hypothesis: Under a real filed 13F quarter update, the value of a dependency certificate is decided by its granularity: an assertion-level certificate certifies ~nothing, a read-set certificate certifies little for aggregate queries, and a validity-condition certificate certifies most answers at a cost proportional to the delta rather than the corpus.
mechanism: 13F restates the full portfolio each quarter, so every assertion is superseded. An argmax reads every position (to prove none is larger), so one changed position kills a read-set certificate. But the argmax *answer* survives whenever no other position overtakes the winner, and that is checkable from the delta alone.
would_change_my_mind: read-set survival above 25% (portfolios are stickier than I think, and the granularity distinction is not the finding), or validity-condition survival within 2x of read-set (the tighter certificate is not worth building)
control: full recomputation of every answer on the new snapshot is the ground-truth anchor; a certificate that certifies an answer which actually changed is a broken certificate, not a weaker one

why_revised: The two filed 13F snapshots carry triples only, no position values, so the argmax-over-values design in v1 is not runnable on them. More importantly, inspecting the delta reframed the question: revalidating a read-set costs the same as recomputing a cheap aggregate, so survival fraction alone is the wrong metric.
hypothesis: The value of a read-set certificate is (cost of recomputation)/(cost of revalidation) times the survival fraction, and it is therefore near-worthless for cheap aggregates and large for solver answers. The certificate pays where the computation is expensive relative to its dependency, not where the dependency is small.
mechanism: Revalidation is |read set| hash lookups against the new snapshot. Recomputation is whatever the query costs. For a count over n rows both are O(n) and the ratio is ~1. For an NP-hard kernel call over a read set of a few hundred facts the ratio is the solve time over a few hundred lookups.

expected.crossover: the certificate breaks even at roughly one aggregate pass and pays above it
expected.global_margin_survival: ~0%, because no security's margin exceeds a 744,136-edge delta

would_change_my_mind: aggregate-query certificate value above 5x (revalidation is cheaper than I think, e.g. the read set is much smaller than the scan), or solver-query value below 10x (solver read sets are not small)
control: full recomputation of every answer on the new snapshot is the ground-truth anchor. A certificate that certifies an answer which actually changed is BROKEN, not weaker; the required count of such false survivals is zero.
prior_art_caveat: Rung R2 is incremental view maintenance and must not be reported as new. What is being tested that IVM does not give: the certificate is produced by a GENERIC recording mechanism over an arbitrary computation, including one that calls an external solver, with no per-query delta rule written by hand.

actual.anchor: 15,300 answers recomputed on the new snapshot, 0 false survivals on every rung
actual.delta: 36,628 of 48,394 keys moved (75.7% churn over one quarter)

prediction_error: Wrong in direction on the headline. I predicted the solver query would show >50x value; it shows 1.0x. I had the speedup right (1,582x, above my >50x) but I predicted survival and speedup as independent factors and they are ANTICORRELATED: the read set that makes a certificate cheap to check is the same read set that makes it likely to be hit. A 12-key read set under 75.7% key churn survives with probability 0.24^12, which is nil. The two factors cancel to ~1.0x across four orders of magnitude of compute cost.
interpretation: The read-set certificate is worthless or a net loss on all four query classes at this update granularity, and it is WORSE than useless on the cheap ones (0.3x) because a digest comparison costs more than a len(). The one rung that worked is the query-supplied stability margin: 93.6% survival against 33.0% for the read set, at O(1) per answer and 0 false survivals. That is not generic and cannot be produced by the recording mechanism.
belief_update: Two beliefs revised. (1) 'The certificate pays where computation is expensive relative to its dependency' is FALSE as stated -- it pays where computation is expensive relative to its dependency AND the dependency is stable, and those pull against each other. (2) HANDOVER item 1, 'make dependency-certification a substrate-wide contract', is now the LOWER-value half: the substrate should carry stability conditions, not read sets. The read set is what you can get for free and it is not what is worth having.
new_question: The measurement is a batch one: one quarterly update, each answer needed once. That is the certificate's worst case. Its value should scale with the FRESHNESS requirement -- if answers must be correct after every filing, the opponent recomputes everything per filing while the certificate recomputes only what that filing touched. 13F filings are the real update unit and are on disk. Predicted crossover: the certificate starts paying when per-update key churn falls below roughly 1/speedup-adjusted read-set size; for the 12-key solver query that is around 0.9% key churn, and one filing touches on the order of 0.8% of keys. So the crossover is predicted to sit almost exactly at 13F's real filing granularity, which would be a sharp and falsifiable claim.

hypothesis: Under a live freshness requirement -- answers must be correct after every FILING, not once per quarter -- the read-set certificate's advantage is approximately (answers maintained) / (facts changed per update), because the opponent must re-derive the whole answer cache per update while the certificate visits only the certs registered on the keys that moved. The batch 1.0x I just measured is the F=1 endpoint of this curve, not the value of the mechanism.
mechanism: An inverted index from fact key to the certificates that read it makes the per-update check O(keys touched), independent of cache size. The opponent -- an LM or retrieval agent that cannot certify non-dependence -- has no such object and must re-answer everything.

expected.advantage_at_filing_granularity: 100-500x for the cheap aggregate, 40x+ for the solver
expected.law: advantage ~ N_answers / keys_touched_per_update, and it should fall to the measured 1.0x as batch size grows to the whole quarter
expected.crossover_batch_size: the advantage should cross 1.0x somewhere between a few hundred and a few thousand filings batched together

would_change_my_mind: advantage below 10x at single-filing granularity (the per-update check is not as cheap as an inverted index suggests, or filings touch far more keys than I think), or a curve that does not return to ~1.0x at full batch (which would mean the two experiments disagree and one of them is wrong)
control: the full-batch endpoint must reproduce the already-measured 1.0x / 0.3x row. If it does not, the freshness experiment is measuring something other than the batch one and neither number is safe.
honesty_note: the opponent's cost is EXTRAPOLATED from measured per-answer compute (300 x 8,000 solver calls is 4.5 hours and is not being run); the certificate side is actually executed. Reported as extrapolated.

prediction_error: Magnitudes inside the predicted band (100-500x cheap aggregate: 165x; 40x+ solver: 37x, just under). The LAW was wrong: I predicted advantage ~ N_answers/keys_touched, which predicts the same 56 for holder_count and portfolio_overlap and got 165x and 1342x. N_answers does not appear in the true law at all.
interpretation: The control endpoint reproduces the batch experiment (0.36/0.71/1.00 against 0.3/0.6/1.0), so the two experiments agree and the batch 1.0x is the far end of a curve rather than the value of the mechanism.

hypothesis: advantage = min(compute_per_answer/check_per_answer, 1/P_hit) with P_hit ~ r*keys_per_update/total_keys, so dependency size sets the ceiling and compute cost only decides whether it is reached.
design: Two independent sweeps that break the confound between cost and dependency size, which every real query class here carries: (A) dependency size r swept 1..48 with the clingo kernel held fixed; (B) kernel cost swept over six orders of magnitude with r pinned at one fact.

actual.A_note: columns are r, measured advantage, 1/P prediction; the two converge as r grows and the invalidation ceiling starts binding
actual.B_note: r pinned at 1. Advantage rises with cost until it saturates at that sample's 1/P ceiling: the last row's P(hit) was 0.371%, and 1/0.00371 = 269.5 against a measured 269.7

prediction_error: none material; both ceilings behaved as predicted and the saturation point matched to three significant figures
interpretation: Confirms the two-regime law and explains the inversion in the freshness table: the 12-key solver is worth 36x less than the 2-key intersection not because it is expensive but because it depends on six times as many facts. Cost helps -- it raises the check-bound ceiling -- but dependency size caps the whole mechanism, and expensive kernels tend to have large dependencies.
belief_update: 'Certificates pay for expensive computations' is FALSE. Certificates pay for SMALL DEPENDENCIES under SMALL UPDATES, and the cost of the computation only decides whether that ceiling is reached. The design consequence is the inverse of the handover's recommendation: the substrate should be pushing kernels toward smaller read sets, not toward reporting read sets.
caveat: A 364.8x measurement at r=1 with P(hit) 0.263% rests on 200 queries and one filing stream; the ceiling formula is the claim, not the third significant figure.

hypothesis: An answer that is an OPTIMUM splits into two bounds with radically different stability, and the split is worth two orders of magnitude. The upper bound (a cover of size k exists) rests on a WITNESS of k edges and survives every addition to the corpus, because more holdings can only make covering easier. The lower bound (no cover of size k-1 exists) is a negative claim that rests on the ABSENCE of a better option and therefore reads the whole holder set of every item. So under a corpus that mostly grows, half the answer is nearly free to maintain and half is not.
mechanism: Set cover's optimum is monotone non-increasing under adding `covers` facts. A witness certificate is invalidated only by DELETION of one of its own edges; an optimality certificate is invalidated by any addition anywhere in the items' holder sets, which is why the recording mechanism correctly read all of them. This also explains why a solver unsat core is NOT a sound stability certificate here: the core proves infeasibility of a k-1 cover under the facts present, and a new edge can destroy that infeasibility.

expected.and: the recorded read set should be indistinguishable from the optimality certificate, because granularity alone does not move P_hit -- a coarse key is hit whenever any edge under it is hit

would_change_my_mind: witness P_hit within 5x of optimality P_hit (deletions are far more concentrated on witness edges than a uniform draw suggests -- plausible, since an optimal cover picks LARGE filers and large filers file the biggest changes), or the edge-granularity read set showing a materially different P_hit from the adjacency one (which would mean granularity does move the ceiling and my law is missing a term)
control: the adjacency-granularity optimality certificate must reproduce the 2.71% P_hit and 37.3x already on disk, or this experiment is not measuring the same thing as the last one

actual.anchor_A: 300/300 witnesses are real edges, cover every item, and name no more filers than the optimum
actual.anchor_B: 13/300 witnesses survive the whole quarter; all 13 re-solved, 0 where the maintained bound was wrong
actual.control: optimality P(hit) 2.8589% against 2.71% on disk, advantage 35.0x against 37.3x -- same measurement, different sample

prediction_error: Well calibrated for once. Predicted witness P_hit ~0.021%, measured 0.0300% (1.4x). Predicted ratio ~130x, measured 95x (1.4x). Both inside the band and in the right direction.
interpretation: An optimum is two claims with a hundredfold difference in what they cost to keep. The upper bound rests on a 12-edge witness and survives 99.97% of filings; the optimality claim rests on every item's whole holder set and survives 97.1%. The 95x is real and it buys HALF an answer -- a maintained `<= k`, not a maintained `= k`.
what_i_got_wrong_inside_the_run: The decomposition row (how much of the saving is monotonicity vs the smaller dependency) is ILL-POSED and returned 1.0x. A witness edge exists in the old snapshot, so it can only be deleted and no addition can touch it -- the row is identical to the deletions-only row by construction. The small dependency is licensed BY the monotonicity; they are one effect. The row is kept in the script labelled degenerate rather than deleted.
also: Anchor A failed 300/300 on its first run and the bug was in the ANCHOR, not the witness: I compared |witness| (12 edges, one per item) against k (4 to 9 distinct filers). The witness was correct throughout. An anchor that fails is doing its job either way, and this one cost five minutes and would have cost a retracted finding.
belief_update: The lever on the ceiling is not read-set size in general -- it is the LOGICAL FORM of the claim. A monotone/existential claim has a witness and a witness is a small, stable dependency. A negative/universal claim has no witness and must read the complement. This subsumes the earlier 'push kernels toward smaller read sets': you cannot shrink an optimality claim's dependency, but you can often split the answer into a half that has a witness and a half that does not.

hypothesis: The 95x witness/optimality gap is not a fact about set cover. It is the NP/coNP asymmetry showing up as a maintenance price, so it should replicate on any problem shape whose answer is an optimum, and the gap should be LARGER for shortest path than for set cover because the search frontier is far bigger than twelve holder sets.
framing: An existential claim ('a cover of size <= k exists', 'a path of length <= d exists') has a short certificate that a verifier can check in polynomial time -- exactly the NP witness. Its universal complement ('no shorter path exists') is coNP and has no short certificate, so its dependency is the explored frontier. The economic content is that this textbook asymmetry has a PRICE on real filed data, and this measures it on a second problem shape to show the first was not a property of set cover.
design: Shortest co-holding path between two 13F filers (filer -> security -> filer), over the same two filed snapshots and the same 8,425-filing update stream. Witness = the path's edges. Optimality = every fact the BFS read, recorded by the same generic mechanism.

expected.witness_r: 4-8 edges for a p50 path of 2-4 hops
expected.optimality_r: thousands of keys -- the BFS frontier over a graph with 8,636 filers and 33,780 securities
expected.optimality_P_hit: near 100% -- a frontier that large is hit by almost every filing
expected.and: the optimality certificate should be effectively worthless here (advantage ~1.0x), because a dependency that spans the graph is invalidated by any update

would_change_my_mind: a gap within 2x of set cover's 95x (which would mean the 95x is about the corpus's churn rate rather than the claim's form), or a BFS read set small enough to stay useful (which would mean I am wrong that the frontier is the dependency)
control: the witness must be re-verified against the new snapshot: if its edges all still exist, a path of that length still exists. Any certified bound that fails re-verification is a broken certificate.

actual.control: 222/300 witnesses intact on the new snapshot, 0 that fail to chain from the source

prediction_error: The numbers I predicted all landed -- witness P_hit ~0.02% (0.0034%), recorded optimality near-worthless (3.3x), gap >1,000x (8,932x). The INTERPRETATION was wrong, and it was the whole point of the experiment.
interpretation: The 8,932x is NOT the NP/coNP asymmetry. Hand-deriving the minimal optimality certificate -- for a 1-hop answer nothing can be shorter, so it is unconditional; for a 2-hop answer 'no 1-hop path' is exactly 'the two portfolios do not intersect', two facts -- collapses the gap to 1.4x. The BFS's recorded read set over-approximates the claim's true dependency by 6,591x. So on shortest path the complexity-class asymmetry is worth essentially nothing, and what the first table measured was the recording mechanism over-reading.
why_set_cover_differs: Set cover's 95x survives this attack, because its optimality read set genuinely IS the dependency: any filer in any of the twelve holder sets could combine to give k-1, so no smaller sound set exists. Whether the recorded read set is tight is a property of the PROBLEM, not of the mechanism.
the_better_result: Once the certificate is minimal, the COMPLETE answer `= d` -- not a bound -- is maintained at 13,987x against re-derivation. That is a stronger claim than the bound-maintenance result it replaces.
belief_update: Retract 'the lever is the logical form of the claim'. The lever is the TRUE DEPENDENCY of the claim, and the recorded read set can exceed it by four orders of magnitude. Logical form is one source of a small dependency (a witness), not the source. This also confirms and extends the dense-graph scout's independent measurement of a 66x over-approximation on the route network -- same phenomenon, two orders of magnitude larger here.
errors_inside_the_run: The FULL ANSWER row was wrong on its first computation: the witness is keyed on edges and the minimal optimality set on adjacencies, and I replayed the union against the adjacency stream alone, so the witness half matched nothing and the row silently reported the minimal row's number twice. Caught because 116 == 116 exactly, which is the same 'a control that confirms to three significant figures is probably broken' shape already in HANDOVER section 8.

hypothesis: The 13,987x full-answer result is a property of a graph with no diameter, not of the certificate. On a graph where shortest paths are actually long, the minimal optimality dependency -- which is the ball that has to be searched to prove nothing shorter exists -- grows roughly exponentially in d, while the witness stays at d edges. So the WITNESS/BOUND stays cheap and the ANSWER stops being cheap, and the bound-vs-answer asymmetry I retracted this morning is restored as the general case with 13F as the special case.
mechanism: To certify 'no path shorter than d' you must know that dst is outside the ball of radius d-1 around src, so the dependency is that ball's edges. Meet-in-the-middle halves the radius and does not change the growth rate. On 13F's co-holding graph d is 1 or 2 and the ball collapses to two portfolios, which is why the hand-derived certificate was 0.5 keys.
design: Openflights route network under a 2,000 km range limit -- 6,072 airports, 37,042 routes, a graph this repo has already measured at amplification 8.3x-44x. Measure witness size and MINIMAL optimality dependency (bidirectional ball) as a function of d. No update stream is needed: the question is whether the minimal dependency stays small, which is a property of the graph.

expected.minimal_optimality_at_d6: a large fraction of the graph
expected.verdict: the full-answer certificate stops being cheap somewhere around d=3-4

would_change_my_mind: the minimal optimality dependency staying within ~10x of the witness at d>=4, which would mean the 13,987x generalises and the bound/answer distinction really is unimportant
control: the d<=2 cases on this graph must reproduce the shape seen on 13F -- small optimality dependency -- or the two measurements are not comparable

actual.graph: 3,225 airports with outbound legs, 27,262 flyable legs at 2,000 km
actual.overall: witness 6.2 edges, minimal optimality 925 edges, ratio 148x, against 13F's 0.2x
actual.control: 21 pairs at d<=2 have median minimal optimality 3 edges -- small, comparable to 13F, so the two graphs agree where they overlap and the comparison across d is not confounded

prediction_error: Held on every axis. Predicted d_p50 3-5 (actual 6), tens of edges at d=2 (actual 4), thousands at d=4 (actual 152 median, 5,828 max -- the median is lower than predicted, the max is not), ratio >100x at d>=4 (actual 38x at d=4, crossing 100x at d=6), and the crossover 'around d=3-4' (actual: 3x at d=3, 38x at d=4, so the crossover is exactly there).
interpretation: The 13,987x full-answer result was a property of a graph with no diameter. On a real graph the minimal optimality dependency is 148x the witness overall and reaches 32% of the corpus at d=10, while the witness stays at d edges. So the bound is maintainable and the ANSWER is not, once shortest paths are actually long.
belief_update: This partly RESTORES the claim I retracted this morning, in a sharper form. 'The lever is the logical form' was too strong and 'the lever is the true dependency' was too weak. The correct statement: an existential claim's minimal dependency is the size of its WITNESS, which grows linearly in the answer; its universal complement's is the size of the SEARCH SPACE that has to be excluded, which grows with the ball. Those coincide on a trivial instance -- 13F's co-holding graph, where every pair is 1 or 2 hops apart -- and diverge by two to three orders of magnitude otherwise. Logical form decides the growth RATE; the instance decides whether you have travelled far enough along it to notice.
method_note: The optimality dependency is measured with meet-in-the-middle (radii ceil((d-1)/2) and floor((d-1)/2)), which is the STRONGEST honest version of the certificate. The naive one-sided ball of radius d-1 would have inflated every number in the direction of the hypothesis.

hypothesis: There is no known small, self-contained, maintenance-cheap certificate for a shortest-path LOWER bound, and the three plausible candidates fail in three different ways. If that holds, the witness/complement asymmetry measured on the route network survives its own named refuter.

candidates.name: ball / meet-in-the-middle
candidates.size: grows with d: 4 edges at d=2, 876 at d=6, 8,745 at d=10 (32% of the corpus)

candidates.name: LP dual / feasible potential
candidates.verification: every edge must satisfy pi(v)-pi(u) <= w(u,v), so ~m reads
candidates.predicted_dependency: the WHOLE graph, so P_hit is 100% under any update
candidates.predicted_verdict: beats the ball on certificate SIZE at large d and loses completely on MAINTENANCE, because a certificate that depends on every edge is invalidated by every update

candidates.name: hub labelling / 2-hop cover
candidates.predicted_dependency: small per query but resting on a GLOBAL 2-hop-cover invariant -- the labels of any two vertices must share a vertex on their shortest path -- whose verification from scratch is APSP-equivalent
candidates.predicted_verdict: an INDEX, not a self-contained certificate. It relocates the coNP cost from per-query to globally-amortised; it does not eliminate it. Literature confirms optimal hub labelling is itself NP-complete and is a special case of SET COVER, which is the same shape as the other experiment in this arm.

expected.route_network_label_size: 50-200 hubs per vertex on a small-world airline network, so a 100-400 hub per-query certificate against the ball's 925 edges -- 2x to 9x, not the 874x collapse that would refute the finding
expected.asymmetry_direction: hub labels are fragile in the DELETION direction (stale labels underestimate distance and become unsound), which is the same direction the witness is fragile in; edge INSERTIONS admit local repair because a new shortest path must travel via the inserted edge

would_change_my_mind: a per-query hub-label certificate that is BOTH small and self-contained (verifiable without trusting a global invariant), or a dual certificate whose dependency is materially smaller than the edge set
sources: Cohen et al., reachability and distance queries via 2-hop labels
Efficient Maintenance of Distance Labelling for Incremental Updates in Large Dynamic Graphs (EDBT 2021)
Efficient Maintenance of 2-Hop Labeling Index on Dynamic Small-World Graphs (VLDB vol 18)
note: Literature-grounded before measuring, and the grounding already changed the design: the interesting quantity is not whether hub labels are small (they are) but whether the global invariant they rest on can be maintained more cheaply than the answers they certify.

hypothesis: The extraction arrow (observations -> typed world) can be priced on real prose for the first time using OpenAlex, and the crossover will land within an order of magnitude of GLEIF's 99,512 -- not because prose is like identifiers, but because the crossover is corpus_tokens/dependency_tokens and BOTH corpora have small per-query dependencies. The number that will differ, and that this repo has never had, is EXTRACTION ACCURACY: a symbolic extractor on prose will lose accuracy that GLEIF's filed structure gave away for free.
why_this_corpus: OpenAlex is open, needs no credentials (CourtListener v4 returned 401 and both bulk listings are closed), carries real prose abstracts, and ships ground-truth structure alongside it: raw_affiliation_strings paired with resolved ROR institution ids. That pairing is a genuine text->entity task with an anchor, and it is the first raw-observation corpus this repo would have.

expected.dependency_tokens_for_institutions_of_X: ~38, close to GLEIF's 41 by coincidence of both being short
expected.crossover_queries: 20,000-100,000, i.e. the same order as GLEIF's 99,512
expected.symbolic_extractor_agreement_with_openal: 70-90% on exact ROR id sets; the failure mode will be multi-institution strings and abbreviations rather than outright misses

would_change_my_mind: a crossover more than 10x from GLEIF's (which would mean the constant IS corpus-dependent in the way HANDOVER section 4 guessed, and the identity found this morning is less general than it looks), or symbolic agreement above 95% (which would mean prose extraction is not the hard step and the first arrow is cheap after all)
honesty_caveat: OpenAlex's institution resolution is ITSELF an automated extractor, so agreement with it is agreement, not truth. This is the same circularity the airport_country audit found, and any accuracy number must be reported as 'agreement with OpenAlex' and never as accuracy. The COST half of the arm does not depend on ground truth at all and is unaffected.
leakage_guard: a name dictionary built from the same works it is evaluated on would be leakage; the dictionary must come from a disjoint split.

after_seeing: 5,000 works, 5,992,167 abstract chars (mean 1,198, as predicted), 44,446 affiliation strings, 42,582 (95.8%) resolving to a ROR id, 4,539 distinct institutions.
design: Two halves. (A) Re-price the crossover on prose: corpus_tokens/dependency_tokens where the dependency of 'which institutions does work X involve' is its affiliation strings. (B) The first extraction-accuracy number this repo has ever had: a symbolic extractor's agreement with OpenAlex's own resolution, on a work-disjoint split.
the_floor_that_decides_it: A FULL-STRING memoriser -- exact normalised affiliation string -> most frequent ROR set, looked up verbatim. Bibliographic text repeats itself, so this floor will be strong, and it is precisely the trap CLAUDE.md calls this repo's oldest: rank on the number a memoriser cannot buy. The headline must therefore be reported SPLIT: agreement on held-out strings whose exact form WAS seen in training, and on strings never seen. The second is the only one that says anything about extraction.

expected.held_out_strings_seen_verbatim: 40-60%, because institutions are written the same way repeatedly

would_change_my_mind: component matching on unseen strings below 25% (prose extraction is much harder than a dictionary can reach, and the first arrow is expensive) or above 85% (it is nearly free, and the arrow is not the bottleneck)

actual.corpus: 5,000 OpenAlex works, 6,337,498 chars = 1,584,374 tokens, $23.77 to read once

prediction_error: Wrong on three of four axes, all in the same direction -- I was too optimistic about how much structure repeats. Predicted 40-60% of held-out strings seen verbatim; actual 15.9%. Predicted memoriser >95% on seen; actual 58.1% exact / F1 0.717. Predicted component extraction 50-70% on unseen; actual F1 0.303. Predicted crossover 20,000-100,000; actual 5,242, a factor of 0.05 against GLEIF.
interpretation_crossover: The crossover formula held and the NUMBER did not transfer, which is what the finding that introduced it already said would happen. The transferable term is the DEPENDENCY, which is corpus-independent: 302 tokens on prose against GLEIF's 41, so a query's necessary context on prose is 7.4x larger. The crossover itself scales with corpus size and is not a constant across corpora -- it must never be quoted as one.
interpretation_ceiling: The most valuable number is one I did not design for. On strings the memoriser has seen VERBATIM, exact-set agreement is only 58.1% (F1 0.717). The same normalised affiliation string maps to different ROR sets in different works, because OpenAlex assigns institutions per AUTHOR rather than per string. So the label is not a function of the input, and 0.717 is a CEILING on what any string-only extractor can reach. Anything scoring above it is using something beyond the string.
interpretation_cost: Cost per CORRECT extraction favours the symbolic extractor by at least 1,766,210x whatever a model scores, because a model cannot exceed F1 1.0. That is a credential-free lower bound on the extraction advantage, and it is the first time this repo has had one: the blocked comparison was symbolic-vs-LM ACCURACY, and this sidesteps it by bounding the model's side at perfection.
belief_update: The first arrow is CHEAP AND BAD. F1 0.303 on unseen strings -- 42% of the task's own ceiling -- builds a world that is mostly wrong, and $/correct-fact winning by a million times does not repair that. This is the arrow where the symbolic approach is weakest and it is the one the programme had never measured. My morning note predicted exactly this would be found and it was right.
floor_not_ceiling: F1 0.303 is a FLOOR for symbolic extraction, not a ceiling. The extractor is a deliberately dumb dictionary with a min-count-2 component vote. String similarity, hierarchical matching, or ROR's own reconciliation service would all do better, and none was tried.

hypothesis: F1 0.303 on unseen affiliation strings is a floor from a deliberately dumb dictionary, and a modestly better SYMBOLIC extractor closes most of the gap to the task's own 0.717 ceiling. If it does, the first arrow is bad only because nobody tried; if it plateaus near 0.35, the programme's weakest arrow is weak for a real reason.
why_it_decides_something: Every advantage this repo publishes sits downstream of this arrow. 42% of ceiling means a mostly-wrong world; 80%+ of ceiling means the bet holds and extraction is not the bottleneck.

rungs.v0: component vote, min count 2 (measured: unseen F1 0.303)

rungs.v1: IDF-weighted components -- a rare component like 'national institute for fusion science' is far more informative than 'usa', and the flat vote treats them alike

rungs.v2: token-overlap similarity against known institution name strings, so an unseen wording of a seen institution can still match

rungs.v3: specificity-first -- take the most specific matching component rather than the union of all of them, which is where the 29.1% precision is going

expected.v3_unseen_f1: small further gain, mostly in precision

ceiling_note: The memoriser on SEEN strings gives precision 72.8% and recall 70.7%, so those are the reachable maxima for any string-only method -- the residual is authors carrying affiliations that their own string never mentions. Report every rung as a fraction of that, never as raw F1 against 1.0.

interpretation: The decision-relevant answer is that the first arrow's weakness is REAL and not an artefact of a lazy first attempt. Three principled improvements over the dumb dictionary bought +0.077 in total and left 47% of the task's own ceiling unreached. That confirms the 'cheap and bad' headline rather than softening it.
the_informative_failure: v2 HURT. Adding a word-overlap fallback for strings where component matching found nothing dropped precision 39.9% -> 36.1% and F1 below v1. The fallback fires exactly where the extractor knows nothing, and its guesses are worse than abstaining -- which is the same shape as the largest harness effect in this repo's history, abstention falling back to the structural prior. ABSTAINING BEATS GUESSING, again.
the_dial: v3 moves precision 29.1% -> 54.7% and recall 35.7% -> 29.1% for a flat F1. So F1 is insensitive to the operating point here and the precision/recall FRONTIER is the object, not the point on it. For building a world to reason over, v3 is the rung to ship despite the flat F1: a world with fewer wrong facts is worth more than one with more facts, and this repo's stated engineering rule is fail-loudly rather than guess.
belief_update: Softens nothing. Symbolic string matching reaches about half of what is achievable on this task, and the residual half needs something that is not string matching. The first arrow stays the programme's weakest link and is now measured twice.

hypothesis: The 0.717 'ceiling the task imposes on itself' that I published today is substantially an artefact of how I built the task, not a property of affiliation linking. My fetcher flattened authorships: for each authorship, for each of its raw strings, it emitted one example labelled with ALL of that author's institutions. So the string 'University of Tokyo' is labelled {Tokyo, RIKEN} whenever its author also listed RIKEN, and no string-only method can ever recover RIKEN from it. Posed at AUTHORSHIP granularity -- all of an authorship's raw strings concatenated, predicting its institution set -- the label becomes far closer to a function of the input and the ceiling should rise.
evidence_it_is_real: 44,446 affiliation entries collapse to 13,288 distinct ror-set groups within works, and 61.9% of those groups carry more than one raw string. Mean 1.94 RORs per entry against a task that asks one string to predict all of them.

interpretation: I published 'F1 0.717 is a ceiling the task imposes on itself, because the label is not a function of the input'. That was wrong and it was my own doing: the fetcher flattened authorships, so a single string was labelled with every institution its author listed. Grouped correctly, the memoriser scores 98.2% EXACT on verbatim-seen strings -- the label IS a function of the input, to within 1.2%.
why_it_matters: The correction makes the finding HARSHER, not softer. The extractor is not missing 47% of a noisy target; it is missing 51% of an achievable one. Every residual is genuine extraction failure rather than label noise.
what_it_localises: 91.6% of held-out authorship strings were never seen verbatim, and the memoriser is near-perfect on the 8.4% that were. So the ENTIRE task is generalising to an unseen WORDING of an institution -- not disambiguation, not multi-label, not noise. That is a knowledge problem before it is an algorithm problem: the dictionary only knows institutions that appeared in 3,500 training works.
next_hypothesis: The extractor fails for want of a GAZETTEER, not for want of a better matcher. ROR publishes a full open dump -- every institution with aliases, acronyms and multilingual labels, CC0, no auth. Giving the extractor real external structure is this repo's own stated principle (external resources are givens) and it is the cheapest thing that could close a 51% gap.

hypothesis: The extractor reaches only 48.9% of an achievable 0.988 ceiling because it lacks KNOWLEDGE, not because string matching is inadequate. Its dictionary knows only the institutions that appeared in 3,500 training works; ROR publishes all 132,706 with their labels, aliases, acronyms and multilingual names, CC0 and unauthenticated. Giving the extractor the registry should close most of the gap.
why_it_is_the_right_test: 91.6% of held-out authorship strings were never seen verbatim and the memoriser is near-perfect on the 8.4% that were, so the entire residual is generalising to an unseen WORDING of an institution. A gazetteer is precisely the object that turns an unseen wording into a known entity. It is also this repo's own stated principle -- external resources are givens, use the real standard rather than re-deriving it -- tested for the first time on the extraction arrow.

expected.unseen_f1: 0.65-0.80, i.e. 66-81% of the 0.988 ceiling, up from 0.483
expected.precision: should rise most: a gazetteer match is evidence, where a component vote was a guess

If precision FALLS, the gazetteer is adding candidates faster than it adds evidence.

fairness_note: Using ROR's own names to predict ROR ids is not cheating: it is what a symbolic system SHOULD do with an authoritative registry, and OpenAlex itself almost certainly uses it. But it does mean the resulting extractor is a registry lookup rather than a general text-to-entity method, and the finding must say so.

the_result_that_matters: A ZERO-SHOT registry lookup, using no training data at all, BEATS a dictionary learned from 3,500 works: 0.522 against 0.483, +0.038, and at 41,668 ns against 96,915. That is this repo's stated principle -- external resources are givens -- working on the extraction arrow for the first time, and it says the learned dictionary was never the point.

The cause is surface variation the registry cannot absorb -- 'univ of tokyo' is not 'university of tokyo', and a component that contains an institution name plus a department does not match it exactly.

The ORDERING of rungs is reliable; the absolute numbers are optimistic. v4 is the exception and is trustworthy in a way the others are not -- it has no training data and no tunable parameter, so there was nothing to fit. The tuned split is the worst of the three. Recorded because the expectation was wrong in the safe direction and would otherwise have stood as an unchecked caveat.
the_diagnosis: ONE string in 6,489 produced no candidate. The extractor is not failing to FIND institutions, it is failing to CHOOSE between them: 'University of Wisconsin' names thirteen ROR campuses and the affiliation string contains exactly what distinguishes them -- Madison, Lancaster, Karlsruhe -- which six rungs never look at, because they match names against names and geography is a different view of the world.
next_arm: A geo constraint on an entity-linking candidate set. ROR's dump carries locations with city and country; the affiliation string carries a city. This would be the first place in this repo where two views genuinely have to compose to answer one question, which is the multi-kernel thesis stated as a bug rather than as an aspiration.
belief_update: Split. POSITIVE for the thesis: zero-shot authoritative reference data beats a learned dictionary on every split, with no training data and at half the cost -- 'external resources are givens' is validated where it matters. NEGATIVE for the strong form: six symbolic rungs plateau at 62% of a 99% ceiling, which builds a world with about four wrong or missing institutions in ten.

hypothesis: The extraction residual is disambiguation, and the discriminating evidence is geography sitting unread in the input. Letting a geo view resolve the candidate sets that a name view proposes should recover most of the 38% of true institutions currently never proposed, because they are not missing -- they are losing to a near-identical sibling.
the_composition: This is deliberately built as two views over one candidate set rather than as a better matcher. The NAME view proposes: every ROR id whose registry name matches a component, INCLUDING the ambiguous ones that v4-v6 discarded by abstaining. The GEO view disposes: ROR ships city, country_subdivision and country per organization, and the affiliation string carries a city. One view's result changes what the other does, which is the multi-kernel claim on a problem that needs it rather than one arranged to need it.
the_change_that_matters: v4-v6 DISCARDED ambiguous name matches (len(hits)>1 -> abstain), which is where the recall went. v7 keeps them and asks geography. So the expected gain is mostly recall, and precision should hold or rise because geo agreement is evidence rather than a guess.

interpretation_hypothesis: Two things changed at once and I conflated them. v7 both (a) RELAXED THE ABSTENTION -- propose() keeps ambiguous candidates that v4-v6 discarded -- and (b) added geography to choose among them. If the relaxation costs more than geography recovers, the composition can be a net loss even when geography is informative. Precision fell 56.0% -> 54.9% while recall barely moved, which is the signature of admitting candidates rather than of choosing badly among them.
why_it_matters_that_the_control_fired: The control was written before the run specifically to distinguish a composition from a decoration, and it is the only reason this is a finding rather than a small unexplained regression. A view that changes 9.8% of answers and is worse on 46.5% of them would have been easy to report as 'roughly neutral, needs tuning'.
next: Two ablations to isolate the mechanism, because a null without one is not yet a result: (A) geography allowed only to RE-RANK, never to add candidates v6 would have abstained on; (B) abstention relaxed with NO geography, ties broken by training frequency. If B is much worse than v6, the relaxation is the culprit and geography is exonerated.

the_result: The second view is informative enough to UNDO a mistake and not informative enough to be worth MAKING one. Geography recovers 81% of the damage that admitting ambiguous candidates does, and never gets ahead of simply abstaining.
the_mechanism_and_the_lesson: I designed this arm from THREE HAND-PICKED failure examples -- Madison, Lancaster, Karlsruhe -- printed from a sample of 1,251 disjoint cases. Those three carry an unambiguous city. The POPULATION does not: 65% of ambiguous components name no place ROR recognises at the granularity needed. That is a slice inversion, which is this repo's oldest and most expensive documented mechanism, and I walked into it while writing a finding that cites the abstention lesson twice.
belief_update: Two. (1) Composition is not free: a second view must beat abstention, not merely beat guessing, and this one only did the latter. (2) The extraction plateau at ~62% of ceiling is now measured against a serious attempt at its diagnosed cause, so it is a harder number than it was an hour ago -- and the diagnosis that produced the attempt was itself derived from a slice.

hypothesis: An exact reasoner over a 55%-correct world does NOT produce 55%-correct answers, and the loss scales with how many extracted facts a query reads. CLAUDE.md says cost is charged to the SYSTEM; this is the first experiment in the repo that can actually charge it.
design: Build two worlds over the same 5,000 OpenAlex works: the REFERENCE world from OpenAlex's own institution labels, and the EXTRACTED world from v4, the zero-shot registry extractor. v4 is used deliberately because it needs no training split, so the world has no leakage anywhere and is what a deployed system would actually produce on a new corpus. Then run query classes of increasing dependency over both and compare against the reference as anchor.

query_classes.institutions_of(work): reads one work's authorships. Depth 1; error should be the extraction error itself

query_classes.collaborators(institution): unions the institutions of every work X appears on. Recall should RISE (an institution is recovered if any one shared work extracts it) and precision should FALL (a spurious extraction anywhere adds a collaborator)

query_classes.works_at(institution): every work involving X; depends on every extraction in the corpus

query_classes.co_affiliation_count(A,B): a NUMBER, so errors cannot cancel into a set -- relative error is the metric

expected.amplification: 1.2-2x, i.e. query error above extraction error
expected.and: the entry point matters more than the aggregate -- if X itself is mis-extracted the whole query is wrong, so a query keyed ON an extracted entity should be worse than one keyed on a given work

would_change_my_mind: queries scoring at or ABOVE the fact-level F1 (union over many noisy extractions is self-correcting, which would be a genuinely good result for the programme and would mean a mediocre extractor is survivable), or amplification above 4x (the first arrow's 62% is fatal downstream and no reasoning advantage can be quoted without it)
anchor: the reference world built from OpenAlex's labels; every number is agreement with it, not truth, as everywhere in this arm

actual.world_size: extracted 2,270 institutions and 8,114 facts against the reference's 4,539 and 15,543 -- HALF the entities and 52% of the facts
actual.ledger: 0.9s and $5.08e-06 to build the world symbolically against $19.03 for a model reading the same text; 3,746,454x on price, and the world is 57.6% F1

prediction_error: Amplification was inside the predicted 1.2-2x band at 1.85x. Everything about the MECHANISM was wrong. I predicted union would raise recall and lower precision; the opposite happened -- precision holds at 84-94% and recall collapses to 20.4%.
the_mechanism_and_it_inverts_a_conclusio: The extracted world has HALF the institutions and 52% of the facts, because v4 ABSTAINS on every ambiguous component. Abstention maximises fact-level precision and F1 -- which is why it won three times today -- and it produces a SPARSE world. Aggregate queries do not pay for precision, they pay for COMPLETENESS: a collaborator that was never extracted anywhere cannot be recovered by any union, and a count over a half-empty world has a median relative error of 100%.
belief_update: 'Abstention beats guessing' is TRUE at the fact level and may be exactly backwards at the system level. The operating point should be chosen on the DOWNSTREAM metric, not on fact-level F1, and I have stated the opposite three times today on fact-level evidence alone.
next_experiment: Re-run end to end with a HIGH-RECALL extractor -- emit every candidate for an ambiguous component instead of abstaining -- and see whether aggregate queries improve despite worse fact-level F1. Predicted: fact F1 falls 0.576 -> ~0.50, collaborators Jaccard rises 0.157 -> 0.25-0.35. If it does, the fact-level operating point this repo has been optimising is the wrong one.

prediction_error: Predicted fact F1 would fall to ~0.50 and collaborators Jaccard rise to 0.25-0.35. Fact F1 fell further (0.455) and collaborators Jaccard rose less (0.196), but the DIRECTION and the inversion are exactly as predicted.
the_finding: The extractor that wins on facts by 0.121 F1 loses on EVERY aggregate query: collaborators +0.085, works_at +0.058, count error halved. Aggregate queries pay for COMPLETENESS, not precision -- a spurious fact pollutes only the queries touching it, a missing entity is unreachable from everywhere.
belief_update: 'Abstention beats guessing' is TRUE at the fact level and BACKWARDS at the system level. I stated it three times today, each time on fact-level evidence alone, which was the only evidence available until now. This is the repo's oldest documented trap in a new costume: a ranking is a property of a metric, and here two defensible metrics rank the two extractors inversely -- with the one this programme has been optimising, fact-level F1, being the one that corresponds to nothing a user asks for.
tension_named: 'No fallbacks -- fail loudly' still stands: it is about a SILENT fallback making a broken component read as working. But world construction and answer construction want opposite defaults and nothing in the architecture says so.

hypothesis: Completeness wins for EXISTENTIAL queries and loses for INTERSECTIVE and UNIVERSAL ones, which would sharpen yesterday's design consequence into the same shape this repo keeps finding -- witnesses, additive bounds, the solver rung, all cases where the cheap existential half of a problem is the useful half.
design: Same two worlds (v4 abstaining vs v4r high-recall) over 5,000 OpenAlex works, but query classes chosen to PUNISH over-generation instead of rewarding it: works_at_both(A,B) (intersection over the inverted index), common_institutions(w1,w2) (intersection of two works), institutions_unique_to(w1,w2) (set difference, a negative claim), is_single_institution(work) (a boolean universal -- 'no other institution is involved').
the_subtlety_worth_naming: Intersection is a natural filter for UNCORRELATED noise: if v4r's false positives were random, intersecting two noisy sets would kill most of them and completeness would keep winning. But v4r's false positives are not random -- they are the thirteen University of Wisconsins, i.e. systematically the SIBLINGS of the true answer. So when two works both say 'University of Wisconsin', both get all thirteen and the intersection keeps all thirteen. Correlated errors survive intersection. That is the mechanism this experiment is really testing.

expected.works_at_both: v4 (precise) wins clearly -- spurious co-occurrence is quadratic in over-generation
expected.is_single_institution: v4 wins; v4r almost never reports a singleton because it emits candidate sets
expected.common_institutions: closest call, and the one that decides the mechanism. If intersection filters the noise, v4r holds up; if the errors are correlated siblings, it does not
expected.institutions_unique_to: v4 wins -- a set difference is a negative claim and over-generation on either side corrupts it

would_change_my_mind: v4r winning on intersective queries too, which would mean completeness wins unconditionally and the extraction operating point is simply 'emit everything' -- a much stronger and simpler design rule than I expect; or v4 winning on ALL classes including the unions already measured, which would mean yesterday's inversion was an artefact I have not found yet
anchor: the reference world from OpenAlex's labels, as everywhere in this arm

common_institutions_intersection.caveat: n=26 -- random work pairs rarely share an institution, so this row is unreliable and is reported only because it agrees with the reliable intersection row

is_single_institution_boolean.caveat: both barely clear a 65.8% majority floor, so this row is inconclusive either way

prediction_error: Wrong on the headline and wrong on the mechanism. I predicted precision would win on intersective queries because the false positives are correlated siblings that survive intersection. It won on only ONE class, the set difference, and completeness won both intersections -- the bigger one by +0.177, the largest margin in either finding.
the_mechanism_and_it_is_better_than_my_g: Intersection FILTERS the noise. v4r's precision runs 36.5% at the fact level, 44.0% and 67.6% on unions, and 95.1% on intersection. The errors are uncorrelated enough between two independently extracted sets that intersecting kills almost all of them. So the QUERY does the disambiguation the extractor refused to do, and over-generation is close to free when the query intersects.
the_unification: The one class where precision wins is the set DIFFERENCE, and the axis is monotonicity. Union and intersection are monotone in their inputs, so extra members can only add candidates that a later constraint can remove. A-B is ANTITONE in B: a spurious member of B wrongly DELETES a true member of A, and nothing downstream can recover it -- v4r's precision there is 38.3%, essentially the raw fact-level rate, unfiltered. That is the SAME axis as the witness finding, where an existential monotone claim had a small stable certificate and its universal complement did not. Monotone tolerates noise; non-monotone does not, and it is now measured twice in two unrelated parts of the programme.
belief_update: Sharpen yesterday's rule. Not 'completeness wins' and not 'completeness wins for existential queries', but: MONOTONE queries tolerate and even repair over-generation, NON-MONOTONE ones do not. The extraction operating point should therefore be chosen by the monotonicity of the workload, and a system serving mixed workloads may need both worlds.

hypothesis: The 36.5% -> 95.1% precision gain from intersection is a NOISE FILTER and therefore requires the two sets' errors to be independent. Where two works share the same affiliation STRING, the extractor makes the same mistake on both, the error is perfectly correlated, and intersection cannot filter it. Precision on shared-string pairs should collapse toward the fact-level rate.
why_run_it: It is the falsifier my own finding names, it is one script against a world that already exists, and if the filter is fragile the design rule published an hour ago is much narrower than it reads.
design: Partition work pairs whose reference intersection is non-empty into (A) pairs sharing at least one normalised affiliation string -- correlated errors by construction -- and (B) pairs sharing an institution but NO string, where the two extractions are independent. Compare the high-recall extractor's intersection precision in each.

expected.group_A_shared_string: precision collapsing to 40-70%, near the 36.5% fact-level rate
expected.if_they_are_equal: the filter is not a filter and I have the mechanism wrong for the second time on this question

would_change_my_mind: shared-string pairs holding above 85% precision, which would mean intersection helps for a reason other than error independence and the whole mechanism needs rewriting

actual.confusable_defined_as: two RORs that some single registry name maps to together -- exactly the correlation the filter is claimed to survive; 4,604 institutions have at least one such sibling

n.confusable: 800 pairs, 356 with a non-empty true answer
n.unrelated: 800 pairs, only 9 with a non-empty true answer, so that row is uninformative and is reported only to show why

prediction_error: Predicted a collapse to 40-70%; the actual collapse is to 8.1%, far past the bottom of my band and BELOW the 36.5% fact-level rate.
the_correction: The 95.1% is real for the population it was measured on -- institution pairs sampled from those that ACTUALLY CO-OCCUR, which are overwhelmingly genuine collaborators and therefore not registry-confusable. It is NOT a property of intersection. Intersection repairs UNCORRELATED noise and AMPLIFIES correlated noise, and the extractor's noise is correlated with precisely the entities anyone would want disambiguated. So over-generation is close to free where you do not need disambiguation and ruinous where you do.
a_slip_worth_recording: My first attempt at this falsifier tested the WRONG QUERY. I partitioned by shared affiliation STRING and measured common_institutions(w1,w2) -- intersecting two works' institution sets -- when the 95.1% came from works_at_both(A,B), which intersects two institutions' WORK sets. Two different intersections carrying the same word in my head. It produced 43.7% vs 33.8%, a null, and I nearly recorded it as one. The correct partition is by registry CONFUSABILITY of the institution pair, and it gives 8.1%.
belief_update: Narrow the published rule. Not 'monotone queries repair an over-generated world' without qualification, but: monotone queries repair INDEPENDENT over-generation and amplify CORRELATED over-generation. The design consequence survives only for workloads whose intersected entities are not registry siblings -- and the whole reason one over-generates is the siblings.

hypothesis: The witness/optimality asymmetry measured at 95x on SEC 13F depends on the corpus GROWING. A witness is monotone under additions and dies only on deletion; the optimality claim is the reverse. 13F opened 411,122 edges against 333,014 closed, so the witness had the easier direction. On a SHRINKING corpus the witness should become the fragile half and the gap should narrow or invert.
design: No new data needed and nothing injected: run cert_bound_asymmetry with the two filed snapshots SWAPPED, so the later one is 'old' and Dec 2025 is 'new'. The same real filings then read as 411,122 closures against 333,014 openings -- a genuinely shrinking corpus made of the same bytes, rather than a simulated one.

expected.witness_P_hit: rises from 0.0300% toward ~0.037%, in proportion to deletions per filing rising 39.5 -> 48.8
expected.optimality_P_hit: roughly unchanged near 2.86%, since it is invalidated by any change in either direction
expected.gap: narrows from 95x to about 77x -- so it does NOT invert, and that is the interesting part: the asymmetry is dominated by the SIZE of the dependency (12 edges vs 12 whole holder sets), not by the direction of the corpus drift
expected.secondary: if the gap inverts instead, the witness's advantage was mostly the growth direction and the finding needs restating

would_change_my_mind: the gap falling below 20x or inverting, which would mean the monotone advantage is about corpus direction rather than dependency size and would revise a claim now cited in three findings

actual.anchors: 300/300 witnesses well-formed and 0 wrong maintained bounds in BOTH directions; the forward run reproduces the published 93x, so the two are the same measurement

prediction_error: Well calibrated. Predicted witness P_hit ~0.037% (actual 0.0351%), optimality roughly unchanged (2.86% -> 2.55%), gap narrowing to ~77x (actual 72x, within 7%).
the_result: The asymmetry does NOT invert on a shrinking corpus. It narrows 93x -> 72x, a 23% reduction that tracks the deletion rate exactly (39.5 -> 48.8 closures per filing, +23%). So the dominant term is DEPENDENCY SIZE -- 12 edges against 12 whole holder sets -- and corpus direction is a second-order effect.
belief_falsified: state.yml held, at confidence 0.8: 'A corpus that mostly SHRINKS inverts the witness asymmetry: the witness becomes the fragile half and the optimality claim the stable one.' That is FALSE. The witness stays ahead by 72x. The belief was recorded precisely so a contradiction would be a finding rather than a surprise, and it is one.
why_it_barely_moves: Reversing swaps openings and closings, but the OPTIMALITY certificate is invalidated by a change in either direction, so its P_hit is nearly unaffected (2.86% -> 2.55%). The witness is hit only by deletions, which rise 23%, and its P_hit rises 15% in step. The gap therefore narrows by the deletion-rate ratio and by nothing else.
method_note: No new data and nothing injected: the same two filed snapshots read in the opposite order, so 'shrinking' is made of real filings rather than a simulation.

hypothesis: A router that reads a query's FORM -- monotone or not, decided without seeing any answer -- and sends it to the precise world or the complete one beats either world alone on a mixed workload. If it does not, the design consequence stated in two findings is decoration.
why_this_and_not_more_extraction: The monotonicity axis is now measured four times, twice before this session and twice in it, and the design consequence has been STATED and never built. It is also the mandate's stated long-term object -- routing computation across heterogeneous components -- and this repo has never measured a routing decision at all.
the_honest_version: Routing by MEASURED per-class performance would be tautological: pick the winner per class and of course it wins. The non-trivial claim is that monotonicity is a STATIC, syntactic property of the query -- readable from its form before it runs -- and that routing on it alone recovers most of the oracle's gain. So the router gets the query's shape and nothing else.
design: Both worlds already exist (v4 abstaining, v4r high-recall). Classify each query class by whether its set expression is monotone in its inputs: union and intersection monotone, difference antitone in its second argument, cardinality-equality non-monotone. Route monotone -> complete world, non-monotone -> precise world. Compare against: each single world alone, and an ORACLE that picks the better world per class after seeing both scores.

expected.routed_vs_best_single_world: +0.03 to +0.08 mean F1 on a mixed workload, because each single world loses badly on the classes it is wrong for
expected.routed_vs_oracle: within 0.01 -- the static rule should recover nearly all of the oracle's gain, since monotonicity is exactly the property that decided every class measured
expected.risk: the boolean universal class went to COMPLETENESS in the measurement despite being non-monotone, which the static rule would get wrong; it was inconclusive against its floor, so it may cost a little

would_change_my_mind: the routed system failing to beat the better single world, which would mean the per-class winners do not generalise and the monotonicity rule is post-hoc; or the oracle beating the router by a wide margin, which would mean form is the wrong signal and something about the DATA decides it

prediction_error: Predicted +0.03 to +0.08 over the better single world (actual +0.015, below the band) and within 0.01 of the oracle (actual -0.026, worse). Form is a real signal and a partial one.
the_refinement_i_declined: The obvious fix from the failures: institutions_of(work) is monotone but its expression is a bare A, so there is nothing to filter against and it inherits the fact-level trade-off where precision wins. That suggests 'monotone AND combining >= 2 sets -> complete'. I checked it against a third case before believing it: works_at(institution) is ALSO arity 1 and ALSO monotone, and completeness wins it by 0.070. The refinement explains one failure and is contradicted by a case it did not come from.
why_that_matters_more_than_the_number: This morning I published a lesson -- a diagnosis derived from a slice must be sized on the population before it is built on -- after designing a whole arm from five printed examples. Here the same temptation arrived with TWO data points and a mechanism that sounded right, and the guard fired. Declining is the result.
belief_update: 'Route by monotonicity' is worth +0.015 and is not the whole story. The design consequence stated in two findings is real but underspecified: form predicts the direction for composing queries and does not predict it for projections, and what separates the two arity-1 cases is not known. Recorded as an open question rather than patched.

the_floor: Predict the N most frequent items in the reference world, where N is the mean true answer size for that class. It uses NO per-query information beyond the answer size, so anything a real method scores above it is what the query bought.

hypothesis: The 1.1M-2.5M x advantage is only available AT ~60% quality, and the moment a model is needed for the residual the advantage collapses to 1/f where f is the escalated fraction. So the programme's real number is not the cost ratio but the KNEE of the quality/cost frontier: how much of the work cheap structure can do CONFIDENTLY, because that is what sets f.
why_this_now: This is the mandate's standing challenge stated as a measurement -- force expensive cognition toward the irreducibly ambiguous boundary cases while cheap structured computation handles everything else -- and it is the frontier the whole programme lives on. Nobody has drawn it. Every cost number so far compares a cheap-and-wrong system against an expensive-and-assumed-perfect one, which is not a choice anyone would actually make.
the_arithmetic_that_makes_it_sharp: A model answer costs $4.54e-03 and ours costs ~2e-09, so if a fraction f of decisions escalate, the hybrid costs about f x 4.54e-03 and the advantage is 1/f. Escalating 50% gives 2x. Escalating 5% gives 20x. The million-fold numbers exist only at f=0.
design: Partition extraction decisions by the confidence the extractor already has -- an unambiguous single registry match versus an ambiguous candidate set or no match at all -- and measure accuracy within each partition. Then sweep the escalation policy and plot quality against cost, with the model's contribution entered at perfect accuracy (the same generous assumption as the ledger, and the same reason: no credentials needed for a bound).

expected.high_confidence_accuracy: 0.85-0.95 -- if it is not high, confidence is not informative and the whole escalation idea fails
expected.the_knee: the number that decides the programme -- if there is a threshold where f is small (say 0.2) and quality is still high (0.9+), the advantage is 5x at near-model quality, which is a real product. prediction_error: Predicted high-confidence accuracy 0.85-0.95; actual 0.666. My pre-registered would-change-my-mind line was 'below 0.7', and it is below 0.7. So by my own criterion, stated before the run: THE EXTRACTOR CANNOT TELL WHAT IT KNOWS.
the_headline_correction: The 1.1M-2.5M x advantage published this session is real only at 52.6% quality. The moment ANY escalation happens the advantage becomes 1/f: escalating the 12.3% of cases where the extractor produces nothing at all collapses it from 2,061,364x to 8.1x, and reaching 83.5% quality costs 2.0x. The symbolic layer buys 2x at usable quality, not a million-fold.
the_repo_said_this_first_again: symbolic_ai_core/cost.py's own module docstring: 'Cheap-and-incapable is not a point on the cost curve; it is a point off the capability axis entirely.' Third instance this session of the repo already knowing what I measured -- after the witness axis in notes/findings/ and the accuracy-above-floor convention in the same file.
the_actionable_half: SILENCE is a better escalation signal than AMBIGUITY. Escalating the silent tier buys 1.00 quality per unit escalated -- perfectly efficient, because those cases score 0.000, so nothing is wasted. Escalating the ambiguous tier buys only 0.48 per unit, because those cases were already 0.516 right and half the spend re-buys what was already there. Escalate where you produce NOTHING, not where you are unsure.
belief_update: The programme's headline metric has been the wrong one. Cost ratio at fixed quality is the comparison anybody would actually make, and by that measure the number is 2x-8x, not 10^6. The million-fold figures are not wrong; they price a system nobody would deploy.

hypothesis: The advantage is 1/f and f is currently the 12.3% SILENT tier -- strings where no registry name matched any component. If most of those strings DO contain their gold institution's registry name somewhere, the failure is the matcher (component splitting, abbreviation, punctuation) and f can fall a long way. If they do not, the string simply does not name the institution recognisably and f is a floor no matching improvement reaches.
why_this_is_the_highest_value_question_a: It is the lever the frontier finding named, and it moves the north star directly and proportionally: f 12.3% -> 6% doubles the advantage 8.1x -> 16x; f -> 2% gives 50x. Nothing else measured this session has that property.
the_diagnostic: For each of the 799 silent strings, ask whether ANY registry name of its gold institution appears as a substring of the normalised string. Yes means recoverable in principle by better matching; no means the string does not contain the name and no matcher can find it without an external association the registry does not carry. Note the gold ids are ROR ids by construction, since OpenAlex resolves to ROR, so 'is it in the registry' is trivially yes and matchability is the only real question.

expected.recoverable_by_substring: 40-60% -- component splitting on commas is the most likely culprit, since an affiliation like 'Dept of Physics, Univ of Tokyo, Japan' splits fine but 'Institute of Physics Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing' does not
expected.irreducible: 40-60% -- non-English forms, transliterations, departmental names that never mention the parent, and genuinely uninformative strings
expected.f_after_fixing_the_recoverable_half: 6-8%, so the advantage roughly doubles to 13-16x at the same quality

would_change_my_mind: recoverable above 80% (the matcher is simply bad and f is nowhere near its floor -- good news and a clear build) or below 20% (f is essentially irreducible by matching, the 8.1x is close to the ceiling for this approach, and the programme needs a different lever entirely)

prediction_error: Predicted 40-60% recoverable; actual 35.9%, just below the band.
the_mechanism_the_samples_show: ROR's canonical name for Purdue's main campus is 'Purdue University West Lafayette'. The affiliation component is 'Purdue University'. Exact component matching fails, and _contained() requires the REGISTRY NAME's tokens to be a subset of the COMPONENT's -- 'purdue university west lafayette' is not a subset of 'purdue university' -- so containment fails in the wrong direction too. The city that would complete the name is in the string, three components later.
the_fix: Match registry names against the WHOLE normalised affiliation string rather than against comma-separated components. That is precisely what the diagnostic's substring test did, which is why it found 35.9%.
the_irreducible_half_is_correctly_classi: 'Department of Chemistry, University of California,' names no campus, and the gold is a specific one. No matcher recovers that from the string alone.
next_prediction: Implementing whole-phrase containment will NOT deliver the projected 12.6x, because the projection assumes perfect recovery at no cost. Matching against the whole phrase matches MORE registry names, so some recovered cases will land in AMBIGUOUS rather than CERTAIN, and the certain tier's precision may fall. Predicted: silent 12.3% -> 8-9%, advantage 10-12x rather than 12.6x, and a small drop in certain-tier F1.

two_fixes: match registry names against the WHOLE phrase, not comma-separated components -- ROR's canonical name is 'Purdue University West Lafayette' while the component is 'Purdue University', and containment was being asked in the wrong direction

gather candidates through the K RAREST KNOWN tokens rather than one -- the single rarest token in a long address is a postcode no registry name contains, which alone left 28.2% of the remaining silent strings silent

the_structural_result: Improving the cheap layer doubles the advantage at LOW quality (13.6x -> 28.7x at 0.60), buys 3-8% in the middle, and buys NOTHING at deployable quality (1.8x at 0.85, unchanged). Once most of the work escalates, the extractor's quality is irrelevant to the price. So the symbolic layer's accuracy matters exactly where nobody would ship it.

I nearly wrote that up as the finding -- a counterintuitive result with a plausible mechanism, which is exactly the kind this repo publishes. It was caught by checking that the shares summed to one. Read the numbers from the run file, not from the terminal.

hypothesis: Advantage = r/f, and r -- how much SMALLER the escalated prompt is than a cold one -- is the only lever that is structurally ours. A cheaper model tier is not: the opponent can use the same one, so the ratio is unchanged. Narrowing IS ours, because producing the candidate set is the symbolic work the opponent would have to do itself.
the_claim: The symbolic layer does not replace the model. It converts an open-ended extraction ('which institutions does this string name?') into a k-way choice ('which of these k?'), and hands over a prompt that is r times shorter. At quality 0.85, f is 56% and r=1 gives 1.8x; r=3 gives 5.4x; r=10 gives 17.9x.
what_decides_it: k, the size of the candidate sets the ambiguous tier produces. Small k means a genuinely easy choice and a short prompt. Large k means the narrowed prompt is no shorter than the string it replaces and the whole argument is decoration.

expected.k_mean: higher with a long tail, maybe 6-15
expected.r_by_tokens: 1.5-3x -- the narrowed prompt is the ambiguous component plus k candidate names, and k candidate names at ~6 tokens each eats the saving quickly
expected.silent_tier_cannot_narrow: by construction: no candidates, so r=1 there, and the silent tier is 5.7% of the workload
expected.verdict_if_r_is_2: advantage at 0.85 goes 1.8x -> 3.6x, which is real but not transformative

would_change_my_mind: r below 1.2 -- the candidate lists are as long as the strings and narrowing buys nothing, which would mean the symbolic layer's only contribution at deployable quality is the 44% of work it answers outright

variants: CANNOT -- the city that separates them is in the string

prediction_error: Predicted r of 1.5-3x. Actual 0.68x. My pre-registered would-change-my-mind line was 'r below 1.2', and it is 0.68.
the_structural_result: You cannot both narrow the choice and shrink the prompt, because THE NARROWING IS INFORMATION. Adding k candidate names to the string makes the prompt 1.5x LARGER; the two prompts that are genuinely shorter (2.11x and 8.19x) are exactly the two that strip the evidence needed to choose, which is the city sitting in the string.
therefore: Advantage = 1/f with no lever available on the escalation side. A cheaper model tier is not ours -- the opponent can use the same one. Prompt narrowing is not available -- it costs tokens rather than saving them. So at 0.85 quality the number is 1.8x, and the only remaining lever is f itself, which the previous experiment showed the extractor's accuracy barely moves at that quality.
belief_update: The cost arc is closed. The symbolic layer's contribution at deployable quality is exactly the fraction of work it answers outright, priced at 1/f, and neither improving its accuracy nor narrowing the model's job moves it. The million-fold figures were a property of accepting 53% quality; the deployable figure is 1.8x.

result: 0 disagreements over 2,360,656 normalised edges, 0 of 8,759 filers.

A 0% disagreement rate between a file and itself says nothing about extraction reliability, and reporting it as evidence for the filed regime would be manufacturing a confirmation. what_survives: Two genuinely independent filed relations still support the regime claim: GLEIF ultimate_parent at 0.216% and the openflights/geonames country disagreement at 4 of 5,882 = 0.068%. Both well under 1%, and both are GENUINE REAL-WORLD CONTESTATION -- disputed ultimate ownership, disputed sovereignty -- rather than extraction error.
the_sharper_mechanism_this_suggests: In the filed regime f is the rate at which the WORLD is contested, which is small and irreducible. In the derived regime f is the rate at which EXTRACTION FAILS, which is large and is a property of the method. That is a cleaner statement of the dichotomy than 'filed versus derived', and it predicts that f in a filed domain should track how contested the property is: ownership 0.216%, sovereignty 0.068%, and holdings -- where one filer is authoritative and there is nothing to contest -- near zero.

hypothesis: The 463x filed-regime headline is too coarse. f is not set by 'filed versus derived' but by HOW MANY IDENTITY BOUNDARIES THE QUERY CROSSES, and a filed-but-CROSS-SOURCE query should sit between the two rungs already measured.

the_correction_to_my_own_headline: 463x is a SINGLE-SOURCE number. Quoting it as 'the filed regime' overstates by 68x for any query that crosses a source boundary -- and crossing boundaries is what a federated substrate is FOR. The gap from cross-source (7x) to derived (2x) is only 4x, so the big cliff is not filed-versus-derived at all: it is inside the filed regime, at the first identity boundary.
the_mechanism: f tracks how many identity boundaries a query crosses. Within one source using its own identifiers there is nothing to contest but genuine real-world disputes. Across two FILED sources with no shared identifier the join goes through names, and one filer in seven matches more than one entity. From unstructured text the whole structure must be derived.
