That is the FOURTH time this session a number I needed was already in the repo, after the witness axis, the accuracy-above-floor convention, and cost.py's cheap-and-incapable docstring.

hypothesis: The 68x cliff at the first identity boundary comes from a 14.7% alignment ambiguity, and 51.3% of ambiguous matches span more than one country -- so adding country to the join key should roughly halve f and double the federated advantage from 7x to ~14x.
outcome: CANNOT BE DONE on available data, and the reason is structural rather than incidental.
what_was_found: SEC entity records carry NO country: `body` is empty on all 44,328 finance/13f entities, and cik_name_2026 has only id/label/kind/same_as.
cik_name's `same_as` is populated 100% but points at kg:company:name:* -- a NAME-DERIVED canonical key, not an external identifier. It is the same name join materialised, not a bridge.
No file on disk links a CIK to an LEI.
GLEIF DOES carry the discriminator -- jurisdiction, legalAddress, headquartersAddress -- so the 51.3% country signal is present on exactly one side of the join.
GLEIF also carries an external identifier, `registeredAs`, and for NVIDIA it is 2862596: the DELAWARE register number, not the SEC CIK of 1045810.
the_structural_result: Federation across two filed sources fails here not for LACK of identifiers but for a SURPLUS OF INCOMPATIBLE ONES. SEC identifies by CIK because it files who is filing; GLEIF identifies by LEI plus a local company-register number because it files who the legal entity is. Each is rich and neither carries the other's key, so the only attribute both sides hold is the NAME -- which is exactly why f is 14.7% and why it is not a matcher problem. The one discriminating attribute that would halve it is present on one side only.
consequence: The 68x cliff is irreducible by modelling. Closing it is a DATA ACQUISITION problem -- a crosswalk -- not an algorithmic one, and that is a different kind of task from anything this repo has attempted.
prediction_error: I predicted f 14.7% -> ~7.2% and advantage 7x -> 14x. Neither is achievable on disk; the experiment could not run and finding out why is the result.

hypothesis: The 68x cross-source cliff is caused by the absence of a shared identifier, not by cross-source-ness itself. Given a REAL identifier bridge, a cross-source join should have f near zero and the advantage should return toward the single-source 463x. GLEIF publishes a free daily ISIN-to-LEI mapping, and US ISINs are literally 'US' + the 9-character CUSIP + a check digit -- and the 13F holdings on disk are CUSIP-keyed. That is an exact-identifier bridge from a filed source to a filed source.
why_this_is_the_right_test: The last finding said closing the cliff is a data-acquisition problem rather than an algorithmic one. This acquires the data and tests whether the claim was right. It also gives the repo its first cross-source join on an IDENTIFIER rather than on names, which is the case the federation layer was built for.

expected.isin_coverage_of_13f_cusips: 40-70% of the 33,780 distinct CUSIPs -- GLEIF's ISIN file covers entities that issue registered securities, and 13F holds plenty of instruments that will not appear
expected.f_for_the_bridged_join: near 0 -- an exact identifier match either hits or misses, and a miss is a coverage gap rather than an ambiguity
expected.advantage_for_bridged_queries: back toward the single-source number, so hundreds rather than 7x
expected.the_caveat_i_expect_to_have_to_state: coverage is not ambiguity. A bridged join with 50% coverage answers half the questions perfectly and none of the rest, which is a different failure mode from a name join that answers all of them ambiguously -- and it may be a worse product even at a better f.

would_change_my_mind: ISIN coverage of 13F CUSIPs below 15%, which would make the bridge real but useless; or the bridged join turning out to be ambiguous anyway, which would mean the cliff is not about identifiers at all

actual.mapping: GLEIF ISIN-LEI, 2,281,221 distinct US CUSIPs carrying an LEI, downloaded free and unauthenticated

prediction_error: Ambiguity exactly as predicted: 0 of 7,503, an identifier join hits or misses. Coverage badly over-predicted: 40-70% expected, 22.3% actual, above my 15% would-change-my-mind line but well below the band. And I predicted the advantage would return 'toward the single-source 463x'; it goes from 6.8x to 8.8x.
the_result_that_matters: The bridge does NOT close the cliff. It CONVERTS it from an ambiguity problem into a coverage problem, and coverage is the larger of the two. A coverage gap escalates exactly as an ambiguity does -- a query the bridge cannot answer still has to go somewhere -- so the identifier join ALONE is far worse than the name join it was meant to improve on: f 77.7% and 1.3x against 14.7% and 6.8x. Only the composite policy helps, and it buys 1.29x.
belief_update: The previous finding's closing claim -- that the 68x cliff is a data-acquisition problem -- is now measured and mostly WRONG. I acquired exactly the data it named and got 29%, not 68x. The cliff is not about the absence of an identifier; it is about the absence of an identifier THAT COVERS THE WORKLOAD, and a mapping built for registered securities covers a fifth of what an institutional portfolio actually holds.
what_this_teaches_about_federation: An identifier bridge and a name join fail in ways that do not compose into a small number. The name join is universal and uncertain; the bridge is certain and partial. A federated substrate needs BOTH plus a policy, and the policy's f is the product of the two failure rates rather than the smaller of them.

hypothesis: The session has measured costs for fifteen cycles and never demonstrated a working capability end to end. The mandate asks for a vertical slice: input, shared world, two or more sources composing, a certificate, a price. The bridge acquired last cycle makes one possible for the first time -- 13F holdings (CUSIP) -> GLEIF ISIN-LEI bridge (LEI) -> GLEIF entities (country) -- which is THREE filed sources and two joins.
the_question: What is the country exposure of a 13F filer's portfolio? Real, valuable, and impossible without federation.
why_it_is_more_than_engineering: The 22.3% bridge coverage means the answer CANNOT be a point estimate. 77.7% of a portfolio's positions have unknown domicile, so the honest answer is an interval -- and this repo already has exact attained bounds (`additive_bounds`) built for precisely that shape. So the slice is also a test of whether the ambiguity machinery composes with a real federated query, which nothing has tried.

expected.bounds_width: wide -- if 78% of positions are unknown, a country's share is bounded between (known-in-C)/total and (known-in-C + unknown)/total, so intervals should span 60-80 percentage points

hypothesis: Collapsing a resolved position to a point treats a lookup as if it SETTLED the question, which it does not -- and that is exactly the collapse this repo's ambiguity machinery exists to refuse. The honest construction widens the band by the worst-case error mass: if k positions are resolved and at most m of them are wrong, widen both ends by the sum of the m largest resolved weights. Coverage should then return to roughly P(errors <= m), a binomial tail, at a width cost of the m largest weights.
the_arithmetic: At k=10 and a=0.95 the expected number of wrong lookups is 0.5, and P(errors <= 1) = 0.914. So widening for a single error should lift coverage from the measured 63.3% to around 91% -- paying only the single largest resolved weight in width.

the_honest_product: At a=0.95 with ten lookups: no lookups gives a 43.5% median band that is always true; naive resolution gives 10.4% and is true 63.3% of the time; widening for ONE error gives 23.7% and is true 96.9% of the time, for the same $0.045. So the band roughly HALVES against doing nothing while staying true 97% of the time -- and the naive version should never ship.
the_principle_and_it_is_the_repo's_own: Do not let an uncertain input collapse a certain output. A lookup does not SETTLE a position, it makes one alternative likelier, and treating it as settled is exactly the collapse this repo's ambiguity machinery exists to refuse. Feeding the lookup's error back in as additional slack keeps the guarantee; additive_bounds needed no change, only the right input.

hypothesis: The robust construction has a consequence I did not notice when I published it. With slack for m=1 error, the band after resolving the k widest positions is sum(w[k:]) + 2*w[0], so the improvement over doing nothing is sum(w[1:k]) - w[0]. At k=1 that is -w[0]: the band is total + w[0], STRICTLY WORSE than not resolving at all. Resolving pays only once the second through kth weights together exceed the largest.
the_prediction: The m=1 band as a function of k should be NON-MONOTONE -- worse than k=0 for small k, crossing over somewhere around k=3-5 because the five widest carry 57.5% of the width and the largest alone carries a large share of that.
why_it_matters: It is a real and counterintuitive operating rule that falls out of taking uncertainty seriously: a few careful lookups are worse than none, because the slack you must carry for the largest one exceeds the width the others remove. Nobody proposing 'just check the top few' would guess it.

the_operating_rule: With slack for one error, checking ONE or TWO positions makes the answer STRICTLY WORSE -- 0.0% of filers improve at k=1 or k=2, and the median band grows by 8.2 points at k=1. You must check at least three, and more is monotonically better thereafter. 'Just check the top few' is worse than doing nothing.
why: Resolving the k widest gives band = sum(w[k:]) + 2*w[0], so the improvement over doing nothing is sum(w[1:k]) - w[0]. At k=1 that is -w[0]. The slack you must carry for the largest resolved position exceeds the width the others remove until enough others accumulate.
what_it_says_generally: Taking uncertainty seriously has a threshold, not a gradient. A partial effort at resolving ambiguity is not a partial improvement -- below the threshold it is a regression, and the threshold is set by the concentration of the thing being resolved.

hypothesis: Everything this session measured is cost and uncertainty; nothing demonstrates REASONING a model could not do, and the Witness contract shipped four cycles ago still has no consumer. Both gaps close with one query: a portfolio's country exposure resolved to ULTIMATE PARENT rather than to the issuer's own domicile. That needs a transitive closure over GLEIF consolidation -- multi-step deduction, not a lookup -- and each answer carries a derivation chain a reader checks by following named edges.
the_question_that_makes_it_load_bearing_: For how many bridged holdings does the ultimate parent's country DIFFER from the issuer's own? If the answer is small, the deduction is decoration and direct domicile suffices. If it is large, direct domicile is actively misleading and the closure earns its place.

question: The closure covers 5.3% of held issuers. Is that our copy's limit or the world's -- i.e. is the reach gap a download away?

actual.repo_has: 3,348,427 GLEIF entities = 98.3% of the 3,405,477 GLEIF publishes

the_answer: The world's, not ours. We hold 98.3% of GLEIF and only 4.1% of its entities report a consolidating parent at all, because reporting is required only under accounting-consolidation circumstances. No download fixes that.
the_mechanism_and_it_is_satisfying: Held issuers are 22x ENRICHED as parents -- 35.8% appear as a parent against 1.6% of the population -- because an institutional portfolio holds the TOP of ownership chains, not the bottom. The closure does not fire because you already own the ultimate parent. It would be load-bearing for a different question, such as who ultimately owns a private subsidiary, and is structurally irrelevant to what a portfolio owns.
how_it_refines_the_programme_conclusion: Reach is the bottleneck, and reach has TWO KINDS: purchasable (a crosswalk, a corpus, a token) and STRUCTURAL (what the world files at all). The extraction gap and the bridge gap are partly purchasable. The ownership gap is not -- it is a property of what GLEIF requires entities to report.

hypothesis: The closure changed 0.8% of portfolio answers because portfolios hold the TOP of ownership chains -- 35.8% of held issuers ARE a parent against 1.6% of the population. If that diagnosis is right, then on the population that DOES have parents the same closure should be strongly load-bearing, and the lesson is about QUESTION SELECTION rather than about capability.
the_test: Over the 137,686 entities that report a consolidating parent, ask how often the ULTIMATE parent lives in a different country from the entity itself -- the same question, on the population the machinery was built for.

expected.depth_where_it_matters: the multi-hop cases should be enriched for cross-border, since a chain that crosses a border usually does so through an intermediate holding company
expected.if_it_is_high: the closure is correct AND load-bearing for its own population, and the 0.8% result is a statement about the QUESTION rather than the kernel
expected.if_it_is_low: the closure is decoration everywhere and the 95.7% agreement is agreement about something that does not matter

would_change_my_mind: under 10% cross-border among entities with a parent -- then ownership chains are overwhelmingly domestic, the closure never changes a country answer for anyone, and the machinery needs a different question class entirely

prediction_error: 35.9% lands inside the predicted 20-40%, and the depth gradient was predicted and is there: chains that cross a border do so through intermediate holding companies, so cross-border rises with depth -- 31.2% at depth 1 to 86.4% at depth 6.
the_result: The closure is CORRECT (95.7% against the filed ultimate) and STRONGLY LOAD-BEARING on the population it was built for: 35.9% of entities with a parent have a cross-border ultimate, 45x the 0.8% seen through a portfolio. At depth 2 or more -- 24,800 entities -- a MAJORITY cross a border, so the single-hop answer is wrong for most of them and transitivity is doing real work.
what_it_settles: The 0.8% was a statement about the QUESTION, not the kernel. Portfolios hold the top of ownership chains, so the closure has nothing to traverse; the same closure over the entities that actually have parents changes a third of the answers.
the_sharpened_programme_instruction: Not 'invest in reach' and not 'build better kernels' but MATCH THE QUESTION TO THE DATA'S SHAPE. The machinery was right in all three arms this session; twice the question did not exercise it and once the data did not reach. Those are different failures and they have different fixes.

note: Applying 'match the question to the data's shape' to my own headline table. It reports CROSS-SOURCE FILED as a single 7x, taken from the SEC-filer-to-GLEIF NAME join at f=14.7%. But the ISIN bridge is also a cross-source filed join, and its f depends entirely on how the workload weights securities: 77.7% per distinct security, 41.2% per position held, 20.9% per dollar held.
the_arithmetic: advantage = 1/f gives 6.8x for the name join, 1.3x for the bridge per security, 2.4x per position, and 4.8x per DOLLAR -- which is the weighting a portfolio question actually uses.
what_would_cap_this: Nothing new is measured here; it is arithmetic over numbers already on disk, so the cap is that all four rows inherit their f from measurements already made and carry those measurements' caveats. Per the calibration lesson this is stated as a fact rather than a band because there is no magnitude being predicted.

mechanism: wikidata notability correlates with corporate size; large corporations have many GLEIF entities sharing a canonical name, so the bridge should preferentially cover the AMBIGUOUS filers and remove more than its share of f.
expected_direction: ambiguity rate among bridged filers HIGHER than the 14.7% base rate
expected_magnitude: bridged-filer ambiguity 16-30% (vs 14.7% base); composite f below the 12.5% independence estimate; gain 1.2-1.5x rather than 1.18x
calibration_note: my magnitude predictions have run over-optimistic 13 times to 0, so this interval is deliberately shaded low and still probably high
would_change_my_mind: bridged ambiguity <= 14.7% means wikidata covers the EASY cases and the bridge buys even less than independence implies; agreement between the bridge's LEI and the name join's candidate set below 50% would mean one of the two joins is badly wrong and neither number can be quoted

hypothesis: Where a filer is both bridged and name-matched, the bridge's LEI is among the name join's candidates.
mechanism: both resolve the same real-world entity; the name join's failure mode is over-generation (too many candidates), not missing the right one.
would_change_my_mind: below 50% agreement invalidates one of the joins

actual: bridge exists: 2,113 CIK->LEI pairs via wikidata. Coverage 15.3% of all filers, 24.9% of matched. Ambiguity among bridged 19.5% vs 13.1% unbridged vs 14.7% base = 1.33x ENRICHMENT toward ambiguous filers. Composite f 9.81% measured vs 11.01% under independence; advantage 6.8x -> 10.2x, a 1.49x gain. Cross-validation 93.0% agreement overall, 90.4% on the ambiguous subset.
prediction_error: direction CORRECT (enrichment > 1). Magnitude 19.5% landed inside the shaded 16-30% interval; gain 1.49x at the top of the predicted 1.2-1.5x. Agreement prediction 60-80% was an UNDER-call: actual 93.0%.
interpretation: deliberately shading magnitude low, after 13 consecutive over-optimistic calls, produced two calls that were correct-to-under rather than over. The over-optimism was a systematic bias, not noise, and correcting for it works.
belief_update: RETRACT: 'SEC and GLEIF share no identifier, the only attribute both hold is the name'. FALSE - wikidata bridges both namespaces. The DEEPER claim survives: 1.49x of a 68x cliff is not closing it. NEW: crosswalk coverage is NOT independent of join difficulty; it is enriched toward the hard cases, so coverage UNDERSTATES a crosswalk's value.

hypothesis: The 1.33x enrichment is caused by CURATION, not by bridging. A human-curated crosswalk selects on notability; a filed/exhaustive one does not. So a curated bridge's coverage should be far more concentrated on high-value entities than a filed bridge's, measured on the same workload.
mechanism: wikidata entities exist because someone thought them notable; GLEIF ISIN-LEI exists because an issuer filed. Notability tracks size; filing does not.
expected_direction: ratio of (coverage by dollar)/(coverage by count) much higher for the wikidata ISIN bridge than for the GLEIF ISIN->LEI bridge, over the same 13F holdings
calibration_note: shading low again given the 13-to-0 over-optimism record
would_change_my_mind: if the curated ratio is not clearly above the filed one, the enrichment is a property of bridging or of entity size generally, not of curation, and the general claim must be stated without the word curated

actual: Raw ratio: filed 2.68x, curated 9.21x, 3.43x apart. But normalised against an oracle picking the best k securities at each crosswalk's OWN k, with random-at-k as the floor: filed attains 66.0%, curated 69.8% — 1.06x apart. Separately: 2,383 curated rows reach 68.8% of $51.4T; 2,281,221 filed rows reach 75.0%. 878x more answered value per row.
prediction_error: filed raw ratio 2.68x was ABOVE my 1.5-2.5x interval; curated 9.21x inside 5-15x. But the MECHANISM prediction is REFUTED: curation is not what buys the concentration.
interpretation: my pre-registered refutation criterion was stated on the raw dollar/count ratio, which has a ceiling of 1/coverage and therefore cannot compare crosswalks of different size. Stated on that statistic the criterion would have CONFIRMED a mechanism that is not there. The floor/ceiling audit — the repo's standing rule — is the only reason this was caught.
belief_update: RETRACT the curation mechanism. Both crosswalks capture ~2/3 of the value achievable at their own size; neither is better targeted. NEW and stronger: purchasable reach SATURATES. Value concentrates so steeply that the first few thousand crosswalk rows carry most of the workload and the next two million carry the tail. The acquisition decision is dominated by the small file, not because it is smarter but because coverage saturates.
meta: a pre-registered criterion is only as good as the statistic it names; registering the DIRECTION without checking that the statistic is comparable across arms is a new failure mode for this ledger.

hypothesis: Ambiguity between GLEIF candidates sharing a canonical name is mostly WITHIN one corporate group, so transitive closure over IS_ULTIMATELY_CONSOLIDATED_BY collapses it for any question asked at the group level — settling filers no crosswalk reaches, at zero acquisition cost.
mechanism: entities share a canonical name because they are Morgan Stanley & Co, Morgan Stanley Bank, Morgan Stanley Capital — members of one group. The name join's over-generation is over-generation WITHIN a group, which is exactly the structure GLEIF's relationship file encodes.
expected_direction: a large majority of ambiguous filers have all candidates under one ultimate root
expected_magnitude: 45-70% determined at group level under consolidation closure alone; +10-20 points adding IS_FUND-MANAGED_BY
calibration_note: shading low again; the 13-to-0 over-optimism correction has now produced two under-calls, so the shade may be slightly too aggressive
would_change_my_mind: below 30% means name-sharing crosses corporate groups and closure buys nothing. AND the permutation control must fail: if shuffling the LEI->root map gives comparable agreement, the result is a base-rate artefact of having few roots, not structure.
scope_caveat: this settles GROUP-level questions only. A question about the specific legal entity stays ambiguous, and that limit is the finding as much as the number is.

actual: 18.2% of ambiguous filers determined at group level unconditionally (109/598), permutation control 0.0%. CONDITIONAL on every candidate appearing in the relationship graph: 81.3% (109/134), control on the same conditional population 0.0%. Relationship graph mentions 348,836 of 3,348,427 GLEIF entities = 10.4%. f 14.66% -> 11.99% by closure alone (1.22x), -> 8.17% combined with the bridge (1.80x vs 1.49x bridge alone).
prediction_error: predicted 45-70% unconditional; actual 18.2% — OVER by a factor of ~3, despite deliberately shading low. But the conditional 81.3% is ABOVE the predicted range. The prediction conflated mechanism strength with data coverage and named only one number.
interpretation: the mechanism is STRONGER than predicted and the data far THINNER. Two bugs were caught en route, both by the result being too clean: (1) roots keyed on full kg:lei:* while lookups used the bare LEI gave a 0/598 with a 0/598 control; (2) membership tested against the root map, which only holds entities with an OUTGOING edge, so a top-level parent read as absent from a graph it is the root of — that version reported 81.8% from n=11.
belief_update: REACH HAS THREE TIERS, not two. Purchasable (saturates — measured this session). Derivable from recorded structure (works at 81.3%, reaches 22.4% of the hard cases). Absent — nobody ever recorded it, which is 90% of GLEIF entities and is NOT a procurement problem. Closure and crosswalks are near-orthogonal: 1.22x and 1.49x compose to 1.80x.
calibration_note: the low-shading correction worked twice then failed badly here. The failure mode was not magnitude but SPECIFICATION: I predicted one number for a quantity that is a product of two independent ones. Predict the factors, not the product.

hypothesis: Tier 3 is 'absent from THIS source', not 'absent'. GLEIF records a relationship for 10.4% of its entities; wikidata's backbone carries owned-by / parent-organization / subsidiary / owner-of edges independently. Closure over the UNION, with wikidata edges mapped into LEI space via the idbridges file, should settle ambiguous filers GLEIF alone cannot.
mechanism: for candidates {LEI_a, LEI_b} unrelated in GLEIF, if LEI_a <- Q1 and LEI_b <- Q2 and Q1 --subsidiary--> Q2 in wikidata, they are one group. Two sources recording overlapping-but-not-identical structure is the federation thesis applied to STRUCTURE rather than to identity.
expected_factor_coverage: 2-8% of ambiguous filers gain FULL candidate coverage from wikidata that GLEIF lacked — the binding constraint, because the bridge holds only 53,198 LEIs and ownership edges are ~50k in the 12M core
expected_factor_mechanism: 60-85% conditional determinacy where covered, at or slightly below GLEIF's 81.3%, because wikidata ownership is coarser and less current
expected_magnitude: marginal gain of +1 to +4 points on the 18.2% unconditional
would_change_my_mind: ZERO additional filers settled would mean the two sources record structure for the SAME entities — that redundancy is itself a finding and a bad one for federation. A permutation control that does not fail invalidates it as before.
why_it_matters_regardless_of_magnitude: the magnitude is secondary. If ANY filer is settled by the second source that the first could not settle, tier 3 is a function of how many sources you federate rather than a wall, and the residual f of 8.17% is not a floor.

actual: NULL. wikidata settles 6/598 ambiguous filers, only 3 that GLEIF could not, against a union permutation control of ~1. The second source buys 1.01x. Mechanism: wikidata holds 1,279,720 ownership edges to GLEIF's 296,491 — 4.3x MORE structure — but only 1.3% of GLEIF's edge count is expressible about LEIs, because only 52,860 of 3,348,427 GLEIF entities (1.6%) carry a wikidata twin. Just 11/598 ambiguous filers have all candidates carrying a QID.
prediction_error: coverage factor predicted 2-8%, actual 1.8% (below). Mechanism factor predicted 60-85%, actual 54.5% but on n=11, a slice, so not scorable. Marginal predicted +1 to +4 points, actual +0.5.
interpretation: my hypothesis was that tier 3 is 'absent from this source' rather than absent, and that federating structure would attack it. The structure IS there — 4.3x more of it — and it is unreachable. The binding constraint is the IDENTITY bridge, not the recorded structure.
belief_update: THE TIERS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT, which corrects the finding published one cycle ago. Relief in tier 2/3 is gated by tier-1 identity coverage, and tier 1 SATURATES. So the residual f of 8.17% is more robust than the three-tier note implied: you cannot route around unrecorded structure by adding sources, because reaching another source's structure requires the identity coverage that already saturated.
dead_arm: federating a second structural source. Cost one note. Do not repeat without first measuring identity-bridge coverage over the candidate population — that single number predicts the yield.

hypothesis: The 1.58% identity coverage that killed the structural-federation arm is an UNWEIGHTED per-entity count, and this repo has been caught by that denominator three times already (22.3% per security vs 58.8% per position vs 75.0% per dollar). Weighted by what the workload actually asks about, wikidata identity coverage should be far higher — because wikidata notability tracks size and the workload concentrates on large entities.
mechanism: identity coverage is prominence-weighted; the missing 98.4% is the tail.
factors: predicting each cell of the 2x2 separately
expected_filers_by_count: 12-25% of 13F filers carry a wikidata twin
expected_filers_by_aum: 55-80% of portfolio dollars sit with a filer that carries one
would_change_my_mind: if the dollar-weighted numbers are also low (<40%), then identity coverage is genuinely thin rather than prominence-weighted, the 1.58% stands as reported, and the reach programme's constraint is much harder than a tail problem. If they are high, the null from the previous arm is about the TAIL and the headline 'structure is unaddressable' needs qualifying to 'unaddressable for the long tail, addressable for most of the value'.
consequence_either_way: this decides whether the residual f of 8.17% is a tail phenomenon (economically minor) or a broad one (economically binding), and nothing measured so far distinguishes them.

actual: SPLITS BY POPULATION. Held securities (issuers): 12.0% by count, 66.3% BY VALUE — 5.5x ratio, 42x the flat rate. 13F filers: 1.6% by count, 23.2% by AUM — 14.3x ratio but only 23.2%, 15x the flat rate. All GLEIF entities unweighted: 1.58%.
prediction_error: issuers correct on both cells (10-20% count / 65-85% dollar, actual 12.0% / 66.3%). Filers WRONG on both and badly: predicted 12-25% by count, actual 1.6%; predicted 55-80% by AUM, actual 23.2%.
interpretation: I assumed prominence tracks SIZE. It tracks ENTITY TYPE. wikidata covers operating companies, not asset managers — and there are 8,755 13F filers, most of them small RIAs with no encyclopaedic existence at any AUM. The 14.3x count-to-value ratio for filers shows the weighting effect is real and strong; it starts from a base so low that it still lands at 23.2%.
belief_update: The 1.58% was indeed a misleading denominator, but correcting it does NOT rescue the filer side. DECISIVE for the arc: the residual f of 8.17% is NOT a tail phenomenon, because the alignment workload where f lives is over FILERS, and filers are 23.2% addressable by the denominator that matters. On the ISSUER side — where the vertical slice operates — 66.3% of held value is addressable, so those answers rest on much firmer ground than the filer alignment does.
new_claim: Coverage is asymmetric in the DIRECTION of the query over the same edge: what a portfolio holds is 66.3% addressable, who holds it is 23.2%. Same bridge, same technology, 2.9x apart.

hypothesis: 'Purchasable reach saturates' rests entirely on how steeply 13F value concentrates — 2,383 crosswalk rows reach 68.8% of $51.4T. The finding names its own refuter: a flatter workload would saturate far later. If concentration is a general property of relational workloads, saturation is a law and the acquisition advice generalises; if 13F is an outlier, the headline is domain-bound.
mechanism: heavy tails are ubiquitous (Zipf), but financial value is concentrated by an additional mechanism — index-tracking and market cap — that citation or activity counts lack.
expected_direction: all workloads steep, with meaningful spread; 13F steepest
expected_magnitude: share of mass held by the top 7.5% of entities: 13F-by-dollar ~95%, GitHub events per repo 70-85%, OpenAlex works per institution 60-80%, patent citations per patent 50-70%, courtlistener citations per case 50-70%
would_change_my_mind: any workload where the top 7.5% of entities holds under ~35% of mass makes saturation domain-bound and the acquisition advice has to be restated as conditional on concentration. If they all cluster above 60%, the headline is a law and gets stronger, not weaker.
why_run_it: it is the refuter I wrote into my own finding two commits ago, it is cheap, and it decides whether the strongest economic claim of this session generalises beyond one asset class.

actual: REFUTED as a law. Share of mass in the top 7.5% of entities: 13F by $ 96.9% (gini 0.976), patent assignees 85.6%, 13F by position count 77.7%, caselaw citations 56.1%, patent citations 55.6%, GitHub events per repo 27.3% (gini 0.373). Spread 27.3% to 96.9%, a 3.5x span.
prediction_error: 3 of 5 in range. 13F ~95% predicted, 96.9% actual. Patent citations 50-70% predicted, 55.6%. Caselaw 50-70% predicted, 56.1%. MISSED: GitHub predicted 70-85%, actual 27.3% — badly over. Patent assignees not predicted separately and came in at 85.6%.
interpretation: I assumed activity concentrates like value. It does not: GH Archive over 5 days is 7.7M events across 3.9M repos, mean 1.98, median 1, 57.3% with exactly one event, max 1,043. There is no head to concentrate in. Verified directly because this outlier carries the whole conclusion.
belief_update: 'Purchasable reach saturates' is NOT a law. It is conditional on the workload's concentration, and concentration spans 3.5x across ordinary relational workloads. The MECHANISM finding survives untouched — both crosswalks still attain ~2/3 of achievable at their own k — but the economic advice has to be restated as conditional.
decision_rule: before acquiring a crosswalk, measure the workload's top-7.5% mass share. 96.9% (13F) means buy the small file and stop; 27.3% (GitHub-like) means a small acquisition buys almost nothing and breadth is the only lever. One cheap statistic decides it.
note: and within ONE edge set the denominator moves it 96.9% -> 77.7% (13F by dollar vs by position count), which is the same denominator trap this repo has now hit four times.

hypothesis: Six arms this session priced DETERMINACY (does the system settle) and silently treated settled as correct. Putting the arc through symbolic_ai_core/cost.py forces two things it never had: a measured accuracy, and a FLOOR. The floor here is strong — 85.3% of matched filers have exactly one name candidate, and a floor that takes the single candidate when there is one already gets those right — so accuracy minus floor will be small and usd_per_solved_episode_above_floor will be far worse than the 6.8x-to-12.2x advantage ratios imply.
mechanism: advantage = 1/f is a COST ratio at assumed equal accuracy. above_floor divides by (accuracy - floor), and the symbolic system's entire contribution is confined to the 14.7% ambiguous slice, so the numerator of the capability it buys is at most ~0.147 before any error.
expected_floor_entity_level: random-among-candidates floor at 88-93% overall, because 85.3% of filers are unambiguous and get the single candidate free
expected_consequence: the above-floor cost is 12x-30x worse than usd_per_solved implies, and the honest headline of the whole arc is a cost-per-CAPABILITY number an order of magnitude less impressive than the cost-per-answer ratios published this session
would_change_my_mind: if the name join's single candidate is frequently WRONG against the bridge ground truth, the floor collapses and the symbolic layer's contribution is much larger than I expect — that would be good news and I do not believe it. Also: if entity-level accuracy on unambiguous filers is below ~80%, the whole alignment premise is weaker than six findings have assumed.
note: the ground truth is the wikidata bridge (1,015 filers), so the bridge must be EXCLUDED from the system being scored or the measurement is circular.

actual: CEILING: the true LEI is among the name candidates for 93.0% of filers. ENTITY level: system+fallback 83.7% vs random-candidate floor 82.9% = +0.9%. GROUP level: system+fallback 87.3% vs floor 87.4% = -0.1%. The symbolic-only resolver DOES NOT BEAT ITS FLOOR and cost.py reports $/solved-above-floor as inf. Hybrid escalating 15.4%: 96.5% accuracy, $1.04e-03 above floor. Model only: 100%, $4.88e-03. The hybrid is 4.7x cheaper per unit of capability above floor.
prediction_error: floor predicted 88-93%, actual 82.9-87.4% (close). System predicted 90-96%, actual 83.7-87.3% (over). Gap predicted 3-8 points, actual +0.9 and -0.1 — badly over, and I predicted the WRONG SIGN at group level.
mechanism: at group level, when closure determines the answer BECAUSE all candidates share a root, picking a candidate at random already lands on that root. The floor gets those right for free. Closure tells you the answer is determined; it does not tell you anything a guess could not.
belief_update: DETERMINACY IS NOT ACCURACY, and six arms this session priced determinacy. The 1.22x from closure, the 1.49x from the crosswalk and the 1.80x combined are COST ratios at assumed equal accuracy — the exact assumption HANDOVER §6 says put four earlier rows out of quotation. Measured against a floor that uses the same candidate sets, the symbolic layer's accuracy contribution is +0.9 points at entity level and ZERO at group level. What it actually buys is KNOWING WHEN IT IS RIGHT, which is certification, not capability — and that is worth 4.7x on $/capability-above-floor via escalation, not the 6.8x-12.2x cost ratios published.
harness_trap: the first version scored abstention as zero and reported the system at -7.5% BELOW floor, comparing a system that refuses to guess against a floor that always guesses. CLAUDE.md lists 'abstention falling back to the structural prior' as one of the largest measured effects in this repo's history and I walked into it anyway.

hypothesis: The resolver buys nothing in accuracy above floor, but if its DETERMINACY signal predicts its own accuracy then certification has real value the ledger cannot see — an escalation policy can target the wrong answers instead of guessing at them.
mechanism: settling means every candidate agrees at the level asked; when they agree the answer is usually the true one, so settled cases should sit near the 93.0% ceiling and unsettled ones far below.
would_change_my_mind: a gap under ~15 points means determinacy does not predict correctness and the symbolic layer buys NOTHING — not accuracy, not certification — which is the starkest possible reading and the one that should end the arc. Note the escalation-frontier finding already answered this question in the OTHER domain and got 0.666 for the confident tier: the extractor could NOT tell what it knew. If this domain agrees, that is two for two and a property of the approach rather than of one extractor.
calibration_note: predicting factors separately per the standing lesson; the gap is the derived quantity, not a fourth independent guess.

actual: HIGHLY informative. Entity level: settled 93.6% (n=817) vs unsettled 32.3% (n=198), gap +61.3%. Group level: settled 95.8% (n=859) vs unsettled 40.4% (n=156), gap +55.4%. Priced via escalation targeting at a fixed 15.4% budget: targeted +9.2 points to 96.5%, blind +2.0 points to 89.2% — knowing which answers are unsafe is worth 4.69x more quality per escalation dollar.
prediction_error: settled predicted 92-96%, actual 93.6/95.8% (correct). Unsettled predicted 40-60%, actual 32.3/40.4% (at or below the low end). Gap predicted 35-50 points, actual 55-61 — an UNDER-call, the third this session since I began shading magnitudes low.
interpretation: this CONTRADICTS the OpenAlex domain, where the confident tier beat the ambiguous one by only +0.150 F1 and the finding concluded the extractor could not tell what it knew. Both tierings are structural, so the difference is not confidence-vs-structure. It is CANDIDATE RECALL: the true answer is in the GLEIF candidate set 93.0% of the time (exact canonical-name match against a registry) and the ROR gazetteer match is lossy. Determinacy can only certify what the generator retrieved.
belief_update: DETERMINACY IS INFORMATIVE EXACTLY WHEN THE CANDIDATE GENERATOR HAS HIGH RECALL, which reconciles two contradictory results with one mechanism rather than picking a winner. And the symbolic layer's contribution is now measured and defensible: NOT accuracy (-0.1% above floor) but escalation TARGETING, worth 4.69x quality per escalation dollar. That is a capability number with a floor behind it, unlike the 6.8x-12.2x cost ratios it replaces.
north_star_gap: $/solved-above-floor prices getting the answer right and prices knowing-you-are-right at ZERO. The 4.69x is invisible in every column of the ledger. That is a real gap in the repo's north-star metric, not a gap in the measurement.

hypothesis: A capability whose value is TARGETING is priced by the savings it enables at a fixed budget, not by the answers it gets right. Adding a Targeting denominator to cost.py — floored by BLIND escalation at the same budget, mirroring Capability's refusal to carry a rate without a floor — should make the 4.69x visible in the same table that printed inf, and should separate the two domains the repo has measured.
verification_not_discovery: the OpenAlex numbers are already on disk in the escalation-frontier finding, so I computed the expected values by hand BEFORE implementing, which makes this a verification of the implementation rather than an experiment. Recording them here so the implementation cannot be quietly fitted to whatever it produces.
expected_ordering: GLEIF determinacy 4.69x > OpenAlex silence 2.13x > OpenAlex ambiguity 1.02x
why_it_matters: if the metric reproduces 'silence is a better escalation signal than ambiguity' as a PRICE rather than a description, it is measuring the right thing. The ambiguity signal coming out at ~1.0x is the sharpest check: that finding said the signal was weak and this should say it is worth nothing.
would_change_my_mind: an implementation that does not reproduce the hand-computed 1.02x and 2.13x has a bug, not a finding.

actual: Implemented Targeting in symbolic_ai_core/cost.py, floored by blind escalation at the same budget. It reproduces the hand-computed values exactly: OpenAlex silence 2.13x, OpenAlex ambiguity 1.02x, GLEIF determinacy 4.69x at $1.31e-03 per quality point. 12 new tests in tests/test_cost_targeting.py; the 41 existing cost tests are unchanged because the two columns render only when a row carries a claim.
prediction_error: none — the hand-computed 2.13x and 1.02x were recorded before implementation and are matched to 0.01.
interpretation: the metric now prices what the escalation-frontier finding could only describe. 'Silence is a better escalation signal than ambiguity' becomes 2.13x against 1.02x, and 1.02x is the sharper statement: the ambiguity signal is worth NOTHING over spending the same budget at random, not merely less.
belief_update: the repo's north star had a real hole and it is now closed rather than noted. A system can read inf on $/solved-above-floor and finite on $/quality-point, and the federated resolver is exactly that row — worthless at producing answers above its floor, worth 4.69x at certifying them.
design_note: the floor discipline is what makes it a metric rather than a ratio. 'We escalated and quality rose' is not a result; buying answers raises quality whoever picks them. Targeting refuses to carry a targeted rate without the blind baseline, mirroring Capability's refusal to carry a rate without a floor.

hypothesis: A read-set certificate invalidates when its INPUTS change; an answer is a function and is often insensitive to input churn. The certificate arm measured soundness (false_survivals = 0 on every row) and never measured PRECISION — how many invalidations were unnecessary. Under the Targeting metric, aim_x = 1/f_flagged for a sound certificate while the ceiling a minimal one reaches is 1/f_stale, so over-approximation destroys targeting value in direct proportion.
sharper_claim: the over-approximation cost is LARGEST exactly where the computation is most expensive, because expensive computations tend to produce coarse answers (a small integer, a boolean) that are insensitive to churn. If true, the recording mechanism is worst precisely where a certificate matters most.

factors.is_widely_held: f_flagged 66.96%; f_stale 6.38% ALREADY KNOWN from the r2 margin row (93.62% survive), so this row is a consistency check not a prediction; cost 10.5x
factors.min_filers_covering: f_flagged 100%; f_stale predicted 8-35%; cost 2.9-12.5x — the interesting one, an NP-hard solve whose answer is a small integer should be extremely stable

would_change_my_mind: if f_stale tracks f_flagged closely on every class, read-set recording is near-optimal and the 6,591x over-read finding does not translate into lost maintenance value — which would be good news for the mechanism and would contradict my reading of the arc. If min_cover's answer is as volatile as holder_count's, the 'expensive computations give coarse answers' claim is dead.
note: is_widely_held is entered as a consistency check with its expected value stated, so a disagreement there indicts the harness rather than the hypothesis.

actual: Over-approximation (f_flagged/f_stale): is_widely_held 79.8x at 739ns, holder_count 1.1x at 748ns, portfolio_overlap 1.6x at 6,048ns, min_filers_covering 2.5x at 6,745,104ns. Realised aim_x per quarter: 1.61, 1.61, 1.01, 1.00. The stability-margin certificate itself over-approximates by 8.2x (bound 6.38% against measured f_stale 0.78%).
prediction_error: the SHARPER CLAIM IS REFUTED. Over-approximation is not largest where computation is dearest -- it is largest at the CHEAPEST class and only 2.5x at 9,000x the compute. Factor predictions: holder_count f_stale 50-62% predicted, 54.3% actual (in range); portfolio_overlap 80-93% predicted, 62.1% actual (over); min_cover 8-35% predicted, 40.7% actual (over -- I expected an NP-hard solve to give a stable small integer and it does not). 1 of 4 in range.
the_controlled_comparison: holder_count and is_widely_held run over the IDENTICAL sampled securities with IDENTICAL read sets and near-identical cost (748ns vs 739ns), and differ 73x in over-approximation. The only variable is the answer function: len(holders) versus len(holders) >= 100. That is as clean a control as this repo has.
belief_update: Over-approximation is a property of the ANSWER'S SENSITIVITY, not of the computation's cost and not of the read set's size. It is INVISIBLE to any mechanism that records reads, because the read set is byte-identical in the two cases that differ 73x. That answers 3b's stated open question -- 'nothing in the mechanism tells you which case you are in' -- with a mechanism: the answer function does, and reads cannot see it.
anchor_note: my anchor asserted f_stale must EQUAL 6.38%. That number is a sound certificate's flagged rate, hence an UPPER BOUND on f_stale, not an estimate. The script correctly reported a disagreement and blamed itself; the design of the anchor was the error. Confusing a bound with an estimate, again.

hypothesis: 3b called the stability margin 'the rung the recording mechanism cannot produce' and treated it as query-supplied. It is DERIVABLE: is_widely_held computes len(holders) >= 100, so the slack |count - 100| is an intermediate the computation already produced and the recording mechanism discards. A certificate that records the numeric intermediate and a per-key Lipschitz bound can revalidate as sum(L_k * |old_k XOR new_k|) < slack, with no per-query delta rule.

factors.is_widely_held: f_flagged drops from 62.1% toward 3-8%. NOT to the 0.78% oracle, because the symmetric difference over-estimates |delta count| -- adds and removes cancel in the count and do not cancel in the XOR. Predicted to land near the hand-built margin's 6.38%, recovering ~10x of the 79.8x and leaving ~8x on the table, which is exactly the measured looseness of the hand margin.
factors.holder_count: no change at 62.1%. Slack is 0 -- any input change moves the count -- and that is correct, not a failure.
factors.min_filers_covering: no change at 100%. No cheap sound Lipschitz bound exists for a set cover's optimum.

expected_headline: the derived margin matches the hand-supplied one without being supplied, on the one class where slack exists
would_change_my_mind: derived f_flagged materially WORSE than 6.38% means the symmetric-difference bound is too loose to be useful and the rung really does need a hand rule. Derived f_flagged BELOW 6.38% would mean the hand margin was not just loose but worse than an automatic one, which I do not expect. Any false survival at all -- valid declared for a moved answer -- kills the mechanism outright, and that check is the anchor.

actual: WORKS. is_widely_held f_flagged 62.22% -> 6.16% with a margin derived from the count the computation already produced. Recovers 10.1x of the 79.8x over-approximation, leaving 7.9x. aim_x 1.61x -> 16.23x; $/quality-point $8.67e-10 -> $3.46e-11, 25x cheaper. holder_count derived == read set exactly (62.22%, recovers 1.0x) because a raw count has slack 0. ZERO false survivals on every arm.
prediction_error: NONE MATERIAL — the closest call this session. Predicted 3-8% (actual 6.16%), predicted 'near the hand margin's 6.38%' (actual 6.16%, marginally BETTER), predicted recovery ~10x (actual 10.1x) leaving ~8x (actual 7.9x), predicted holder_count unchanged (it is, exactly).
interpretation: 3b called the stability margin 'the rung the recording mechanism cannot produce' and treated it as query-supplied. It is DERIVABLE, and the derived version slightly beats the hand-built one. The slack was never hidden — is_widely_held computes len(holders) >= 100 and the count is an intermediate it already had. Only the DISCARDING of it was the problem.
belief_update: a certificate should record the numeric intermediate and a Lipschitz bound, not only the reads. That is a strictly larger contract than 'report your read set' and it costs one extra number per answer. The residual 7.9x is the symmetric-difference bound: an add and a remove cancel in a count and do not cancel in a XOR, which is the documented price of not knowing what the query does with its inputs.
what_it_does_not_do: nothing for holder_count, portfolio_overlap or min_filers_covering — slack 0 for the first two, no cheap sound Lipschitz bound for the third. The mechanism pays exactly where the answer is coarse, which is the same place the waste was.

hypothesis: Last cycle's headline — derived margin 25x cheaper per quality point, 'from recording one extra number per answer' — priced RECOMPUTE for both arms and omitted REVALIDATION from both. That is not apples-to-apples: a read-set check is one digest comparison, while the derived check is a symmetric difference over the whole holder set. 3b's own formula is advantage = min(compute/check, 1/P_hit), and I improved only the second term.
mechanism: the derived margin saves (62.22% - 6.16%) = 56.1% of recomputes, worth 0.561 x 739ns = 414ns per answer. A frozenset XOR over a mean holder set (roughly 54 elements) costs microseconds in Python. Saving hundreds of nanoseconds by spending several microseconds is a net LOSS.
expected_verdict: NET LOSS at 739ns query cost; break-even query cost roughly 5-15 us
expected_delta_supplied_regime: if the update stream supplies |old XOR new| per key — which it does, changed_keys already computes deltas once per update and amortises over every query touching that key — the derived check is a multiply-and-compare and is nearly free, so the 10.1x stands
would_change_my_mind: if the XOR is cheap enough that derived wins outright at 739ns, my worry is unfounded and last cycle's claim needs no qualification. If even the delta-supplied regime loses, the mechanism is elegant and economically inert and last cycle's finding needs a hard correction rather than a caveat.
why_run_it: it is a direct attack on the headline I published one commit ago, and the repo's standing rule is to prefer the experiment that could embarrass you.

actual: Ceilings at q->inf: read set 1.05x, derived margin with delta SUPPLIED 2.91x, derived margin RECOMPUTING its own diffs 0.05x. The delta pass costs 6,634ns/key against the digest pass's 853ns -- 7.8x dearer. Revalidation per answer is CHEAPER for the derived margin (80.1ns vs 94.2ns) but the XOR recomputed per query costs 5,911ns against a 277.5ns recompute. Derived(supplied) overtakes the read set at 34.3 queries per key and exceeds 1.00x at 36.4.
prediction_error: direction correct on the recomputed regime and I under-called its severity — predicted 'net loss', actual 0.05x, a 20x loss. Predicted break-even query cost 5-15us; the first version measured 11.6us, inside the range. But the REAL variable turned out not to be query cost at all: it is QUERIES PER KEY, because the cost is an amortised per-key pass and my first script sampled ~1 query per key, the worst possible case, which crushed the supplied-delta arm to 0.08x.
interpretation: my previous headline — '25x cheaper per quality point, from recording one extra number per answer' — priced RECOMPUTE for both arms and omitted REVALIDATION from both. The extra number is not the whole cost: the delta pass is 7.8x dearer per key than the digest pass.
belief_update: the derived margin is still the better arm and is the FIRST thing in the certificate programme to exceed 1.0x on this workload (2.91x against the read set's 1.05x ceiling) — but only above ~36 queries per key, and it is a 20x LOSS if the delta must be recomputed per query. 3b's maintenance framing implicitly assumes answers are re-served many times, which is exactly the condition; a one-pass analytical workload does not meet it.
correction_needed: the previous finding's 25x figure must carry the revalidation cost and the queries-per-key condition beside it.

hypothesis: If the update stream supplies |old XOR new| rather than it being recovered by diffing snapshots, the derived margin's advantage becomes a flat 2.91x at every queries-per-key and the 36.4 crossover moves to ~1.
derivation: revalidation 80.1ns + amortised 0 + flagged 5.47% x recompute 277.5ns = 95.3ns against a 277.5ns recompute = 2.91x, independent of q.

A Delta type would be consumed only by a test, the shape the egraph-witness decision declined earlier this week.

hypothesis: Every certificate in this repo is SOUND — it never declares valid for an answer that moved — and soundness has never been priced. The derived margin flags 5.47% where 0.78% actually moved. Relaxing the margin by a factor alpha (flag iff delta >= alpha*slack) trades correctness for fewer recomputes. Under the Targeting metric aim_x should RISE with alpha, because the flagged share falls faster than the quality does — which would mean the instrument I built last cycle can be GAMED by unsoundness.
mechanism: aim_x = (rate_targeted - base) / (flagged * (1 - base)). Relaxing cuts the denominator linearly in flagged while the numerator loses only the answers that actually moved in the relaxed band, which is a small fraction of a small fraction.
expected_direction: aim_x rises monotonically with alpha over the useful range while rate_targeted falls below 1.0
expected_magnitude: aim_x roughly 18x at alpha=1 rising to 30-60x by alpha=8, with error rate climbing from 0 to somewhere around 0.2-0.5% of all answers
what_this_tests: not whether to ship an unsound certificate — the repo's answer to that is no — but whether the TARGETING METRIC has a hole. If aim_x alone ranks an unsound arm above a sound one, then aim_x must never be read without the rate column, and Targeting should say so itself.
would_change_my_mind: if aim_x FALLS with alpha, the metric is self-protecting and no guard is needed. If the error rate explodes immediately (>2% by alpha=2), unsoundness is not even tempting here and the question is academic on this workload.

actual: 0.76% of answers actually moved. Sound margin (alpha=1): 6.22% flagged, 0 wrong, aim 16.1x. Relaxing: alpha=1.5 -> 24.8x at 0.060% wrong; alpha=8 -> 65.8x at 0.440%; alpha=16 -> 76.8x at 0.620%; alpha=64 -> 65.8x at 0.740% (aim PEAKS and falls). Oracle flagging exactly the movers: 131.6x, sound but unattainable.
prediction_error: direction correct. Predicted aim rising from ~18x to 30-60x by alpha=8 with error 0.2-0.5%: actual 16.1x -> 65.8x at 0.440%. Slightly over on the aim floor, over-delivered on the ceiling. I did not predict the PEAK at alpha=16 followed by a fall, which happens because the numerator collapses once almost nothing is flagged.
interpretation: soundness costs 8.2x of aim on this workload -- the sound margin reaches 16.1x of an available 131.6x -- and relaxing recovers 4.77x of that at 0.62% wrong answers. But the finding is about the INSTRUMENT: aim x ranks the unsound arm first, so the column I added two cycles ago can be gamed by unsoundness.
belief_update: the accuracy column DOES catch it ($/solved>floor: alpha=1 $7.31e-11 against alpha=16's $3.97e-10) but nothing in the table said the two columns disagreed. Added targeting_regime() and a TARGETING REGIME warning mirroring the existing perverse_regime check, plus 5 tests. This is the SAME lesson 3i already taught -- 'advantage AT FIXED QUALITY, the only comparison that is fair across extractors' -- rebuilt by me in a new column.
instrument_note: the oracle is deliberately not a ledger row. It is a bound, not a system: flagging exactly the movers requires knowing which answers moved, which is the thing being certified. Including it ranked a thing nobody can build above the things they can, and suppressed the warning.

hypothesis: I framed 8.2x as 'the cost of soundness'. It is not — it is the looseness of ONE sound bound. moved_elements uses the symmetric difference, where an add and a remove cancel in a count but not in a XOR. A bound on |delta count| is equally sound and much tighter, so the 8.2x decomposes into XOR-vs-magnitude looseness and a residual magnitude-vs-signed looseness that no sound bound can remove without computing the answer.
mechanism: |delta count| still over-flags: a rise of +1000 while already above the threshold cannot flip the answer, but its magnitude exceeds the slack. So the magnitude bound sits strictly between the XOR bound and the oracle.
expected_magnitude: the |delta count| arm flags 1-2% against the XOR's 6.22% and the oracle's 0.76%, i.e. it recovers most of the gap; aim_x roughly 50-100x against 16.1x and 131.6x
would_change_my_mind: if |delta count| flags close to 6.22%, the XOR was not the problem and the looseness is intrinsic to bounding a threshold by input movement. If it flags essentially 0.76%, the over-flagging on large same-side moves is negligible on this data and a sound certificate is effectively optimal here.
why_it_matters: it decides whether the 8.2x is an argument about EXACTNESS (soundness is expensive) or an argument about ENGINEERING (this bound is loose). Those have opposite implications for the programme.

actual: |delta count| bound: 1.74% flagged, ZERO wrong, aim 57.5x — against the XOR bound's 6.22%/16.1x and the oracle's 0.76%/131.6x. Of the 8.2x total looseness, 3.6x is the XOR over-counting a count and 2.3x is what no sound bound removes without computing the answer.
prediction_error: none material. Predicted 1-2% flagged and 50-100x aim; measured 1.74% and 57.5x.
interpretation: my framing of the previous arm was wrong and this corrects it. 8.2x was never 'the cost of soundness' — it was the looseness of one bound. Soundness costs 2.3x. And the consequence reverses the trade: the tighter SOUND bound at 57.5x beats every unsound arm up to alpha=8, which serves 0.44% of answers wrong, while serving nothing wrong. You do not give up soundness to get the aim; you stop using a loose bound.
belief_update: the exactness thesis is in better shape than the first measurement suggested, and for a reason that is engineering rather than philosophy. Also: the parked Delta decision now has a SECOND independent motivation worth 3.6x, since |delta count| is deployable only from signed adds and removes -- computing len(new) from a snapshot is the recompute it was meant to avoid.
next_level_down: the residual 2.3x is over-flagging on large SAME-SIDE moves (a rise of +1000 while already above the threshold). A signed-delta bound removes that too and reaches the oracle exactly, so 2.3x may be the price of taking a magnitude rather than the price of soundness. The decomposition probably goes one level deeper than measured.

hypothesis: The certification value this session measured on federated data (aim_x 4.69x escalation, 16.1x-57.5x maintenance) is ABSENT from the repo's 51 language models, for a structural reason: aim_x ~ 1/f_flagged needs the flagged set to be SMALL, and these models abstain on most positions so they flag 65-99%. An abstaining model looks epistemically virtuous and has no certification value at all -- it is just a model that does not answer.
derivation_from_numbers_already_on_disk: symbolic_ai_models/models/symbolic.py:343 records 'ilp answers 35% of nodes at 0.525 against a floor of 0.332; synth answers 1% at 1.000'. Taking acc|abstained = the fallback (context prior, ~the floor): ilp base = .35*.525+.65*.332 = .3996; targeted = .1838+.65 = .8338 (gain .434); blind = .3996+.65*(1-.3996) = .7899 (gain .390); aim_x = 1.11x. synth flags 99%, and escalating 99% is nearly escalating everything, so aim_x = .99(1-f)/.9801(1-f) = 1.01x regardless of the floor.
expected_magnitude: aim_x between 1.0x and 1.3x for every rule-based model measured; no model above 1.5x
would_change_my_mind: a model with a high vote rate AND a large accuracy gap between voted and abstained positions would break this -- it would flag little and flag well. If one exists, the certification thesis transfers to the language substrate and that model is the one to build on. Also: if acc|abstained is materially BELOW the floor, the fallback is weaker than documented and the base rates above are wrong.
why_verify_rather_than_assert: two examples from a docstring is a slice, and this repo has had slices invert results ten times. The instrumentation is cheap: s_conf is already computed in _forward_graph and a position with s_conf == 0 is an abstention.
method_note: expose s_conf as a channel; do NOT add a readout, because a readout carries floor obligations and a column in every published table. If the answer is interesting it earns one later.

actual: Five models with a reportable abstained set: routes-001 1.48x, ruleinduce-001 1.45x, ilp-001 1.37x, syllogism-001 1.09x, synth-001 1.02x. Three never abstain at all (corefer, ptrgen, vsa_perm). Two abstain on exactly ONE position of 5,233 and are slices, not reported. Every aim x sits at or just under 1/(1-label_acc).
prediction_error: MAGNITUDE CORRECT, MECHANISM WRONG. I predicted 1.0x-1.3x with none above 1.5x; measured 1.02x-1.48x. But I predicted it because 'these models abstain on most positions so they flag 65-99%' -- and in fact three flag ~0% and the vote rates span 2.1% to 100%. The flagged share turns out to CANCEL exactly.
the_closed_form: aim = (1-v)(1-a_abstained) / [(1-v)(1-base)] = (1 - a_abstained)/(1 - base). The flagged share cancels, so since a_abstained >= 0, aim <= 1/(1 - label_acc). That single bound explains every number this session produced: the models are 7.7%-32.9% accurate so their ceiling is 1.49x; the federated resolver at base 0.873 reached 4.69x; the maintenance oracle's 131.6x is exactly 1/(1-0.9924).
belief_update: A MODEL CAN ONLY CERTIFY TO THE EXTENT IT IS USUALLY RIGHT. Certification value is not governed by how much you flag nor by how WELL you flag -- synth-001 has the strongest determinacy signal in the repo, voting on 2.1% at 0.759 against 0.062 elsewhere, a +0.697 gap, and it is worth 1.02x. Signal quality is not the binding constraint; base accuracy is.
corrections_made: the script first printed a canned 'middle regime' conclusion the algebra contradicts, and reported grammar-001 and evidence-001 -- which abstain on ONE position each -- as measurements. Both fixed: the conclusion is derived, and a minimum abstained set of 30 is required to report.

hypothesis: I recorded in state.yml that strengthening the structural back-off RAISES accuracy and LOWERS certifiability, 'both real and pulling opposite ways'. Working the closed form, that may be wrong. aim = (1 - a_abstained)/(1 - base). Turning the back-off OFF lowers a_abstained (numerator UP, aim up) and lowers base (denominator UP, aim down). Which dominates is a magnitude question, and for the models where the back-off matters most the base effect should dominate -- so the back-off would be strictly better on BOTH axes and there is no trade.
mechanism: the prior is attached at EVERY hidden node, not only abstained ones, so a model that votes with low confidence keeps most of its mass on it. symbolic.py records ruleinduce voting on every node at 0.192 and scoring 0.076 before the change; it now scores 0.329.

factors.base_label_acc: ON higher than OFF by +0.05 to +0.25, largest for ruleinduce-001 which the docstring names as the case the change was made for
factors.acc_voted: ON higher, most for low-confidence voters
factors.aim: ON HIGHER than OFF for ruleinduce and routes; possibly lower for models whose base barely moves

expected_headline: the back-off wins on both accuracy and aim for at least 3 of 4 models, i.e. no trade
would_change_my_mind: if aim rises with the back-off OFF while accuracy falls, the trade is real and the TARGETING REGIME guard should fire on the pair -- which would be the guard doing its job on a real comparison rather than a constructed one. Either outcome is informative and they need opposite entries in HANDOVER.
cost_note: synth-001 dropped from this arm: it takes ~20 minutes to fit and its 1.02x is already understood as a base-accuracy consequence.

actual: THE TRADE IS REAL, for 2 of 4 models. ilp-001: back-off ON label_acc 0.312 / aim 1.37x, OFF 0.291 / 1.41x. syllogism-001: ON 0.146 / 1.09x, OFF 0.116 / 1.13x -- and OFF falls BELOW its 0.143 floor, so its $/solved-above-floor reads inf. ruleinduce-001: label_acc identical 0.329 both ways (the back-off helps abstained positions 0.003 -> 0.030 and hurts voted ones 0.397 -> 0.391, cancelling exactly), aim 1.45x on vs 1.49x off. routes-001: byte-identical both ways.
prediction_error: WRONG. I predicted the back-off would win BOTH axes for at least 3 of 4 on the reasoning that the base effect dominates. Measured 0/4 win both, 2/4 trade, 2/4 neutral. My state.yml claim that the two effects pull opposite ways was RIGHT, and this cycle's algebraic 'correction' of it was wrong -- the algebra was right in form and wrong on magnitudes.
interpretation: the back-off buys +0.021 and +0.030 label_acc and costs 0.04x of aim. Since aim is capped at 1.49x for these models and the accuracy difference is what puts syllogism above its floor at all, the accuracy column wins decisively. The trade exists and is economically one-sided.
belief_update: 3t's consequence -- strengthening the back-off lowers certifiability -- is TRUE and economically irrelevant. It costs 0.04x of a metric capped at 1.49x while buying the difference between beating the floor and reading inf.
instrument_finding: the TARGETING REGIME guard DID NOT FIRE on this table, because it compared the global aim winner against the global rate winner and ruleinduce-001 off held both. The inversions here are PAIRWISE within a model. Strengthened to find any inverted pair and report the sharpest; it now names ilp-001 bo-off (1.41x, rate 0.2907) above ilp-001 bo-on (1.37x, rate 0.3124). Third strengthening of a ratio guard this session, and the second found by using the instrument on real rows rather than by constructing a fixture.

hypothesis: Two settings this session produced the same form. Escalation: aim <= 1/(1 - accuracy). Maintenance: the oracle reached 1/f_stale = 131.6x. Both are 1/(fraction of cases that actually need the expensive path). If that is a LAW rather than a coincidence of two settings, it should retrodict every certification number the repo has measured -- including ones recorded in 3b before this session began.
the_law: ceiling = 1 / P(this case needs the expensive path); realised = ceiling x (1 - a_flagged)/(1 - a_needed) <= ceiling, with equality iff the certificate flags exactly the cases that need it.
test: for each certification number on disk -- witness verification 247x, maintenance 93x/72x, optimality 2.0x, the 13,987x full answer, escalation 4.69x, the curriculum models 1.02x-1.48x -- recover the underlying fraction and check the measured value does not exceed 1/fraction, and that the ORACLE rows attain it.
expected: the law holds as a CEILING everywhere (no measured value exceeds its 1/fraction), and the oracle rows attain it within rounding. Where a measured value sits far below, the gap should equal the certificate's over-approximation, which was measured independently at 8.2x for the XOR bound and 2.3x for |delta count|.
would_change_my_mind: any measured advantage EXCEEDING 1/fraction breaks it outright -- that would mean certification buys more than the work it avoids, which should be impossible. A large unexplained gap on a row whose over-approximation is known would mean the realised form is wrong even if the ceiling holds.
why_this_and_not_accuracy: state.yml names raising curriculum accuracy as the next action, but that is the repo's oldest question and CLAUDE.md deprioritises moving a model up the existing table. This costs one script over numbers already on disk and either promotes the law toward RESEARCH_LOG.md or kills it.

actual: The unification holds and is ALGEBRA, not a measurement. realised = recall/f_flagged, ceiling = 1/f_needed, attained iff precision = recall = 1. 3b's advantage = min(compute/check, 1/P_hit) is the sound case. Across 12 rows the worst error is 1.2% -- but 7 of them are IDENTITIES that reproduce the definitions their own inputs came from. Only 5 rows are independent (measured from timings and USD, predicted from invalidation counts): 3b's four witness rows and the one maintenance class where the 1/P term binds. Worst independent error 1.2%. No arm exceeds its ceiling.
the_near_miss: the first version of this script presented all 12 rows as confirmations and reported '1.2% worst error across 11 arms spanning five orders of magnitude'. For maintenance, aim = (1-base)/(flagged x (1-base)) = 1/f_flagged BY CONSTRUCTION; for the curriculum rows predicted rearranges to (1 - a_abstained)/(1 - base), which is the expression aim was computed from. I nearly published a tautology as a validation, and the 1.2% was rounding in hand-entered constants.
prediction_error: the ceiling claim survives (nothing exceeds 1/f_needed) but the TEST I designed could not have falsified it for 7 of 12 rows. That is a design failure, not a magnitude error.
belief_update: the contribution is a DERIVATION -- escalation targeting and certificate maintenance are one expression, and the achievable ceiling is 1/f_needed rather than 3b's 1/f_flagged, the two differing by the certificate's over-approximation. The empirical content was already 3b's. Labelled accordingly rather than promoted.
status: NOT promoted to RESEARCH_LOG.md. A derivation with one pre-existing empirical anchor is not a finding that something independent has tried to break.

hypothesis: APPROACH.md names five properties a reportable benchmark needs and says work moving toward them outranks work moving a model up the existing table. Four of the five ALREADY EXIST in symbolic_ai_models/agent.py: episode-level verdicts (CurriculumReport, n=1432), whole-continuation scoring with no true prefix, and a floor that is max(uniform, per-lesson majority, best parameter-free shortcut) -- literally 'a floor built from every feature the model sees'. What is missing is that NO MODEL HAS EVER BEEN RUN THROUGH IT. runs/agents-full179 contains only five baseline policies, and the best of them beats the floor by +0.0009.
the_question: does any model in this repo beat the episode-level floor of ~0.264?
mechanism: position-level label_acc runs 0.19-0.36 against a 0.143 floor, which is a real lift. But an episode-level verdict requires ranking whole answer strings, and rule-based models predict labels at masked graph nodes rather than scoring free text -- their text path may abstain entirely, leaving uniform logits and an effectively random choice.
expected_magnitude: most rule-based models land within +-0.02 of the 0.264 floor; at most one or two show a lift above +0.03; none exceeds +0.10
would_change_my_mind: a model with a lift above +0.10 would mean the episode-level benchmark is already discriminating and the repo has an unreported capability result. Alternatively, if score_choices ERRORS for rule-based models, the answer is that the episode-level benchmark cannot score them at all -- a different and more actionable finding about the instrument.
why_this_over_the_alternatives: it is the work APPROACH.md ranks first, it needs no new benchmark, and the number it produces -- an episode-level verdict against a shortcut-aware floor -- is the one the repo says it wants to report and does not have.

hypothesis: The flood pipeline needs a near-perfect reader -- losing 1 claim in 6 puts it at a non-reasoning floor -- and the only reader is a regex template matched to the generator's own phrasings. corrupt() perturbs the recovered WORLD; nothing perturbs the TEXT. So the front's real starting point is: what does recovery do when the surface changes but the world does not?
mechanism: each claim kind is recovered by one regex keyed to one phrasing. A paraphrase that moves a single word ('posted at' -> 'limited to', 'unladen mass' -> 'kerb weight') takes that regex to zero recall for the whole kind at once. Recovery should therefore be a STEP function in the number of paraphrased kinds, not a curve in a paraphrase rate.
expected_direction: reader recall collapses per-kind and all-or-nothing; end-to-end answer accuracy hits the floor as soon as one important kind is paraphrased
expected_magnitude: paraphrasing any ONE of load_limit / flooded / mass / capacity should drop exact-set accuracy to at or near the 0.333-0.383 floor region the fidelity table shows at p>=0.20, because losing a whole kind is a 100% drop rate for that kind
would_change_my_mind: graceful degradation under paraphrase would mean the regexes overlap enough to be robust, which I do not believe. A more interesting refutation: if paraphrasing 'link' barely matters while paraphrasing 'flooded' is fatal, the ORDERING differs from the dropout ordering the fidelity finding measured -- and that finding says its ordering prediction was wrong, so the two channels disagreeing would be worth knowing.
why_this_first: it is the honest zero of the new front. Every later reader is measured against it, and it costs one text-side channel that the repo does not have and needs anyway.

derived: S = F + (1-F) q^k fitted to the existing parse-fidelity sweep: k = 9.35, F = 0.338, rmse 0.0151 against a reported +-0.029 at N=300, largest residual +0.037.
correction_forced: the finding read its own curve as 'roughly >= 90% per-claim recall'. Solving the fitted law, q=0.90 buys S=0.585 -- barely above that pipeline's strongest floor of 0.450. Reaching S=0.90 needs q=0.9826, a 6x smaller allowed error rate.
decomposition: k is additive across claim kinds: mass 2.31, capacity 2.16, link 1.61, demand 0.73, load_limit 0.68, flooded 0.28, sum 7.77 against aggregate 9.35 (17% gap). Entity attributes carry ~8x the leverage of the flooding relation.
strategic: S is more sensitive to k than the sweep suggests -- at q=0.95, halving k from 9.35 to 4.7 moves S from 0.66 to 0.85. Anything that reduces how many claims the answer depends on is worth as much as a much better reader, which argues for emitting ambiguity and letting kernels bound over it rather than for a bigger parser.
epistemic_status: empirical scaling law. Two parameters, ten points, one domain, one metric. q^k assumes independent losses and equally-necessary claims; the 17% sum-vs-aggregate gap is where that assumption pays.
next_test: does fitted k equal the answer's dependency size, which the certificate machinery measures directly? Agreement promotes it toward a mechanistic model; disagreement kills it.

hypothesis: The reader survival law S = F + (1-F)q^k fitted k = 9.35 to the flood pipeline. If k is a real COUNT of answer-critical claims rather than a fitted constant, it should match the dependency size measured directly by single-claim ablation: drop each claim, re-solve, count how many change the answer. Agreement promotes the law from an empirical scaling law toward a mechanistic model and makes required recall PREDICTABLE for a new task without sweeping it.
refinement_registered_before_running: the law fits E[q^d] across cases, and by Jensen E[q^d] >= q^E[d] whenever d varies. So fitted k should come out BELOW mean d, with the gap growing in Var(d). k = E[d] exactly only if d is constant across cases. This is a directional prediction that a naive 'k should equal d' would miss.
expected_magnitude: mean d in 10-14 (28 claims per world: 3 mass, 3 capacity, 8 link, 5 load_limit, 5 bridge_on, 1 each flooded/depot/needs/demand, of which many are non-binding); fitted k = 9.35 should sit below mean d by 10-30%
expected_per_kind: the per-kind k from the law -- mass 2.31, capacity 2.16, link 1.61, demand 0.73, load_limit 0.68, flooded 0.28 -- should track the per-kind ablation counts in the same ORDER, with mass and capacity near their full counts of 3 and load_limit far below its count of 5
would_change_my_mind: mean d far above k (say > 2x) means most claims are individually critical but the law's exponent is much smaller, so q^k is not counting claims and the fit is coincidence. Mean d BELOW k would be worse -- it would mean the answer depends on fewer claims than the exponent, which the independence model cannot produce, and the law would be dead.
cost: about 40 cases x 29 solves; the fidelity sweep did 3,000 solves so this is cheaper.

actual: mean d = 6.95 (sd 4.74, min 0, max 15) over 40 cases with 28.5 claims each. k_eff from the measured d distribution = 5.76 against fitted k = 9.35, a 38.3% gap. The population is bimodal: many cases have an EMPTY answer set and d ~ 2.
prediction_error: I predicted mean d in 10-14 and fitted k BELOW mean d by Jensen. Measured mean d = 6.95 and fitted k is ABOVE both mean d and k_eff. Wrong on magnitude and wrong on direction.
interpretation_to_test: single-claim ablation counts only claims that individually move the answer. Under random dropping several go at once, so pairs that are individually harmless and jointly fatal are invisible to ablation. That would make d a LOWER bound on the effective exponent and explain k > k_eff. Not yet established -- the alternative is a population difference, since the sweep used 300 seeds and exact-set while this used 40.
next: run the drop sweep on the SAME 40 cases and fit k directly, so the comparison is like-for-like and the interaction effect is isolated from any population difference.

actual: PROMOTED, after the first verdict was wrong. Same-population sweep: all 40 cases fit k=5.71 F=0.400 rmse 0.072; NON-EMPTY answers only fit k=8.31 F=0.014 rmse 0.018. Interaction effect -0.9% -- ablation k_eff (5.76) matches same-population fitted k (5.71). Empty-answer share 0.450 against all-cases fitted floor 0.400, and against the published 'strongest floor' of 0.450.
the_correction: the published parse-fidelity floor is NOT a reasoning baseline -- it is the fraction of cases whose correct answer is the empty set, which survive any corruption for free. On cases with a real answer the pipeline is a pure power law with NO floor, decaying to 0.018 at q=0.5. Required recall on real cases is q=0.987 for 90% success, and q=0.90 answers only 41% of them.
prediction_error: I predicted mean d 10-14 and fitted k below mean d by Jensen. Pooled mean d = 6.95 (below range) because 45% of cases have an empty answer. On non-empty cases mean d = 11.05, inside the predicted range, and fitted k = 8.31 IS below it as predicted. The first script's KILLED verdict compared across populations and was wrong.
status_change: empirical_scaling_law -> mechanistic_model. Both parameters now have referents: k is the ablation-measured dependency size, F is the corruption-proof case share. Accuracy ~30%, not 1% -- the pooled 0.9% agreement is two component errors cancelling and must not be quoted as precision.
strategic: report the two populations separately; a pooled score on this task is 45% a measure of case mix. And k is measurable per task WITHOUT a sweep, so required recall for a new domain can be computed before its reader is built.
