hypothesis: The template reader's regexes are keyed to the old report's phrasings. On the new five-paragraph surface it should recover essentially nothing, and what it does recover should be a DISTRACTOR: _LINK matches '(region_d) to (region_d)' and the only surviving 'X to Y' phrasing is 'A disused track once ran from region_88 to region_94', between two regions that are not in the world at all.
expected_claim_precision: near 0 -- the one match is spurious
expected_end_to_end: POOLED accuracy near 0.45 and NON-EMPTY accuracy near 0.00. The pooled number is the empty-answer share from the previous finding: a reader that recovers nothing still 'gets' every case whose correct answer is the empty set.
would_change_my_mind: pooled accuracy near 0 would mean the flow errors rather than returning empty on a degenerate world, which changes what 'no reader' scores and hence the floor every arm is measured against. Recall above 0.2 would mean the surface is not as different as intended and needs to be harder.
why_it_matters: this is the concrete demonstration that a pooled score on this task is 45% case mix. If the template reader scores 0.45 while recovering one spurious claim, no reader arm can be reported on the pooled metric again.

actual: claim P 0.000, claim R 0.000, dependency recall 0.000, pooled accuracy 0.450, non-empty accuracy 0.000 -- IDENTICAL to a world with no claims at all. The oracle world and the template reader on the OLD report both score 1.000/1.000.
prediction_error: none. Predicted recall below 0.05, precision near 0, pooled near 0.45 and non-empty near 0.00; measured 0.000/0.000/0.450/0.000.
interpretation: the repo's only reader recovers 100% of the world from one surface and 0% of the same worlds from another. That is what 'a template reader proves nothing about parsing' means as a number, and it is the honest zero of the text->world front.
operational_consequence: the pooled metric is dead on this task -- it cannot distinguish a reader that recovers nothing from having no reader. Every arm from here is reported on the non-empty column. This is the previous finding's 45%-case-mix point demonstrated rather than argued.

hypothesis: A deterministic reader written FOR this surface should reach the oracle, and its ablations price the two mechanisms the surface was built to require. Coreference carries three claims per case -- the pronoun load_limit ('it is now rated for N'), the pronoun capacity ('It can take a further N'), and the demand ('It is for N kg of supplies'). Distractor rejection is carried by pattern specificity: 'is rated for' vs 'was rated at', 'weighs N kg empty' vs 'is committed elsewhere', 'joined by a surfaced road' vs 'once ran from'.

expected.rules_full: claim R 1.000, non-empty accuracy 1.000 -- if it does not reach the oracle the surface is unfair, not hard
expected.rules_no_coref: loses 3 of ~28 claims so global recall ~0.89, but one of them is the DEMAND, which the dependency ablation found critical in 55% of cases, and one is a CAPACITY (k_kind 2.16). Non-empty accuracy 0.20-0.50, far below what 0.89 global recall would suggest.
expected.rules_greedy: precision falls as distractor links and the superseded limit are admitted; false links open routes that do not exist, so non-empty accuracy 0.30-0.70
expected.lexical_retrieval: a genuinely different mechanism -- match each sentence to the claim template with highest lexical overlap. Recall 0.5-0.8, precision lower, non-empty accuracy 0.1-0.4

the_law_test: this is the first PREDICTIVE use of the survival law. no-coref has global recall ~0.89 but its DEPENDENCY-weighted recall should be much lower, and the law says end-to-end success tracks the dependency-weighted number, not the global one. If non-empty accuracy for no-coref lands near q_dep^k rather than q_global^k, the law earns its keep.
would_change_my_mind: rules_full below 1.000 means the surface states something the reader cannot recover and the alignment is lying. no_coref scoring near rules_full would mean the three pronoun-mediated claims do not matter, and the surface is not exercising reference resolution.

actual: non-empty accuracy: oracle 1.000; rules-full 1.000; rules-no-coref 0.000; rules-distractors-admitted 0.682; lexical cue routing 0.136; template 0.000. Global claim recall for no-coref is 0.895 and dependency recall 0.835.
prediction_error: rules_full predicted 1.000 -- it first measured 0.682 and my stated criterion was 'if it does not reach the oracle the surface is unfair'. It was: the naming sentence said 'X is the lightest' while the capacity after it belonged to the first vehicle by id, so the TEXT asserted something false. Fixed, and the arm then hit 1.000 exactly. no_coref predicted 0.20-0.50, measured 0.000 -- I under-predicted the severity because I did not notice the demand is pronoun-stated in EVERY case. distractors predicted 0.30-0.70, measured 0.682. lexical predicted 0.1-0.4, measured 0.136.
the_law_test: FLAT LAW FAILS. q^k with k=8.31 predicts 0.222 for the no-coref arm and the truth is 0.000 -- no single-q model can produce a zero from 84% recall, because it assumes losses are exchangeable and readers lose whole KINDS. The per-kind product S = prod q_kind^d_kind gets that exactly, but moves mean error only 0.137 -> 0.116 and still over-predicts the lexical arm 3.5x (0.476 vs 0.136).
status_change: reader_survival DEMOTED from mechanistic_model to screen_not_predictor, superseded by the per-kind form. Use it to rule out arms that lose a kind; do not forecast a number with it.
answered: is reference resolution more important than semantic parsing? On this task, decisively yes -- the parsing was already perfect and the system answered nothing.

hypothesis: Arm 1 reaching 1.000 proves the surface is FAIR and nothing about reading -- I wrote its patterns for that exact phrasing, so it is arm 0 for a different template, the same artefact read.py's own docstring warns about. The discriminating measurement is a generalisation curve: give each claim kind V alternative phrasings, draw one per case deterministically, and evaluate readers whose patterns were written against variant 0 only.
mechanism: a pattern set keyed to one phrasing recovers roughly 1/V of each kind as V grows. By the per-kind law a kind whose recall falls sends the product toward zero, so end-to-end accuracy should collapse much faster than recall does.

expected.rules_V2: global recall ~0.6-0.7, non-empty accuracy 0.0-0.15 -- the demand and capacity kinds are pronoun/pattern bound and losing either in half of cases is fatal
expected.lexical: degrades more gracefully than rules IF cue words survive paraphrase, but I am deliberately varying the cue words too (weighs / kerb weight / unladen), so I expect it to collapse as well -- just less steeply, maybe 2x the accuracy of rules at V=4

the_real_question: does ANY hand-authored mechanism survive surface variation? If both collapse, that is a strong negative result and the argument for a learned or retrieval-based reader is made by measurement rather than by assertion.
would_change_my_mind: lexical holding above 0.5 at V=4 would mean cue-word routing genuinely generalises and hand-authored readers are viable; rules holding up would mean my variants are not real paraphrases.

actual: rules arm: V=1 recall 1.000 acc 1.000; V=2 recall 0.542 acc 0.000; V=3 recall 0.362 acc 0.000; V=4 recall 0.280 acc 0.000. lexical arm: V=1 acc 0.136; V=2 onward acc 0.000. Alignment complete at every V.
prediction_error: qualitative prediction CONFIRMED -- both collapse and nothing survives at V=4. Magnitudes: predicted rules V=2 recall 0.6-0.7 (actual 0.542, below) and accuracy 0.0-0.15 (actual 0.000); predicted V=4 recall 0.35-0.45 (actual 0.280, below). I predicted lexical would hold roughly 2x rules at V=4; both are exactly 0.000.
law_confirmation: the PER-KIND law's first clean predictive success. One pattern set against V phrasings gives q_kind = 1/V for every kind, so S ~ V^-6.95 using the ablation-measured mean dependency: 0.008 at V=2 against a measured 0.000 over 22 non-empty cases. Its failure mode is now characterised rather than vague -- it works on pure recall loss and over-predicts when claims are recovered with the WRONG VALUE.
result: no hand-authored reader survives the words changing. The argument for a learned or retrieval-based reader is a measurement now, not an assertion. And the benchmark has full 0->1 headroom at V>=2.
self_criticism_that_prompted_it: arm 1 reaching 1.000 proved the surface fair and nothing about reading -- I wrote its patterns for that phrasing, reproducing the artefact read.py's own docstring warns about.

hypothesis: Both failed arms were LEXICAL -- they keyed on words, and the words vary. A reader can instead key on the TYPE SIGNATURE of what a sentence mentions (how many regions, how many vehicles, how many quantities) plus its paragraph position, which the world IR gives for free and which paraphrase does not change. That should be near-invariant to phrasing by construction.
the_signature_analysis: signatures alone are ambiguous: (2 regions, 0 qty) is link OR bridge_on; (1 truck, 1 qty) is mass OR capacity; (1 region, 0 qty) is flooded OR depot OR needs. Paragraph position resolves all but link/bridge_on, and THAT resolves because every bridge in the generator carries a load_limit -- so the bridge pairs are exactly the pairs appearing in the quantities paragraph, and links are the pairs in the infrastructure paragraph.

expected_V4.claim_recall: 0.85-0.98 -- the mechanism is phrasing-invariant, so V should barely matter
expected_V4.precision: 0.80-0.95 -- the disused-track distractor has signature (2 regions, 0 qty) in the infrastructure paragraph and will be read as a link

expected_V1_vs_V4: nearly flat, unlike rules (1.000 -> 0.000) and lexical (0.136 -> 0.000). Flatness is the claim; the absolute level is secondary.
would_change_my_mind: a large V1->V4 drop would mean the signature still leaks lexical dependence somewhere. Recall below 0.6 at any V would mean position is not as informative as the paragraph structure suggests -- possible, since the pronoun capacity and the demand both have signature (0 entities, 1 quantity) and are separated only by which paragraph they sit in.
note: this also sets up the ambiguity question: where the signature genuinely cannot decide, the right move per the critical invariant is to EMIT the ambiguity rather than collapse it, and see whether the kernels can bound over it.

actual: EXACTLY FLAT across V: claim recall 0.971, dependency recall 0.946, non-empty accuracy 0.318 at V=1,2,3,4 to three decimals. At V>=2 it is the only reader above zero (rules 0.000, lexical 0.000).
prediction_error: recall predicted 0.85-0.98, measured 0.971 (in range). Flatness predicted and confirmed exactly. Accuracy predicted 0.4-0.8, measured 0.318 (below range).
failure_diagnosis: ONE mechanism. capacity recall 0.725 (33 of 120 missing, 0 spurious); every other kind recall 1.000 with zero spurious, except one spurious link per case from the disused-track distractor. The pronoun 'It can take a further N kg' attaches by RECENCY but its antecedent is named by a SUPERLATIVE ('X is the lightest of them'), so recency picks the last vehicle in the roster and the lightest loses its capacity, dropping out of the fleet.
boundary_found: type signature + paragraph position recover every claim whose role is fixed by what it mentions and where it sits, and stop exactly at reference mediated by MEANING. A rule for 'lightest' is lexical and dies under paraphrase (smallest, least heavy) exactly as the pattern arm did -- so this is the first place in the front where a lexical resource or a learned component is the only mechanism available rather than a shortcut.
regime: crossover. Hand-authored wins 1.000 vs 0.318 on a fixed surface; signature wins the moment the surface varies at all.
law_note: per-kind law predicts 0.725^1.20 = 0.673 from capacity recall alone against a measured 0.318 -- the same over-prediction it shows whenever loss is structured rather than exchangeable, since a missing ATTRIBUTE removes an entity from the answer's domain.

hypothesis: The signature reader resolves its ambiguities using paragraph POSITION, which is a property of this generator's template. Ablate position and the ambiguities become real: (1 vehicle, 1 qty) is mass OR capacity, (1 region, 0 qty) is flooded OR depot OR needs, (0 entities, 1 qty) is pronoun-capacity OR demand. The critical invariant says the reader should EMIT that ambiguity and let the kernels bound over it rather than guess. This measures whether the bound is tight enough to be worth having.
the_ambiguity_is_bounded: link vs bridge_on resolves STRUCTURALLY even without position, because bridge pairs are exactly the pairs carrying a load limit. What remains is per-vehicle role assignment (2 readings x 3 trucks = 8), the three single-region roles (3! = 6), and the bare-quantity pair (2) -- about 96 candidate worlds, which is enumerable.

expected.collapse_by_prior: 0.0-0.15 non-empty accuracy. Swapping a mass for a capacity is fatal: it changes both which vehicles exist and what they can carry.
expected.bound_soundness: 1.000 by construction -- the true answer must lie inside the enumeration, and if it does not the reader is unsound and that is a bug not a finding
expected.bound_width: the interesting number. If most vehicles come out UNDETERMINED the bound is vacuous and preserving ambiguity buys nothing here; if certainly-in plus certainly-out covers most vehicles, ambiguity beats guessing.

expected_width: 1-2 undetermined vehicles of 3, i.e. partially informative but not decisive
would_change_my_mind: a vacuous bound (all vehicles undetermined in most cases) would mean the critical invariant is right in principle and worthless at this ambiguity level, which is a genuine negative worth publishing. A tight bound would make emitting ambiguity strictly better than guessing and would be the first measured argument for the world IR carrying alternatives.

actual: Position fully ablated: collapse 0.250 exact-set accuracy; bound 1.000 sound and decides 0.0% of the fleet over 72 worlds. Regime sweep: vehicle alone 4 worlds decides 75.8%; bare alone 2 worlds decides 45.5%; region alone 9 worlds decides 36.4%; region+bare 18 worlds decides 4.5%. Soundness 1.000 on every row.
prediction_error: I predicted the bound would leave 1-2 of 3 vehicles undetermined and be 'partially informative'. At full ablation it leaves 3.00 of 3 -- completely vacuous, worse than predicted. The regime sweep was not predicted at all and is where the result is.
two_results: (1) carrying ambiguity is always sound and rapidly vacuous -- useful only up to 4 worlds, nothing at 72, and 72 worlds is computationally trivial, so the bound dies long before enumeration gets hard. (2) decidedness is NOT a function of world count: 2 worlds of 'bare' decide less than 4 worlds of 'vehicle'. An ambiguity budget cannot be counted in worlds.
the_expensive_ambiguity: 'bare' -- which number is the DEMAND. Same claim this session keeps finding critical: pronoun-stated, its loss took the no-coreference arm to 0.000, and being merely unsure about it costs more per world than any other ambiguity here.
invariant_verdict: right and not sufficient. Never collapsing is free soundness; soundness alone is not actionable. The design consequence is to carry ambiguity AND spend reader effort on the distinctions whose ambiguity is expensive, which is measurable per group before the reader exists.
bugs_caught_by_the_soundness_check: two, both of which would have produced publishable-looking numbers. The enumeration dropped leftover bare quantities so one vehicle had no capacity in every world (unsound on 19 of 22). And it assumed exactly one flooded region while the generator can flood two, making the true assignment unreachable on seed 25 (sound on 21 of 22 -- a near-miss that reads as noise).

hypothesis: The reader machinery -- type-signature routing plus section position, exact span->claim alignment, and the arm harness -- should transfer to a structurally opposite task. Solvency has no routing, no subset answer, a trivial kernel, and a bitemporal core. If signature routing works here too, the approach is architectural rather than a flood trick.
the_sharp_transfer_test: in flood a superseded value was a DISTRACTOR and 'take the latest number' was correct. In solvency the revision is the substance and 'take the latest' is exactly WRONG, because a figure filed after the decision date was not knowable. The same surface feature is a trap in one domain and the answer in the other, so a flood-derived heuristic arm should MISFIRE here and by a measurable amount.

expected.signature_reader: accuracy 0.85-1.00 -- the signatures are cleaner here than in flood (2 members = owns; 1 member + 1 USD + 1 date = revenue; 1 USD alone = threshold; 1 date alone = decision date), with no coreference at all
expected.flood_heuristic_latest: substantially worse -- it uses post-decision revisions. Magnitude depends on how often the latest filing crosses the threshold boundary; I expect 0.5-0.75
expected.ignore_dates_first_filed: also wrong but differently -- it misses legitimate pre-decision revisions

expected_floor: majority-class baseline; solvency answers are boolean so the floor is high, likely 0.5-0.7, and any arm must be read against it
would_change_my_mind: if the signature reader needs domain-specific hackery to work here, the approach does not transfer and the flood result was a template in disguise. If the flood heuristic scores the SAME as the date-aware reader, the bitemporal trap is not actually load-bearing in this generator and the transfer test is vacuous.

actual: signature reader 1.000 at V=1,2,3,4; flood's latest-value rule 0.850 at every V; first-filed 0.900; majority-class floor 0.583. Filing recall 1.000 for ALL arms at V=4.
prediction_error: signature predicted 0.85-1.00, measured 1.000 (top of range). Flood heuristic predicted 0.5-0.75, measured 0.850 -- I over-predicted the damage. Floor predicted 0.5-0.7, measured 0.583.
the_result: the machinery transfers and the heuristic inverts. Type-signature routing, exact span->claim alignment, the variant sweep and the arm harness all carried over unmodified to a task with no routing, no subset answer and no coreference. But 'take the latest value', correct in flood where a revision supersedes, costs 0.150 here where the question is what was KNOWABLE.
the_sharpest_part: filing recall is 1.000 for every arm, so the 15-point gap is not extraction at all -- it is entirely how transaction_time is used. A representation carrying transaction time gets this right; one carrying only values cannot, however good the extraction. That is the strongest argument the world IR has been given, and it came from a task chosen to be structurally opposite to the one it was exercised on.
honest_caveat: solvency is EASIER for a reader than flood -- no coreference, cleaner signatures, no withheld entity ids. 1.000 claims the machinery transfers, not that the tasks are of equal difficulty.
consequence: the temporal policy is hand-written per domain just as the flood rule was, which argues the reader should EMIT the time and let a kernel decide rather than resolving it itself.

hypothesis: The reader survival law S = F + (1-F)q^k was derived on flood and its two parameters were given referents there: F is the share of cases whose answer is corruption-proof, k is the ablation-measured dependency size. If those referents are real rather than flood-specific, both should predict solvency BEFORE the sweep is run.
the_generalisation_of_F: in flood the degenerate answer (no claims recovered) is the EMPTY SET, and F was the share of cases whose true answer is empty. In solvency the degenerate answer is FALSE, because with no filings the total is 0 and decide returns not-cleared. So the general form is F = P(truth == degenerate answer), and here that is the False-share, measured at 35/60 = 0.583.
expected_F: 0.583 +- 0.05, and it should coincide with the majority-class floor only because the degenerate answer happens to BE the majority class in this generator
expected_k: MUCH smaller than flood's 8.31. The verdict is a sum against a threshold, so dropping one filing flips it only if that filing straddles the boundary. I predict ablation-measured mean dependency d of 1-3 and a fitted k in the same range, giving a SHALLOW survival curve where flood's was steep.
why_this_is_the_test: a law whose parameters are refitted per domain explains nothing. If F is predictable from the degenerate answer and k from ablation, both WITHOUT the sweep, the law transfers. If k has to be refitted, it is a curve-fit with a story.
would_change_my_mind: F far from 0.583 kills the degenerate-answer referent. A fitted k far from the ablation d kills the dependency referent -- and on flood that agreement was only good to ~30%, so a second domain agreeing poorly would mean the k referent never held.
note: solvency ships CORRUPTIONS already (drop_owns, drop_filing, misread_value, drop_period, drop_publication_date), so the sweep needs no new corruption machinery.

actual: BOTH PARAMETERS TRANSFER. F predicted 0.583 from the degenerate answer with no corruption, fitted 0.590 -- 1.1% error, and the curve asymptotes to 0.583 exactly at p=0.50 and p=0.80. k predicted 8.25 from ablation on the non-trivial population, fitted 9.92 -- 20.2% error, better than flood's own 31%. rmse 0.0070.
the_clean_part: the trivial population has dependency EXACTLY 0.00 on all 35 not-cleared cases -- not approximately zero. F and k describe two disjoint populations rather than two knobs on one curve, and it is cleaner here than in flood where the empty-answer cases still had d=1.94.
prediction_error: F correct. k BACKWARDS: I predicted 1-3, reasoning that a sum against a threshold makes single terms non-decisive. It is 9.92, slightly larger than flood's 8.31 -- to CLEAR a threshold every contributing filing matters, and the reasoning I used holds only for cases that fail, which are exactly the ones in F.
error_i_repeated: computed k_eff over the POOLED population first, got 2.06 against 9.92 and printed 'k does NOT transfer' at 381%. Same error as flood. The tell was printed and I read past it twice: mean 3.48 with sd 4.15 and min 0 is visibly bimodal.
mechanism_i_tested_and_rejected: hypothesised interactions -- pairs harmless alone and fatal together. Measured pair survival 0.589 against an independence prediction of 0.606, gap +0.016. NO interaction effect. Testing it instead of asserting it is what forced the population reading.
consequence: required reader recall is now computable for a NEW domain with no sweep: run the kernels on an empty world for F, ablate single claims on the non-trivial cases for k.

hypothesis: Scheduling has something neither previous domain had: a tunable decision margin (slack). So the question is not 'does the law hold a third time' -- which I could largely write up in advance -- but 'what governs its parameters'. If F = P(truth == degenerate answer) is a real referent, then sweeping slack should move F in a way that is predictable WITHOUT any corruption sweep, because slack directly controls the feasible share.
degenerate_answer: with no claims there are no jobs, so every job is vacuously assignable and the ASP kernel should return feasible = True. So F should equal the FEASIBLE SHARE at each slack, measurable by generating cases and reading .feasible.
expected_F_by_slack: F rises monotonically with slack, from well below 0.5 at slack 0.05 to near 1.0 at slack 0.5, and at each setting the fitted asymptote should match the feasible share to within a few points
expected_k: k is the ablation dependency on the NON-TRIVIAL population -- here the INFEASIBLE cases, since degenerate is True. Predicted to RISE as slack tightens: at large slack an infeasible case is infeasible for one blunt reason (a capability nobody has) and few claims matter; at tight slack it is infeasible by a narrow margin and nearly every duration and capacity matters.
would_change_my_mind: F not tracking the feasible share kills the referent on its first parametric test. k FALLING as slack tightens would mean my account of what makes a case non-trivial is backwards -- which has already happened once this week on solvency, where I predicted k small and it was large.
note: the degenerate answer being TRUE rather than the empty set or FALSE is itself the test of the generalisation: F is defined by whatever the kernels say on an empty world, not by any particular value.

actual: F's REFERENT survives its third domain: the degenerate answer on an empty world is True here (empty set in flood, False in solvency), and at p=1.0 accuracy is exactly the feasible share -- 0.850 at slack 0.60. But the law's monotone FORM fails: the corruption curve is U-shaped (slack 0.30: 0.575, 0.400, 0.375, 0.575, 1.000), rmse 0.08 against solvency's 0.007, and the fit reports F = 0.593 where the true value is 0.850.
the_mechanism_measured: P(answer=True) by channel at slack 0.30. Dropping JOB claims (duration, needs_capability) rises monotonically 0.575 -> 1.000; dropping MACHINE claims (capacity, has_capability) falls monotonically 0.575 -> 0.000. Each channel alone is monotone and they run in OPPOSITE directions; the U is their superposition, supply dominating in the middle and demand winning at the limit.
the_scope_result: the law's precondition is that every claim is evidence in the SAME direction for the answer. Flood and solvency satisfy it -- losing a claim only ever destroys the answer. Scheduling mixes demand and supply and does not. Checkable before any sweep by dropping each claim kind alone.
prediction_error: I predicted F would track the slack knob AND be recoverable from the fit. It tracks the knob as a referent and is NOT recoverable from the fit, because the fit is of the wrong shape -- my prediction conflated the parameter with the fitted value, which is exactly the distinction the result turns on. My k prediction is unanswerable rather than wrong: a fitted k on a U-shaped curve means nothing.
why_better_than_confirmation: the law now has a stated scope and a task outside it, rather than three agreements and unknown limits.

hypothesis: The scheduling corruption curve is U-shaped because job claims and machine claims are opposite-signed evidence. Rather than fit a two-term curve, DERIVE it. An instance reads feasible iff every surviving job has a capable surviving machine. A job is a constraint only if both its claims survive: probability (1-p)^2. A job becomes unsatisfiable only if ALL m_j machines carrying its capability lose it: probability p^m_j. Assuming independence across jobs, P(answer=True | p) = prod_j [1 - (1-p)^2 p^m_j].
why_this_is_the_right_kind_of_model: every quantity in it is STRUCTURAL and read off the world -- m_j is the capability multiplicity for job j -- so there is nothing to fit. It predicts the U by construction: the product goes to 1 at p=0 (no capability lost) and to 1 at p=1 (no job survives as a constraint), and dips where (1-p)^2 p^m is largest.
expected: predicted A(p) within 0.10 of measured at every p on the slack 0.30 population, with the minimum located within one grid step. The shape should be right even where the level is off.
known_omission: the model ignores CAPACITY entirely and models only capability. At slack 0.30 there is 30% spare capacity so capability should be the binding constraint, but at tight slack the model should degrade -- that is a prediction too, and a discriminating one.
would_change_my_mind: a predicted curve that is monotone, or whose minimum is in the wrong place, would mean the demand/supply account is wrong rather than incomplete. A good fit at slack 0.30 that does NOT degrade at slack 0.05 would mean capacity never binds and the generator's margin knob does something other than what its docstring says.

actual: The derived form works on originally-feasible cases: mean |err| 0.070 (slack 0.30, n=29) and 0.069 (slack 0.60, n=47), both endpoints exact, trough located, 0.751 predicted against 0.750 measured at p=0.1. Nothing fitted.
the_correction: my first derivation had a machine survive with (1-p), modelling only capability loss. Right shape, HALF the depth -- trough 0.678 against a measured 0.336, mean |err| 0.234 and 0.172. A machine also needs its CAPACITY claim to be usable; requiring both takes mean error to 0.070/0.069, a 2.5x improvement from one exponent, predicted from structure rather than fitted to the residual.
prediction_error: I predicted within 0.10 at every p and got 0.069-0.070 mean -- but only AFTER the correction, and only CONDITIONED on originally-feasible cases. Unconditionally the model is badly wrong (mean |err| 0.319) because it says every case is feasible at p=0 and 42.5% are not. My stated omission -- 'ignores capacity' -- turned out to be two distinct omissions: capacity as a machine-usability claim (fixed, worth 2.5x) and capacity as a binding constraint on the original instance (not fixed, co-dominant).
status: derived mechanistic model, unfitted, scope stated: predicts how corruption moves a FEASIBLE instance, not which instances are feasible.
residual: largest at p=0.8 (0.527 measured vs 0.799 derived), which is where few machines survive and job competition is strongest -- consistent with independence-across-jobs being the assumption that pays.

hypothesis: The boxed pipeline is text -> world IR -> multi-kernel flow -> structured output + TEXT, and the last box is unbuilt. A renderer is only worth having if its output is CHECKABLE, so the design commitment is that every factual assertion in the paragraph carries a citation to a claim or a kernel output, and an unsupported assertion is detectable mechanically.
design: render_answer(case, answer, outputs) -> Answer with .text, .citations and .structured. The structured answer stays canonical and the paragraph is strictly downstream, so generation quality cannot contaminate reasoning evaluation -- that separation is the point, not a nicety.
what_makes_it_non_trivial: the interesting paragraph is the NEGATIVE one. 'No vehicle can make the delivery' is easy; saying WHY -- which vehicle failed on which crossing at what laden mass -- requires reading the load_report and the load_limit claims together, and it is where an ungrounded renderer would invent a reason.
expected: groundedness 1.000 by construction on both answer polarities, and a deliberately corrupted renderer (asserting a limit that is not in the world) caught by the checker. The real test is whether the checker can FAIL -- a groundedness metric that cannot detect an invented fact measures nothing.
would_change_my_mind: if the flow's outputs do not carry enough to explain a NEGATIVE answer -- if load_report only reports successes -- then the renderer can state the verdict and not the reason, and grounded explanation needs kernel changes rather than a renderer.

actual: Built. 40/40 flood cases fully grounded, both polarities explained. 8 tests, three of which exist to make the checker FAIL: an invented quantity, an invented entity, and a false ordering of real regions -- all caught.
two_false_assertions_the_checker_caught_: (1) a false route ORDERING: the flow reports a route as an unordered edge SET, and my first version printed endpoints in list order, producing 'region_0 to region_3 to region_4 to region_5' for a route that runs region_0 -> region_5 -> region_4 -> region_3. Every token was grounded -- they are all real regions -- so token-level grounding passed a false ordering. ungrounded() now checks ADJACENCY too. (2) a verdict with no reason: when the demand site is unreachable per_vehicle is empty and the paragraph fell silent, asserting 'No vehicle can make the delivery' and stopping. It now names the cut, cited to the flooded claims.
prediction_error: I predicted groundedness 1.000 by construction and a checker that can fail -- both hold. What I did not predict is that my OWN renderer would be the thing the checker caught, twice, and that token-level grounding would be too weak to see a false ordering.
design_point_that_earned_itself: the structured answer stays canonical and the paragraph is strictly downstream, so generation quality cannot contaminate reasoning evaluation. A test pins it: an empty-string renderer changes no structured answer and is trivially grounded.
known_gap: grounding is token-and-adjacency, not semantic. A real number asserted about the wrong entity would pass. Role-level binding is the next tightening and is the same shape of gap as the ordering bug.

actual: Milestone table delivered at V=4 on the non-empty population. Oracle world 1.000 task acc at $1.39e-08/correct, grounded 1.000. Signature reader claim R 0.971 but task acc 0.318 at $3.95e-08. Rules 0.280/0.000, lexical 0.256/0.000, template 0.000/0.000. Kernel ablations from the oracle: no SMT 0.500, no datalog 0.818, no ASP route search 0.864.
the_headline: READER LOSS 0.682 EXCEEDS EVERY KERNEL LOSS (worst 0.500, no SMT). World construction costs more than any single kernel contributes -- the programme's own thesis, measured in one table rather than asserted. Every kernel still earns its place.
cost_moves_the_wrong_way: $/correct rises 2.8x from oracle to best reader (1.39e-08 -> 3.95e-08) because the kernels run at nearly the same price and produce fewer correct answers. A weaker reader does not save compute, it wastes it.
recall_is_not_capability: the signature reader recovers 0.971 of claims and answers 0.318 of tasks. That gap is why the dependency-weighted and end-to-end columns exist.
bug_caught: first run reported $/correct as exactly 0.00e+00 because I read Context.cost_usd, which is None -- the flow prices per artifact (routes.cost.usd for ASP, load_report.usd for SMT). A cost column of exactly zero is the kind of number that looks like a result.
stated_limits: one domain; the reader arms are hand-authored and three score 0.000 at V=4 for the known reason; $/correct prices the KERNELS only and excludes the reader's own compute, so it is a lower bound on system cost.

hypothesis: I claimed the capacity failure needed a lexical resource or a learned component because the antecedent is named by a SUPERLATIVE ('X is the lightest of them') and a rule for 'lightest' dies under paraphrase. That claim is probably WRONG. The naming sentence has type signature (1 vehicle, 0 quantities) and sits immediately before the pronoun sentence, so the antecedent is recoverable by POSITION AND SIGNATURE with no content word consulted. My reader simply never handled that signature in the quantities paragraph -- a sentence with a vehicle and no number falls through every branch, so last_vehicle is never updated and the pronoun binds to whatever the roster left.
the_fix: one clause: in the quantities paragraph, a sentence mentioning exactly one vehicle and no quantity is a NAMING sentence and sets last_vehicle. Purely structural, no lexicon, so it should stay flat across phrasing variants.
expected: capacity recall 0.725 -> 1.000; claim recall 0.971 -> ~1.000; task accuracy 0.318 -> near 1.000, matching what the rules reader achieved at V=1 with full recall. And still FLAT across V=1..4, since nothing lexical was added.
would_change_my_mind: if capacity recall improves but task accuracy does not follow, then capacity was not the binding constraint and the 40 spurious links or something else is. If the fix works only at some V, it leaked a lexical dependence.
what_it_would_correct: notes/findings/2026-08-18-type-signatures-are-phrasing-invariant-and-stop-exactly-at-meaning.md says signatures 'stop exactly at reference mediated by meaning' and that this is the first place a lexical resource is the only mechanism available. If a structural fix closes it, that boundary was drawn in the wrong place and the finding needs correcting.

actual: CONFIRMED and larger than predicted. One clause -- handling the (1 vehicle, 0 quantities) naming signature in the quantities paragraph -- takes the type-signature reader from claim recall 0.971 / task acc 0.318 to 1.000 / 1.000, flat at V=1,2,3,4. The milestone table now reads: oracle 1.000 at $1.97e-08, signature reader 1.000 at $2.03e-08 -- a 3% cost premium and ZERO reader loss.
two_published_claims_withdrawn: (1) 'type signatures stop exactly at reference mediated by meaning; this is the first place a lexical resource is the only mechanism available' -- wrong, the antecedent is the nearest preceding lone-vehicle mention and is recoverable from position and signature with no content word read. (2) 'reader loss 0.682 exceeds every kernel loss 0.500' -- wrong, reader loss is 0.000 and the kernel losses now dominate.
the_mechanism_of_my_error: a failure localised to ONE claim kind, in a sentence that really did contain a superlative, with a generalisation argument that really is true of a 'lightest' rule. Everything fit -- and the fit was to a story about the domain rather than to the code that produced the numbers. I never asked whether my reader had a branch for that input shape.
what_to_take_from_it: the surface is SATURATED, not solved. A reader reaching the oracle means the benchmark stopped discriminating -- the same trap the rules arm hit at V=1, walked into from the other side. The surface still hands over section headings and a fixed paragraph order, and position does most of the disambiguation. The honest frontier is a surface without them, where this same reader leaves 72 consistent worlds and a bound deciding 0.0%.

hypothesis: With position ablated the reader leaves 72 consistent worlds and a bound deciding 0.0% of the fleet. Consistency pruning has nothing to bite on -- every ambiguous reading is internally coherent, and the invariants I verified (depot never flooded, needs never flooded) are automatically satisfied by any role permutation. But EXTERNAL KNOWLEDGE does bite: the generator draws masses from {1200,1800,2600,3200}, capacities from {1500,2500,4000} and demands from {900,1400,2100}, and mass n capacity = {} and demand n capacity = {}. A value registry should therefore collapse the vehicle group (4 -> 1) and the bare group (2 -> 1) outright, leaving only the region group.
expected: worlds 72 -> 6-12 (region only); decided 0.0% -> about 36% by the regime table's 'region alone' row; soundness must stay 1.000 -- if the registry ever excludes the true reading it is unsound and that is a bug not a result.
what_it_answers: the programme's own question, can external ontologies dramatically reduce required learning. Here the answer would be that a value vocabulary does the work of paragraph position, which is a much cheaper thing to have than a document template.
honesty_label: the registry is taken from the generator's own draw sets, so it is unusually clean external knowledge -- a real registry would be noisier and overlapping. This measures the CEILING of what a value vocabulary buys, and it must be reported as such and be ablatable.
would_change_my_mind: decided staying near 0% would mean the region group alone is the binding ambiguity and value knowledge is irrelevant. Any unsoundness means the registry is excluding true readings.

actual: no external knowledge: 72 worlds, sound 1.000, decided 0.0%. + value registry: 9 worlds, sound 1.000, IN 0.91, OUT 0.18, open 1.91, decided 36.4%. The 9 worlds and 36.4% match the ambiguity-regime sweep's 'region alone' row exactly, confirming the registry collapses the vehicle and bare groups completely.
prediction_error: none. Predicted 6-12 worlds and about 36% decided from the regime table; measured 9 and 36.4%.
consistency_pruning_found_useless: I verified over 200 cases that the depot is never flooded, the demand site is never flooded and depot != needs -- real domain invariants. They prune NOTHING, because any assignment giving three roles to three distinct regions satisfies them automatically. Every ambiguous reading here is internally coherent, so the world IR can carry the ambiguity and the task offers no constraint that collapses it. Branching and bounding are available; resolution by consistency is not.
the_claim: a value vocabulary does the work of paragraph position for two of three ambiguity groups, and a registry is a far cheaper thing to possess than a document template. That answers the programme's 'can external ontologies dramatically reduce required learning' with a number on this task.
honesty: the registry is the generator's own draw sets, so this is the CEILING of what a value vocabulary buys; a real one would overlap. And 36.4% decided is still not actionable -- the registry moves this task to the EDGE of the useful-bound regime, not into it.
residual: the region group survives because flooded/depot/needs are all bare region mentions with no quantity. Closing it needs relational knowledge, a different kind of external knowledge from a value list.

hypothesis: State says the residual region group needs RELATIONAL knowledge. Before accepting that -- having just published a boundary that was my own missing branch -- there is a structural signal unused. The surface says 'A request has come in from region_3. It is for 1400 kg of supplies.' Once the value registry identifies which bare quantity is the DEMAND, the needs site is the lone region immediately preceding it. That is coreference by adjacency, the same mechanism that fixed capacity, applied to a second referent, and it reads no content word.
expected: the region group's choices fall from 6 (ordered pairs over 3 lone regions) to 2 (needs pinned, depot chosen from the remaining two), so worlds 9 -> about 3 and decided 36.4% -> 55-75%. Soundness must stay 1.000.
what_remains_after: depot vs flooded among the two leftover regions. Both readings are internally coherent and give DIFFERENT answers, so nothing structural separates them -- that residual really may need lexical or relational knowledge, and this arm establishes where the structural signal genuinely runs out rather than assuming it.
would_change_my_mind: if adjacency does not pin the needs site -- because the demand sentence is not always adjacent to its region mention across the four phrasing variants -- then the signal is a property of variant 0 and not of the surface. Any unsoundness means the adjacency rule excludes the true reading.

actual: worlds 72.0 -> 9.0 -> 2.5; decided 0.0% -> 36.4% -> 60.6%; soundness 1.000 on every arm. 60.6% at 2.5 worlds is inside the <=4-world band the ambiguity-regime finding identified as actionable.
prediction_error: none material. Predicted about 3 worlds and 55-75% decided; measured 2.5 and 60.6%.
the_claim: paragraph position is a CRUTCH. A value vocabulary plus adjacency-based recency replaces it entirely for two of three ambiguity groups, with no content word read and no lexicon beyond a value list. A registry and a recency rule are both far cheaper things to possess than a document template.
boundary_established_not_assumed: the residual is exactly depot vs flooded among the two leftover regions. Both readings are internally coherent, give different answers, and are unseparated by signature, adjacency, value vocabulary OR the domain invariants (which I verified over 200 cases and found useless, since any assignment of three roles to three distinct regions satisfies them automatically). Having just published a boundary that was my own missing branch, this one is stated WITH the list of what was tried.
honesty: adjacency is a property of this surface's discourse -- the demand follows its region mention here, and a document stating the demand first would defeat it. It is recency, not understanding. And 60.6% decided is a bound, not an answer: a caller still gets 'one of these, we cannot say which' on 1.18 vehicles per case.

hypothesis: The milestone's 'grounded 1.000' column rests on a checker that verifies TOKENS and route ADJACENCY. I flagged the gap myself: a real number asserted about the wrong entity passes. The sharpest missing check is not role bindings though -- it is that the paragraph must never CONTRADICT the structured answer. A forged 'truck_1 runs <real route> and clears 4500 kg' uses only real tokens on a real route, so both existing checks pass it, while asserting the opposite of the canonical decision.
the_design_point_it_protects: the whole separation between reasoning and generation is that the structured answer is canonical and the paragraph is downstream. That separation is worth nothing if the paragraph can assert a different answer and no check notices.
expected: my current renderer derives each vehicle's polarity from the flow's feasible flag, so it should pass the tightened check unchanged and grounded stays 1.000. The value is that the checker gains a class it could not see, and a forged contradiction is caught.
would_change_my_mind: if my renderer FAILS the tightened check, the 'grounded 1.000' column overstated and the milestone needs correcting again -- which is the outcome worth having, since I predicted more bugs of this shape.

actual: Added a CONTRADICTION check: every '<vehicle> runs' / '<vehicle> cannot' in the paragraph must agree with whether that vehicle is in the structured answer. The renderer passes unchanged, 40/40, and the milestone's grounded column is 1.000 on every row under the tightened checker. Three new tests make the check fail -- claiming a refused vehicle runs, denying an able one, and confirming an honest paragraph is not flagged. 11 tests total.
prediction_error: none. I predicted the renderer would pass unchanged and that the value is the checker gaining a class it could not see; both hold. I also predicted I might find another bug of the ordering shape and did not -- this time the published column was right.
the_sharper_form: the gap I had named was 'a real number asserted about the wrong entity'. The sharper missing check is CONTRADICTION: token grounding and adjacency both pass a sentence asserting the opposite of the decision using only real tokens on a real route. The separation between reasoning and generation is worth nothing if the paragraph can disagree with the decision and nothing notices.
remaining_hole: a real quantity attached to the wrong entity when no route or polarity claim is made. Role-level binding would close it; the three levels now are token, route adjacency, and contradiction.

hypothesis: The grounding CONTRACT -- structured answer canonical, paragraph downstream, unsupported and contradictory assertions caught mechanically -- should transfer to a structurally opposite domain. Solvency's answer is one boolean, not a set, so 'contradiction' means the paragraph asserting cleared when the decision says not.
the_interesting_part: the explanation is BITEMPORAL. A covenant fails not because a number is small but because a filing POSTDATES the decision: 'sub_3's only return is dated 2026-06-01, after the 2026-05-30 determination, so it could not be counted.' That is what transaction_time is for, and it is the first explanation in this repo that has to cite a date rather than a value.
expected: grounding 1.000 across cases once dates are added to the known-token set; the contradiction check needs a boolean form rather than the per-vehicle polarity form; and the interesting failure mode is a paragraph that cites a figure WITHOUT noting it was unusable, which is true-but-misleading rather than false.
would_change_my_mind: if the flood grounding checker transfers with no change beyond the token set, the contract is more general than I think. If it needs a domain-specific rewrite, then what transfers is the IDEA of a checkable paragraph rather than any mechanism, which is a weaker claim and should be stated as such.

actual: 60/60 grounded. The paragraph explains bitemporally: 'The covenant was not met. On the information available at 2026-05-30, consolidated revenue was 450.98 USD against a requirement of 651.22 USD. Excluded as not yet knowable: sub_3 filed 169.91 USD dated 2026-06-01, after the determination.' 8 tests, four of which make the checker fail (a verdict disagreeing with the decision, an invented date, an invented entity, an invented figure).
prediction_answered: I asked whether the flood checker would transfer with nothing but a new token set. It did NOT. The contradiction check needed a BOOLEAN verdict form rather than per-vehicle runs/cannot polarity, and a DATE channel. So what transfers is the CONTRACT -- tokens, a domain-specific relation, contradiction against the structured answer -- and not any line of code. That is the weaker of the two outcomes I named in advance and is the honest one.
the_domain_specific_slot: the middle check is the interesting one: route ADJACENCY in flood, DATE VALIDITY here. Both answer 'what relation can this paragraph get wrong while using only real tokens?' and the answer differs per domain.
bug_that_fired_loudly: first version reported 0/60 grounded because _NUM matches the digit runs inside dates -- every 2026-05-30 contributed three spurious numbers -- and my guard tested whether the TOKEN was a full date, which 2026 is not. A checker that flags everything is obvious; one that flags nothing looks like success.
first_of_its_kind: this is the first explanation in the repo that must cite a DATE rather than a value, which is exactly what transaction_time is for. A representation carrying only values could state the verdict and not the reason.

hypothesis: Scheduling is the third domain and it discriminates a claim I made loosely. Solvency showed the grounding CONTRACT transfers while the MECHANISM does not -- but solvency and scheduling both answer a BOOLEAN, so if solvency's contradiction check works here unchanged, the truer claim is that the mechanism transfers within an ANSWER-TYPE CLASS rather than not at all.
reader_expectation: the signature reader should work well and possibly better than flood's, because entity prefixes (job_ vs machine_) plus quantity presence separate all four claim kinds outright: (machine, qty) = capacity, (job, qty) = duration, (machine, no qty) = has_capability, (job, no qty) = needs_capability. No coreference is needed at all.
the_external_knowledge_slot: capabilities are a closed vocabulary {cut, paint, weld} -- the same slot the value registry filled in flood, but lexical rather than numeric. That is a second instance of the same architectural need and worth noting as such.
expected: reader claim recall near 1.000 and flat across phrasing variants; the boolean contradiction check reusable from solvency with only the verdict wording changed; grounding 1.000.
would_change_my_mind: if the boolean check needs a scheduling-specific rewrite, then answer type is NOT the unit of reuse and the contract-only claim stands as published. If the reader needs coreference here, my read of the signatures is wrong.

actual: Reader claim precision and recall exactly 1.000 at V=1,2,3,4 with NO coreference. Renderer 40/40 grounded and distinguishes a capability failure from a packing failure. 14 tests pass.
the_sharpened_claim: solvency concluded 'the contract transfers and not any line of code', drawn from two domains with DIFFERENT answer types. Scheduling is also boolean and discriminates: boolean_contradiction is now SHARED CODE between solvency and scheduling, parameterised only by the verdict phrases, with a test asserting they are literally the same function object. So the mechanism transfers WITHIN an answer type and not across -- flood's set answer needs per-element polarity and keeps its own.
the_decomposition: one check shared per answer type; one check always bespoke (route adjacency in flood, date validity in solvency, capability validity in scheduling); a token vocabulary always bespoke.
external_knowledge_slot_again: capabilities are a closed vocabulary {cut, paint, weld} -- the lexical counterpart of flood's numeric value registry, second instance of the same architectural need, and it doubles as the distractor filter since the withdrawn machine and cancelled job carry neither quantity nor capability.
prediction_error: none material. Predicted near-1.000 recall flat across variants (measured exactly 1.000), the boolean check reusable with only wording changed (it is, and is now shared code), and grounding 1.000 (40/40).
honest_caveat: scheduling is the EASIEST of the three to read -- entity prefixes carry the type -- so 1.000 says the signatures are clean here, not that reading is solved. Flood needed coreference and reached 1.000 only after a bug fix; solvency needed dates.

hypothesis: Directive 11 asks the training path to accept a replayable dataset with bounded memory, a resumable cursor and a tokenizer fitted from bounded deterministic samples. The abstraction is done and tested -- 18 tests including constant memory on a 10^12-address split -- but that test iterates ds.keys() only, and build_tokenizer takes a Sequence[Episode]. So the untested claim is that the FULL path (tokenizer, episodes, batches) stays bounded, not just key enumeration.
scope_decision: NOT rewriting train(). Fifty-one published models depend on that path, and the directive warns against a refactor detached from capability. The honest deliverable is the acceptance test itself plus the one missing piece -- a tokenizer fitted from a bounded deterministic prefix of the stream.
expected: peak memory for a 10^12-address dataset within a small constant of a 24-address one across the WHOLE path; the streaming tokenizer deterministic (same vocabulary from the same prefix, twice) and covering the curriculum comparably to the materialised one; the cursor round-tripping through a checkpoint dict and resuming at the same next batch.
would_change_my_mind: if peak memory grows with the address space once episodes are generated rather than keys enumerated, then something downstream of keys() materialises and the abstraction is not as done as its tests suggest -- which would be the finding.
known_limit_to_state: floors and rule-based one-pass fitting both genuinely want the whole training set, so streaming benefits the batch-consuming path only. That path is the neural control, which CLAUDE.md keeps off by default -- so this closes a named requirement without claiming it changes capability.

actual: Generating EPISODES from a 6,000,000,000,000-address split peaks at 239.5 KiB (40 episodes) and 271.0 KiB (400) against 418.2 and 473.4 KiB from a 24-address split -- ratio 0.57x, and 10x the episodes costs +13%. The huge split is CHEAPER because the finite one does extra epoch bookkeeping. Tokenizer fits from a bounded deterministic prefix: 1024 ids from 64 episodes of 6e12 addresses, with two fits of the same prefix required to agree exactly. Cursor round-trips through a checkpoint dict and a resumed stream continues. 7 new tests.
prediction_error: none. Predicted bounded memory across the whole path, a deterministic prefix tokenizer, and a round-tripping cursor; all three hold.
what_was_actually_missing: the existing 18 streaming tests cover key enumeration, replay, sharding, pinned eval and resume -- but the constant-memory test iterates ds.keys() ONLY. Enumerating addresses cheaply is worth nothing if turning an address into an episode materialises the corpus, and nothing measured that. build_tokenizer also took a Sequence[Episode].
scope_decision_stated: train() deliberately untouched. Fifty-one published models depend on it; floors and one-pass rule induction genuinely want the whole training set (and this repo has more dead claims from floors than anywhere else); and only the batch-consuming learner benefits, which is the neural control CLAUDE.md keeps off by default. The named requirement is closed WITHOUT claiming it changes capability.

hypothesis: Directive 13 says collect execution traces before learning any routing policy, and gives the rule to derive against: escalate when p*L > c1 - c0. The milestone table already suggests the answer -- the cheap arm (first_route_only) costs $1.85e-08 against the full flow's $1.97e-08, only 6% cheaper, while dropping accuracy from 1.000 to 0.864. If that holds per case, the derived policy is ALWAYS TAKE THE EXPENSIVE ARM, because the cost gap is too small to justify ever risking a wrong answer.
the_derivation: with c1 - c0 = 0.12e-08 and cheap-arm failure p = 0.136, escalation pays whenever L > (c1-c0)/p = 0.88e-08 -- i.e. whenever one wrong answer costs more than about a hundredth of a microdollar. That is trivially true for any real use, so the threshold is met everywhere and there is no regime where routing helps.
what_this_means_for_the_directive: the precondition 'multiple valid strategies actually differ' is met on SUCCESS and not on COST. Collecting traces is still the right step 1; the finding would be that step 2 -- learning a policy -- is not justified on this task, which is a negative result that saves the work rather than a reason to do it.
expected: per-case cost gap between the full flow and each ablation under 30%, cheap-arm failure concentrated rather than uniform, and a derived escalation threshold so low that the expensive arm always wins.
would_change_my_mind: a large per-case cost spread -- some cases where the full flow costs 10x the cheap arm -- would mean the aggregate hides a real routing opportunity, and then whether cheap-arm success is PREDICTABLE from pre-run world features becomes the question worth answering.

hypothesis: Flood showed the cheap kernel PAYS FOR ITSELF -- dropping datalog made the flow 1.78x more expensive, an escalation threshold that is negative. Scheduling has the same shape with a sharper mechanism: capacity_gate is a SOUND ONE-SIDED check that only ever proves infeasible, and infeasible is exactly the side ASP has to EXHAUST the search space to establish. So the gate should prune precisely the most expensive instances, and unlike flood's constant 1.78x its value should GROW with instance size.
the_open_question: does clingo find the global capacity argument by itself? Each machine's #sum is a separate propagator, and deriving 'total demand > total capacity' means aggregating across all n_machines of them -- a cutting-plane style inference. If clingo does it, the gate is REDUNDANT and saves nothing. If it does not, the gate converts an exponential into arithmetic.
expected: clingo does NOT find it cheaply, so UNSAT instances cost far more than SAT ones and the gap widens with n_jobs. Gate fires only at negative slack, by construction.
would_change_my_mind: UNSAT instances costing the SAME as or LESS than SAT ones would mean clingo aggregates the sum constraints, the gate is redundant, and flood's 1.78x was about datalog shrinking the GROUNDING rather than about pruning search -- a different mechanism with a different generalisation.
note: prediction on the flood arm was WRONG in the useful direction: I said every cost gap under 30%, and no-datalog came in at +78%.

hypothesis: Chasing the routing traces found a hang, and instrumenting the phases separated it cleanly. The ASP budget WORKS -- seed 3 at n_jobs=20 cut off at exactly 2.000s with exhausted=False, correctly refusing to call an unfinished search a proof. The hang is in ctl.ground(), which runs BEFORE the async handle and is therefore unbounded. My hypothesis for why grounding explodes: ops.py sets SCALE=100 to keep two decimal places, so every duration and capacity enters the #sum weight constraint multiplied by 100, and clingo's translation of a weight constraint scales with the WEIGHTS and not just the atom count.
expected: grounding time at n_jobs=30 collapses when SCALE is reduced, with the answer unchanged on instances whose durations are representable at the coarser scale. If so, the dominant cost of this kernel is a PRECISION CHOICE IN THE ENCODING, not the search.
why_this_matters_for_routing: directive 13 wants a router choosing between execution paths on cost. If encoding cost dominates search cost by orders of magnitude, then routing between kernels is second-order and the first-order lever is how the problem is written down. That would reframe the routing question rather than answer it.
would_change_my_mind: grounding staying slow at SCALE=1 would mean the blowup is combinatorial in jobs x machines and the weights are innocent, which puts the cost back in the search where a router could reach it.

hypothesis: With the oracle fixed the scheduling domain reaches 80 jobs, so the routing question is finally measurable: does the cheap SOUND capacity gate fire where the expensive kernel's cost actually lives? The gate can only fire at slack<0, where capacity is below demand. Hardness in packing problems concentrates at the feasibility boundary.
expected: cost peaks NEAR slack 0 and the gate fires only strictly below it, so the gate catches the arithmetically-obvious infeasible cases -- the ones that are easy for clingo too -- while the expensive region sits just where the gate is structurally unable to reach. If so the principle for routing is that a cheap SOUND check is ANTI-CORRELATED with cost, and buys less than its fire rate suggests.
the_genuine_uncertainty: at n_jobs=20 slack=-0.02, three seeds finished instantly and one hit the 2s budget. So SOME gate-firing instances are hard for clingo. If the hard ones concentrate at slack just below 0 -- barely infeasible -- then the gate catches exactly the expensive region and the principle inverts to the opposite of the above.
would_change_my_mind: either direction is a result. What would refute BOTH is cost being flat in slack, which would mean this domain has no phase transition and the whole framing is wrong for it.
note: three predictions on this thread have now been wrong -- gate prunes an exponential (no), SCALE causes the blowup (no), budget_ns not binding (it binds). Confidence set to 0.5 deliberately.

verdict: partly right, and wrong in the direction that mattered
measured: per-case cost gaps: no ASP search 0.83x, no SMT 0.83x, no datalog 1.78x. Escalation thresholds 9.37e-09, 2.63e-09 and NEGATIVE (-3.30e-08) USD. Per-case spread p50 1.08x, max 2.14x, 2.5% above 2x.
right: the derived policy is always take the expensive arm, and no per-case spread hides an opportunity.
wrong: I predicted every gap under 30%. no-datalog came in at +78% -- dropping the cheap kernel made the flow MORE expensive, which the tier framing has no slot for.

verdict: wrong, and the reason was outside the system
measured: UNSAT/SAT 0.83-1.43 with no widening across n_jobs 6-18, every instance under 2ms.
why: the sweep never reached a hard regime, and the thing that stopped it was the ground-truth oracle -- an exhaustive itertools.product costing 53s per 18-job instance. Two sub-hypotheses also died: budget_ns not binding (it binds exactly), SCALE=100's weights (innocent). All three wrong the same way: looking inside the system for a cost that was in the harness.

verdict: WRONG, and the opposite is true
measured: the gate removes 87.7% of solver time on 50.0% of instances -- 1.75x better than its fire rate. Cost peaks at slack -0.03 (62.9% of all solver time) where the gate fires 100%.
i_predicted: anti-correlation: a sound cheap check fires where the problem is easy and buys LESS than its fire rate. Stated at 0.5 confidence with the alternative written down.
mechanism: cost concentrates at BARELY infeasible, where no single machine's constraint is violated by any partial assignment and the contradiction exists only in the sum ACROSS machines. clingo's propagators are per-constraint; the gate does that cross-machine sum in O(n). The cheap check performs exactly the inference the expensive kernel cannot express locally.
consequence: the escalation rule p*L > c1-c0 is the wrong model for these domains: it prices the cheap arm as a SUBSTITUTE, and in both flood and scheduling it is a COMPLEMENT -- c1 depends on whether c0 ran.

hypothesis: state.yml says the flood surface is SATURATED -- a reader consulting no content word reaches the oracle. Reading read_signature confirms why and it is worse than 'position helps': the function branches on pi==0,1,2,3, HARD-CODED PARAGRAPH INDICES. The milestone headline 'signature reader 1.000, zero reader loss' is a reader that knows the generator's five-paragraph template by position. Breaking it by shuffling is not worth running -- I can write that up in advance. The open question is what SURVIVES.
the_real_question: are paragraph ROLES recoverable from content instead of position? Mechanism: the paragraph containing trucks-with-masses is the roster, so its lone one-region sentence is the DEPOT; the paragraph containing 'Which vehicles...' is the tasking, so its one-region sentence is NEEDS; the remaining all-one-region paragraph is overnight, so those are FLOODED. That resolves the known depot/flooded residual by CO-OCCURRENCE rather than position, and consults no content word.
expected: index-based read_signature collapses to near 0 non-empty accuracy on a surface with headings dropped and paragraphs shuffled. A role-assignment reader recovers most of it -- I put 0.6 on it reaching >=0.75. If it reaches the oracle, position was a crutch and the honest headline survives; if it lands in between, the gap is the real reader loss the milestone has been hiding.
would_change_my_mind: the role-assignment reader failing near 0 would mean the paragraph grouping ITSELF was carrying the signal, and the honest frontier is a surface with sentences interleaved rather than merely reordered.
note: paragraph-level shuffle is chosen deliberately over sentence-level: every pronoun in this surface resolves WITHIN its paragraph (capacity, load_limit, demand), so shuffling paragraphs keeps every sentence TRUE. Sentence-level shuffle would make the ground truth wrong rather than the reader, which this repo has already done once.

hypothesis: Paragraph co-occurrence replaced position and held 1.000 -- but GROUPING is still a template property. A real report does not put every road in one paragraph. Interleaving shuffles sentences globally, destroying grouping, with each pronoun kept glued to its antecedent so every sentence stays true. Crossed with paraphrase (V=1 vs V=4) this is a 2x2, and I expect the two readers to fail on OPPOSITE axes.
expected: rules (regex phrasings) survives interleaving -- its patterns are position-independent -- and dies at V=4, which is already established. read_signature_roles survives V=4 -- the signature is flat across phrasings, established -- and dies interleaved, because with one paragraph has_demand and has_mass are both true and depot/flooded/needs collapse into one branch. So NO arm survives both axes, and the honest frontier is the paraphrased-and-interleaved cell.
what_makes_it_worth_running: the 2x2 is the falsifiable version of a claim this repo keeps making one axis at a time. If some arm survives both, the surface is still saturated and I have been measuring the wrong axis; if none does, the empty cell is the frontier and directive 19's answer applies -- EMIT the ambiguity rather than collapse it, which signature_worlds can already do soundly.
would_change_my_mind: roles holding up interleaved would mean grouping was never load-bearing and the registry plus adjacency carry everything, which would make the surface saturated on BOTH axes and send the frontier somewhere else entirely.

verdict: right, and one half was stronger than expected
measured: index reader 1.000 -> 0.000 non-empty when paragraphs are shuffled, claim recall 1.000 -> 0.197. read_signature_roles holds 1.000 on the shuffled surface. Section headings worth EXACTLY NOTHING -- no reader consulted them.
corrects: state.yml's '72 consistent worlds, 0.0% decided' was an artefact of signature_readings flattening the document with text.replace(chr(10)+chr(10),' '), discarding paragraph MEMBERSHIP along with ORDER. Membership carries the disambiguation and survives a reorder.

verdict: right, at 0.7 confidence
measured: V=1 grouped: rules 1.000, roles 1.000. V=1 interleaved: rules 1.000, roles 0.000. V=4 grouped: rules 0.000, roles 1.000. V=4 interleaved: ALL 0.000.
conclusion: the two mechanisms fail on orthogonal axes and their intersection is EMPTY. What is missing is a reader invariant to phrasing AND arrangement at once -- a sharper statement of the front than 'the surface is saturated'.
constructive: in the empty cell the sound enumerating arm is the only thing that works: soundness 1.000 on every rung, decided 0.324, median 2.5 worlds with registry+adjacency. Directive 19 vindicated with numbers.
surprise: adjacency still helps after interleaving (0.147 -> 0.324). The atom rule that keeps each pronoun with its antecedent -- there to keep the document TRUE -- preserves exactly the adjacency that binds the demand to its site. A property of the task, not a leak.
my_error: first ran the emit ladder with registry=None, which means NO registry, and nearly reported 72 worlds as the arm's number when it is the number with its declared knowledge switched off.

hypothesis: Before building readers for the empty V=4-interleaved cell, ask whether it is reachable at all. The residual that stops the enumerating arm at 2.5 worlds / 32.4% decided is DEPOT vs FLOODED, and both are realised as one-region, no-number, no-vehicle sentences. A reader consulting no content word observes only: entity types, numbers, value-registry membership, and which sentences mention which entity. If the depot's content-free FINGERPRINT -- the multiset of signatures of every sentence mentioning it -- is identical to a flooded region's, then NO content-free reader can separate them, whatever its architecture.
expected: identical fingerprints in the large majority of cases. If so, 32.4% is a CEILING for content-free reading on this surface, not a property of my particular arm, and closing the gap REQUIRES reading content -- which converts the lexical resource from a shortcut into a necessity and redirects the whole front.
would_change_my_mind: a systematic fingerprint difference -- e.g. the depot appearing in a different number of link sentences than a flooded region -- would mean a content-free reader CAN separate them and the empty cell is merely unsolved rather than closed. That is the better outcome for the programme and the one I would rather find.
note: this is cheap and could embarrass me: I have just published that the intersection is empty, and a systematic difference would show I stopped one step short.

verdict: prediction RIGHT (closed), but my first test said the opposite and I nearly published it
measured: fingerprints distinguishable in 93.3% of cases -- which is asymmetry, not information. The feature they differ on is node degree in the road network. Rule 'depot is the highest-degree lone region': 33.3% against 28.5% chance. Architecture-independent collision test: rank-normalised observation -> role is NOT A FUNCTION, 21/21 role-slots ambiguous, every one of the 7 distinct observations carrying all three roles.
conclusion: the V=4 interleaved cell is CLOSED to content-free reading. 32.4% decided is a CEILING, not an implementation limit. Settling depot vs flooded REQUIRES content, which makes a lexical resource a necessity rather than a shortcut -- the first place in this programme where that is measured rather than assumed.
the_error: I measured DISTINGUISHABLE when the question was IDENTIFIABLE. Anything with incidental variation is distinguishable. Lesson written; the script now runs all three tests and prints the corrected verdict so it cannot mislead a later session.

hypothesis: Flood's reader collapses under interleaving and its residual is closed to content-free reading. Is that a property of flood or of the pipeline? Proposed law: A DOMAIN IS STRUCTURE-DEPENDENT EXACTLY TO THE EXTENT THAT ITS ENTITY NAMES DO NOT CARRY THEIR ROLES. Flood names every place region_N, and region_0 may be the depot, a flooded district or the needs site -- so structure has to assign the role, and destroying structure destroys the reading. Scheduling names them job_3 and machine_1: the prefix IS the type, state.yml records precision and recall exactly 1.000 with NO coreference for that reason.
expected: scheduling's read_signature is IMMUNE to interleaving -- accuracy unchanged -- while flood's collapses to 0.000 (already measured). If so the law holds with a mechanism, and it predicts where the text->world front is hard BEFORE building a reader: look at whether the entity vocabulary is role-typed.
would_change_my_mind: scheduling collapsing too would mean structure carries the reading regardless of naming, and the law is wrong -- the flood result would then be general and the front is harder everywhere. Scheduling being immune for some OTHER reason (e.g. one sentence per claim with no cross-sentence binding at all) would make the law untested rather than confirmed, so I check the mechanism and not only the number.

verdict: law survives, but ONLY after the confound I predicted was found and killed
measured: at V=4 interleaving costs flood 1.000 (role-typed 0.571) and scheduling 0.000 (role-typed 0.917). The aggregate looks like clean confirmation and the script said so -- it is CONFOUNDED: scheduling is 100% self-contained against flood's 75.5%, so it would be immune whatever its names were.
what_settled_it: per-kind decomposition. Every claim flood loses is SELF-CONTAINED -- depot 1.000, flooded 1.000, needs 0.725, each naming its own region and realised by no pronoun -- while the two kinds realised ENTIRELY by a pronoun, capacity and load_limit, lose 0.000. Worst drop among pronoun-bound kinds 0.000; among self-contained kinds 1.000. Cross-sentence binding is not the mechanism.
restated_law: structure is load-bearing exactly where a sentence's SIGNATURE DOES NOT DETERMINE ITS PREDICATE. Role-typed naming is one way to get determinacy, which is why role_typed tracks it, but determinacy is the mechanism. This predicts where text->world is hard BEFORE a reader is built, and it explains the closure result rather than merely coexisting with it -- the residual no content-free observable settles is exactly the group the signature leaves open.
status: mechanism confirmed by decomposition on two domains, NOT a law confirmed by manipulation. The missing cell -- flood renamed so prefixes carry roles, everything else identical -- is the next test and it is cheap.

hypothesis: The structure-dependence law is confirmed by decomposition on two domains but not by MANIPULATION. The missing cell is flood renamed so entity prefixes carry roles, everything else identical. Sharper version: type the ambiguous roles ONE AT A TIME, which turns a binary law into a quantitative one. Flood's ambiguous group is {depot, flooded, needs}, all sharing signature (1 region, 0 numbers, 0 vehicles).
expected: a THRESHOLD, not a gradient. The survival theory in the ledger says a reader loses whole KINDS and a lost kind sends S = prod q^d to zero, so partial typing should buy nothing until the last answer-critical ambiguity is gone. Typing 2 of 3 is already full determinacy by elimination, so the informative points are 0, 1 and 2 typed.
the_genuine_uncertainty: adjacency ALREADY pins needs -- it is what lifted the enumerating arm from 0.147 to 0.324 decided, and it survives interleaving because the atom rule keeps the demand quantity beside its site. So typing DEPOT alone may cascade: depot by prefix, needs by adjacency, flooded by elimination. If that happens, one rename restores immunity and the curve is a step at 1 rather than at 2.
would_change_my_mind: a genuinely graded curve -- accuracy rising smoothly with the number of typed roles -- would contradict the whole-kinds account in the theory ledger and mean the survival law's product form is wrong about how readers fail.

verdict: law confirmed causally; the SHAPE was neither of the two I framed
measured: interleaved accuracy across the ladder 0.000 -> 0.500 -> 1.000 -> 1.000 as depot, then flooded, then needs get role-carrying prefixes. Grouped stays 1.000 throughout (the control: renaming buys nothing while arrangement is readable).
causal: only the entity NAMES changed -- phrasings, arrangement, claims and answer identical -- and interleaved accuracy moved 0.000 to 1.000. Arrangement was load-bearing ONLY because the signature left the predicate open.
shape: a PARTIAL CASCADE. I predicted a threshold at 0.5 confidence and wrote the cascade alternative down. Typing one role of three recovers exactly half: depot by prefix, needs by adjacency, flooded by elimination -- but adjacency only fires sometimes, the same partiality that capped the enumerating arm at 0.324 decided. Partial determinacy buys immunity only through a SECOND mechanism, never on its own.
near_miss: the first run scored 0.000 in EVERY cell including grouped, which would have read as 'renaming does not help'. Cause: I hand-rolled claim assembly instead of importing _assemble. The tell was the control column, whose value is known in advance -- worth including for exactly that reason.

hypothesis: The V=4 interleaved residual -- depot vs flooded vs needs -- is CLOSED to content-free reading (21/21 role-slots ambiguous). So content is required. The question is HOW LITTLE content, and whether it generalises across paraphrases. Cheapest arm first: a hand-declared anchor lemma set per role, exact match, no external resource.
protocol_note: these are DOMAIN-CONCEPT words -- what someone told the task but not the generator would name. I have previously seen the flooded variant 'Water rose through {w} during the night...' and the link/bridge_on variants; I have NOT read the depot or needs variant lists. Choosing anchors after reading them would be memorising the generator, which is this repo's oldest trap.
expected: anchors cover most but not all of the 4 variants per role, because a paraphrase set written to vary wording will include at least one variant that avoids the obvious lemma. So I expect V=1 interleaved to go 0.000 -> ~1.000 and V=4 interleaved to land partial, somewhere around 0.4-0.8, with the gap being exactly the variants no declared anchor reaches.
what_the_gap_would_justify: a measured coverage gap is the honest justification for installing WordNet and expanding the anchors by synonymy -- an external resource earning its place against a number rather than being reached for first. If the plain anchors already reach 1.000, WordNet is unnecessary here and I should say so rather than build it.
would_change_my_mind: anchors scoring near 0.000 would mean the variants share no concept vocabulary at all and the residual needs distributional rather than lexical knowledge.

verdict: beat the prediction, and the control corrected an earlier finding of mine
measured: read_content_roles scores 1.000 in ALL FOUR cells of phrasing x arrangement -- the first reader here invariant to both. I predicted 0.4-0.8 in the hardest cell.
why_it_beat_the_prediction: the anchors DO miss variants exactly as expected ('Vehicles are dispatched from {w}', '{w} is asking for resupply' reach no declared anchor) but elimination and adjacency cascade over the misses -- the same partial-cascade mechanism the renaming manipulation measured.
control: emptying the anchors costs 1.000 -> 0.618 in the hardest cell, so content IS load-bearing (+0.382). But the content-free floor is 0.618, NOT the 0.000 my earlier finding quoted.
correction_i_owe: the 'empty cell' was empty FOR THE ARMS THAT EXISTED. Two of this arm's gains are content-free and were simply missing before: binding needs by adjacency rather than paragraph membership, and never defaulting an unresolved region to flooded.
