At claim level with anchors emptied, needs recall is 1.000 (adjacency solves it outright), depot 0.471, flooded 0.632 -- so the CLOSURE finding stands at the claim level and only the answer-level 'empty' was overstated.
which_content_matters: one vocabulary, and it is FLOODING. Removing flooded anchors costs most (0.853); removing needs costs NOTHING (1.000); depot between (0.941). Structural reason: needs is pinned by adjacency and depot is single-valued so elimination reaches it, but flooding is the MANY-VALUED role and elimination cannot pin a set whose size it does not know.
wordnet: NOT NEEDED, and state.yml's claim that it is on disk is FALSE -- ~/nltk_data/corpora holds only `words`. Five concept words closed the cell; installing a resource before measuring the gap would have been reaching.

hypothesis: read_content_roles scores 1.000 in all four cells with five declared flooding words. The four flooding phrasings happen to use water/submerged/inundated; a phrasing written ADVERSARIALLY against the declared anchors is the honest floor test, and I just published 1.000 so this is the run that could embarrass it. Adding variants 5-8 that avoid every declared word for all three residual roles: depot 'Every lorry is garaged at {w} overnight', flooded '{w} is cut off and nothing may pass through it', needs '{w} has called in an order'.
what_i_can_already_state: making ONE role adversarial should cost nothing, because elimination covers it -- anchored depot plus adjacency-pinned needs leaves flooding by elimination, and anchored flooding plus adjacency leaves depot as the single unresolved. So the informative case is when SEVERAL roles draw an adversarial phrasing in the SAME case.
expected: at V=8 (half the draws adversarial) accuracy lands between the 0.618 emptied-anchor floor and 1.000, with the loss concentrated in cases where depot AND flooded both draw adversarial forms. I put the hardest cell around 0.75-0.90.
the_risk_worth_measuring: a declared vocabulary can be WORSE than none if it MISFIRES -- an anchor firing on a sentence it was not written for assigns a confident wrong role, where an empty vocabulary would have left it to elimination. If the all-adversarial arm scores BELOW 0.618 that is what happened, and it is a real defect rather than a missing word.
would_change_my_mind: 1.000 surviving all-adversarial phrasings would mean the content is not doing what the ablation says it does and elimination is carrying everything, which would contradict the +0.382 ablation result.

verdict: prediction close on the number, and the risk I flagged did NOT occur
measured: original 4 phrasings 1.000/1.000 (grouped/interleaved); 8 with half adversarial 0.853/0.794; 4 ALL adversarial 0.765/0.618 -- EXACTLY the emptied-anchor floor to three decimals. I predicted 0.75-0.90 for the hardest cell at half-adversarial and it came in at 0.794.
result_1: the published 1.000 is a CEILING, not a capability. The arm is invariant to the paraphrases it HAS WORDS FOR, which is a weaker claim than 'invariant to phrasing' and the one the evidence supports.
result_2: the anchors never MISFIRE. All-adversarial equals emptied-anchors exactly, so a declared word never fires on a sentence it was not written for and pre-empts elimination. The arm's failure mode is SILENCE, not error -- the right failure mode for a component feeding a symbolic pipeline, and why the loss stops at the floor instead of going through it. Degradation is graceful and monotone 1.000 -> 0.794 -> 0.618 as the adversarial share goes 0 -> half -> 1.
what_it_justifies: lexical generalisation against a MEASURED gap: the 0.382 between floor and ceiling is exactly the value of having the right word, so WordNet or a distributional resource now earns its place against a number. That was the standard I set when declining to install it and it is now met.
what_it_does_not_justify: enlarging the hand-declared list. Adding garaged/cut off/called in would recover this adversarial set and demonstrate nothing -- memorising the generator one variant later, which is the trap the rules arm already sits in.

hypothesis: The adversarial test measured a 0.382 gap between the anchor vocabulary's ceiling (1.000) and its floor (0.618), which is exactly the value of having the right word. That justifies a lexical resource. WordNet installs and loads.
procedure_declared_before_running: for each declared anchor lemma, take every synset; collect (a) all lemma names in those synsets, (b) all lemma names of their direct hyponyms, (c) all lemma names of their direct hypernyms, (d) derivationally related forms. Lowercase, split on underscore, keep tokens of 3+ characters. NO hand curation, NO inspection of the adversarial variants while choosing the procedure. Match by the same token-prefix rule.
expected: LITTLE RECOVERY. The adversarial phrasings describe the roles by CONSEQUENCE AND FUNCTION, not by synonymy: flooding as 'cut off' / 'nothing gets through' / 'written off' / 'traffic ceased'; depot as 'garaged' / 'the fleet sleeps' / 'the yard' / 'crews sign on'; needs as 'called in an order' / 'an appeal' / 'is short' / 'they are out'. A thesaurus bridges flood->inundate, not flood->nothing gets through. I expect interleaved to move 0.618 -> somewhere in 0.65-0.75, and I put 0.7 on it staying below 0.85.
the_downside_worth_measuring: expansion can MISFIRE where the tight vocabulary provably did not. A large expanded set may fire on sentences it was not written for and pre-empt elimination, which would push the ORIGINAL-phrasing score BELOW 1.000 and the adversarial score BELOW the 0.618 floor. So both are measured, and a drop on the original set is the more important number.
what_a_negative_result_would_mean: if WordNet recovers little, the gap is not lexical at all: settling this residual needs knowledge about what a role DOES -- a depot is where vehicles are kept, flooding is what makes a region unroutable -- which is closer to the kernel's own semantics than to a thesaurus. That would redirect the front from 'get a better lexicon' to 'let the reader emit role CONSEQUENCES and let the kernel bind them', which is a different and more interesting programme.

verdict: negative, and STRONGER than predicted -- the resource is actively harmful
measured: expansion 6/6/5 -> 507/224/593 tokens. Adversarial phrasings 0.618 -> 0.588 interleaved (recovers -0.029 of the 0.382 available, i.e. WORSE than no vocabulary). Original phrasings 1.000 -> 0.735 (-0.265). Filtering tokens shared across roles helps the original slightly (0.794) and makes the adversarial MUCH worse (0.412), because shared-token ambiguity was acting as a brake: two roles matching returns '' and falls through to elimination, one WRONG role is assigned confidently.
i_predicted: little recovery, 0.65-0.75, at 0.7 confidence it stays below 0.85. Recovery was NEGATIVE. I did explicitly predict the misfire downside and it materialised at -0.265.
mechanism: the tight vocabulary's value was PRECISION, not coverage. Six words make a match almost certainly right; five hundred make most matches spurious, and a confident wrong role pre-empts the elimination that would have got it right. For a component feeding a symbolic pipeline -- where a wrong claim propagates and a missing one merely fails to help -- PRECISION DOMINATES COVERAGE and a bigger lexicon is a worse one. Automatic expansion trades away exactly the silence-not-error failure mode the adversarial test identified as the arm's virtue.
why_the_gap_was_never_lexical: the adversarial phrasings name roles by CONSEQUENCE -- flooding as 'nothing gets through', a depot as where the fleet sleeps. A thesaurus bridges flood->inundate, not flood->nothing gets through, because that is not a fact about words. What settles them is knowledge of what a role DOES, which is the KERNEL's semantics rather than a dictionary's.
redirect: front moves from 'get a better lexicon' (closed by measurement, in the strong form that more words are actively harmful) to LETTING THE READER EMIT CONSEQUENCES AND THE KERNEL BIND THEM.
not_ruled_out: a DISTRIBUTIONAL resource rather than a taxonomic one might bridge a situational relation where WordNet cannot. Untested, and the one thing this does not close.

hypothesis: Three findings now say the same thing: structure is load-bearing exactly where a sentence's signature does not determine its predicate; the residual that no content-free observable settles is exactly the group the signature leaves open; and the content needed is only for the many-valued role in that group. That implies a REUSABLE INSTRUMENT -- for a new domain, ask which claim kinds share a sentence signature BEFORE building a reader -- and turning a finding into an instrument is worth more than another finding.
expected: the audit reproduces both known answers, which is what validates it: flood shows a three-way collision on (1 entity, 0 numbers) covering depot/flooded/needs, and scheduling shows NO collision because job_/machine_ prefixes fix the predicate. Solvency is the genuine unknown; its surface realises only `owns` (two entities, no number) and `revenue` (one entity, a number, a date), which are different shapes, so I expect ambiguity mass near 0 and therefore a reader immune to interleaving without any content at all.
the_point: if solvency audits clean and then survives interleaving, the instrument PREDICTED a domain's difficulty before a reader existed for it -- which is the whole claim. If it audits clean and then COLLAPSES, the instrument is incomplete and something outside sentence signature carries the reading, which would be the more interesting result.
would_change_my_mind: a collision in solvency I did not anticipate would mean the audit is finding structure I could not see by reading the generator, which makes it more valuable rather than less.

verdict: prediction held, after a broken reader nearly confirmed it for the wrong reason
measured: audit reproduces both known answers -- flood 0.617 ambiguity mass (irreducible part 141/1141 = 0.124, exactly the depot/flooded/needs group), scheduling 0.000. Solvency audited 0.000 with NO READER IN EXISTENCE; the reader built afterwards scores 1.000 answer accuracy and 1.000 filing recall in all six cells of V x arrangement.
the_near_miss: the first solvency reader scored 0.583 in all six cells -- identical across V and arrangement, which is EXACTLY the signature of structure-independence I was predicting. 0.583 is the majority-class floor: it was answering False on all 60 cases. Cause: solvency names its parent `group` with NO NUMBER, breaking the name_number convention, so an entity pattern requiring the suffix dropped all 78 parent filings. The same bug was in the audit's generic pattern, so solvency's 0.000 had been computed with one of its two entity types invisible.
what_caught_it: NOT accuracy -- a constant scores the floor and 0.583 reads as a plausible weak reader. The OUTPUT DISTRIBUTION caught it in one line: 60 False / 0 True against a truth distribution of 35/25. Now a test.
also_caught_before_it_mattered: the audit's date regex matched only ISO, and solvency renders half its corpus as '1 June 2026' -- which would have been read as two bare numbers, silently changing every signature in half the corpus.
limits_recorded: the audit sees only CLAIM spans (solvency's threshold and determination date are prose the answer depends on); it assumes a naming convention unless given an entity pattern; and it measures collisions rather than CONSEQUENCES -- link/bridge_on costs nothing, depot/flooded costs everything. Dependency weighting would make it cardinal. Untried.

hypothesis: The audit is ordinal: it counts collisions, not consequences. flood's biggest collision by span mass is bridge_on/link at 520 spans and it costs NOTHING (the flow treats a bridge as a link carrying a limit, and the limit sentence identifies it); the 141-span depot/flooded/needs collision costs everything. Weighting by dependency alone does not fix this, because both involve high-dependency kinds -- what differs is RESOLVABILITY, which is currently human-judged.
the_move: do not reason about resolvability -- MEASURE the consequence directly. For each colliding signature group, permute the predicates among the claims whose spans share that signature, in the TRUE world, and solve. That is the cost of being unable to tell those kinds apart, and it is computed from the world and the surface WITHOUT A READER, which is the property that makes the audit predictive in the first place.
expected: depot/flooded/needs permutation costs 0.7-1.0 of answer accuracy; bridge_on/link costs ~0.000; capacity/load_limit is moderate. If so the audit becomes CARDINAL: the cost-weighted mass predicts the magnitude of the interleaving drop rather than only its sign, and scheduling/solvency stay at 0 because they have no collisions to permute.
would_change_my_mind: bridge_on/link costing significantly would mean the flow does NOT recover bridges structurally and my account of why that collision is harmless is wrong. depot/flooded/needs costing little would mean random role assignment is survivable and the interleaving collapse has a different cause than the collision -- which would undercut the whole instrument.

verdict: right, and the fix was simpler than the dependency weighting I planned
measured: depot+flooded+needs 141 spans (0.124 share) costs 0.625 over 40 cases; capacity+load_limit 43 spans (0.038) costs 0.550; bridge_on+link 520 spans (0.456) has ZERO PERMUTABLE CASES.
the_refinement: a sentence-signature collision is real ambiguity only if the colliding kinds also share a ROLE SIGNATURE. link carries (a,b) and bridge_on carries (a,b,via): identical in text, flood's largest collision at 456 per thousand spans, and there is NOTHING TO PERMUTE. With that filter flood reads 0.617 raw -> 0.161 real, and the two remaining collisions are exactly the ones that hurt.
honesty_note: the zero for bridge_on/link is STRUCTURAL, not empirical -- the permutation never fires, so the table reports permutable=0 rather than a cost measured over 40 cases. Reporting it as a measured zero would claim evidence never gathered.
span_mass_is_the_wrong_weight: the largest collision by mass costs nothing and the second smallest costs 0.550. Any weighting by how OFTEN kinds collide ranks these exactly backwards.
what_it_did_not_need: the ablation-measured dependency sizes I planned to use. Role signature settles which collisions are real; direct permutation in the true world settles what they cost. Both need NO READER, which is the property that lets the audit speak before one exists.

hypothesis: The audit sees only CLAIM spans. Two things are therefore invisible to it: information the answer depends on that is rendered as prose (solvency's covenant threshold and determination date -- I checked those BY HAND, which is what an instrument exists to stop), and DISTRACTOR sentences that share a signature with a real claim kind, which is a false-positive risk rather than an ambiguity.
expected: scoring every sentence should independently rediscover something already measured by hand: flood's 'Districts region_88 and region_91 lie outside the affected area' and 'A disused track once ran from region_88 to region_94' are both two regions with no number -- the LINK signature -- and the reader is already known to admit the disused track as a road. If the audit flags a prose/link collision without being told, it has found a real defect from the surface alone.
also_expected: solvency's prose should collide with nothing: its threshold sentence is (no entity, 1 money, no date) and its determination-date sentence is (no entity, no money, 1 date), neither of which any claim kind occupies. That is WHY reading them by shape worked, and the audit should now be able to say so instead of me.
would_change_my_mind: a prose collision in solvency I did not anticipate would mean its reader is fragile in a way the 1.000 in all six cells hides -- which would be worth knowing, since that reader is new and its 1.000 is doing a lot of work in the last two findings.

verdict: right on both counts, and the scan earned its place by rediscovering a known defect
measured: three flags across three domains, resolving three different ways. FLOOD 'A disused track once ran from X to Z' reads as link -- REAL: the reader admits one spurious link in every one of 20 cases, a defect previously found by hand and now rediscovered from the surface alone. SCHEDULING 'machine_90 is withdrawn' reads as has_capability -- NEUTRALISED: the reader admits 0 of 20, because the capability vocabulary doubles as the distractor filter. FLOOD 'The relief operation covers 6 districts' reads as load_limit -- FALSE ALARM: the audit counts any bare number while the reader requires the unit, so the audit's notion of a number is COARSER than the reader's.
solvency: zero prose collisions, exactly as predicted. Its threshold is (no entity, 1 money, no date) and its determination date (no entity, no money, 1 date), and no claim kind occupies either -- which is WHY reading them by shape works, and the audit can now say so instead of me checking by hand.
the_general_observation: in BOTH flood and scheduling the declared external knowledge does DOUBLE DUTY -- it settles signature collisions and it filters distractors. flood's value registry and scheduling's capability vocabulary are the same mechanism playing both roles.
status: the prose scan is a RISK REGISTER, not a defect list: each flag costs one check against the reader's declared knowledge. Better than reading the generator and hoping I noticed everything, which is how the flood defect was found the first time.

hypothesis: The prose scan found a real defect: flood's reader admits one spurious link in every one of 20 cases, from 'A disused track once ran from X to Z; it has not carried traffic for years.' That sentence carries exactly the link signature. It is currently HARMLESS because the generator draws its endpoints from _OUTSIDE = (region_88, region_91, region_94), which appear nowhere else in the world -- so the phantom edge connects nothing. The defect is masked by a GENERATOR CHOICE, not by reader design, and a real report could describe a disused track between two real places.
expected: pointing the distractor at two REAL, unlinked regions should break the reader: the phantom edge creates routes that do not exist, so answers become too permissive -- vehicles admitted that cannot actually reach the site. I expect a substantial accuracy drop, larger where the phantom edge bypasses a flooded region or a low bridge.
the_deeper_point: by the audit's own logic this is unresolvable without content. The disused-track sentence has EXACTLY the link signature -- two regions, no number -- so no content-free observable separates it from a real road, and distractor rejection is another instance of the closure result rather than a separate problem. That also explains why scheduling's capability vocabulary works as a distractor filter: it is CONTENT.
would_change_my_mind: the reader surviving would mean the flow is robust to phantom edges -- plausible if every route it finds is re-checked against bridge limits and flooding, in which case a phantom edge only adds candidate routes that get pruned. That would be a real robustness property of the FLOW rather than the reader, and worth knowing.

verdict: right, and it corrects one of my own headlines
measured: pointing the disused-track distractor at two REAL unlinked regions -- nothing else changed, same claims, same phrasings, same answer, same span alignment -- costs 1.000 -> 0.367 grouped and 1.000 -> 0.383 interleaved. Two region ids in one sentence are worth -0.633.
the_sharper_detail: the interleaved rows admit TWICE the spurious links (2.00 vs 1.00 per case), because interleaving destroys the paragraph grouping that picks the network paragraph so the 'districts lie outside' distractor gets in too -- and they still scored 1.000 published, because both phantom edges are inert. The reader was being scored on a surface where its false claims could not matter.
corrects: the 'signature+content scores 1.000 in all four cells' headline. It is bounded TWICE over: by the phrasings it has words for (the adversarial-variant ceiling) and by a distractor the generator declined to arm. Honest range 0.333-1.000 depending which props are removed.
unification: the sentence has EXACTLY the link signature, so no content-free observable separates a disused track from a road -- the same closure that holds for depot vs flooded, reached from a completely different direction. Distractor rejection is not a separate task from role assignment; both are the signature failing to fix the predicate, and both need content. That also explains why scheduling's capability vocabulary works as a distractor filter: it IS content.
alternative_rejected: I wrote down that the flow might absorb phantom edges by re-checking every route against flooding and bridge limits. It does not -- those checks pass, because the edge itself is the lie.
shipped: render_observation(hard_distractors=True), default False so every published number keeps its meaning.

hypothesis: The milestone table is the programme's north-star measurement -- $ per solved episode with the reader in front -- and it is doubly stale. It uses read_signature, whose 1.000 is now known to be hard-coded paragraph indices, on the EASY surface: grouped paragraphs, section headings, and a distractor whose phantom edge connects regions appearing nowhere else. Every prop that has been removed this week is still in place there.
expected: re-running it honestly -- V=4, interleaved, hard_distractors=True, with the readers that actually exist now -- should INVERT its central conclusion. The published decomposition says reader loss 0.000 and the KERNEL losses dominate (no SMT 0.500, no datalog 0.818, no ASP search 0.864). With an honest surface the best reader lands near 0.333, so reader loss ~0.667 should exceed every kernel loss, and $/correct should rise roughly threefold because the same spend buys a third of the correct answers.
the_number_i_actually_want: not the accuracy -- the DECOMPOSITION. Where does the loss sit once the surface stops helping? If reader loss dominates, the programme's marginal effort belongs in reading rather than in kernels or routing, and that is a different allocation from the one the published table implies.
would_change_my_mind: reader loss staying below the kernel losses would mean the honest surface is still easier than the kernels are hard, and the published allocation survives. Grounding falling below 1.000 would be a separate and worse finding -- it would mean the renderer cites claims the reader invented, so a false claim would reach the user as a grounded sentence.

verdict: prediction half right; the important finding was one I had not predicted at all
measured: honest surface (V=4, interleaved, hard_distractors=True): oracle 1.000 at $1.78e-08; signature+content 0.500 at $3.69e-08 (2.1x); signature/roles, signature/index, rules and lexical all 0.000. Reader loss 0.500 MATCHES the worst kernel loss (no SMT 0.500) rather than exceeding it -- I predicted ~0.667 exceeding everything. The published table says reader loss 0.000 and kernels dominate.
unpredicted_and_more_important: CLAIM RECALL IS THE WRONG READER COLUMN. signature+content scores 0.998 recall with 0.500 accuracy, because its failure is a claim it ADDS and recall cannot see a false positive. The milestone reports recall as its reader-quality column.
the_finding_i_nearly_inverted: grounding reads 1.000 in every row including the half-wrong ones, and my script's first draft printed 'grounding intact -- a false claim does not reach the user as a grounded sentence'. FALSE. ungrounded() builds its admissible edges from the routes the flow computed FROM THE READ WORLD, so a route over an invented claim is self-consistent and passes. Demonstrated on seed 1: true answer EMPTY, rendered as 'truck_0 runs region_0 to region_3' over a road existing in no claim, ungrounded() returns []. The property is INTERNAL CONSISTENCY WITH THE WORLD AS READ, not truth -- it catches renderer errors and cannot by construction catch reader errors.
shipped: scope in ungrounded()'s docstring, and tests/test_grounding_scope.py pinning BOTH halves -- that a grounded paragraph can walk a non-existent road, and that a paragraph contradicting the structured answer is still rejected. The second is what stops the first reading as an excuse.

hypothesis: The grounding finding leaves one honest response open. Nothing downstream of a reader can see the true world, so no check catches an invented claim -- but the reader can DECLINE TO COLLAPSE. The audit already says, offline, that flood's (2 regions, 0 number) signature is shared with prose. The reader cannot tell WHICH link sentence is the distractor, but it knows the kind is suspect, so it can emit the ambiguity and let the flow answer only where every candidate world agrees. That is directive 19 applied to distractors rather than roles, which the last finding showed are the same problem.
the_bound: enumerating all subsets of suspect links is exponential and would be vacuous, so the hypothesis is bounded: AT MOST ONE link is spurious. That gives k+1 worlds for k links -- the full set, plus each single-link deletion -- which is cheap and is exactly the generator's actual situation.
expected: soundness 1.000 by construction (the true world is among the candidates when at most one link is spurious), and decidedness LOW, because most links are load-bearing and dropping one changes the answer. I expect decided somewhere in 0.2-0.5, which would mirror the earlier result that carrying ROLE ambiguity is sound and rapidly vacuous.
why_run_it_rather_than_assume: the direction is predictable; the MAGNITUDE is not, and it decides whether this is a usable policy or a dead end. Decided 0.5 converts a silent 50% error rate into a sound half-answer and is worth shipping; decided 0.05 is vacuous and the note should say so.
would_change_my_mind: soundness below 1.000 would mean the at-most-one-spurious hypothesis is wrong for this generator -- worth knowing, since it is stated as exact.

verdict: soundness as predicted; decidedness far better than predicted, and the sets are IDENTICAL
measured: collapse answers everything at 0.383 accuracy. Carrying at-most-one-spurious gives soundness 1.000 with 0.383 decided, median 16 candidate worlds per case. The decided set and the collapse-correct set are the SAME 23 cases: 0 decided-but-wrong, 0 correct-but-undecided.
i_predicted: decided 0.2-0.5 and expected it to MIRROR the earlier role-ambiguity result of sound-but-vacuous. It landed at 0.383, in range, but the identity of the two sets was not predicted -- the policy gives up NOTHING and flags EVERY error.
the_important_distinction: decided => correct is PROVABLE by construction (true world among candidates + all agree => the common answer is true). correct => decided is EMPIRICAL -- a collapsing reader could be accidentally right while candidates disagree, and on 60 cases it never was. Nothing guarantees it; on less redundant road networks it would fail, and the policy would still be sound while starting to pay coverage. The test is NAMED for that fragility and its docstring tells a later session to treat failure as information rather than regression.
the_arc_it_completes: carrying ROLE ambiguity was measured sound and rapidly vacuous (72 worlds deciding 0.0%). Carrying DISTRACTOR ambiguity is sound and here free. The difference is the BOUND: role permutation enumerates a combinatorial space with no structure, at-most-one-spurious is a single bounded hypothesis the generator satisfies. Ambiguity is cheap to carry when the hypothesis about it is small.
why_it_matters: 0.383 correct with no way to tell which is a SILENT error rate; 0.383 decided at soundness 1.000 is a BOUNDED one. For a pipeline arguing its reasoning is inspectable rather than inferred, that is the difference between a component you can build on and one you cannot.

hypothesis: I ended the last finding with a general claim -- AMBIGUITY IS CHEAP TO CARRY WHEN THE HYPOTHESIS ABOUT IT IS SMALL -- on the strength of one comparison: unbounded role permutation was sound and vacuous (72 worlds, 0.0% decided), bounded at-most-one-spurious-link was sound and free. One comparison is not a principle, and the two differ in the claim KIND as well as the bound, so the variable is confounded.
the_clean_test: take the SAME ambiguity -- flood's depot/flooded/needs role assignment, the one measured vacuous -- and vary only the bound. Enumerate worlds within k role swaps of the reader's reading, for k = 0, 1, 2, 3, and measure soundness and decidedness at each. Same domain, same reader, same collision; hypothesis size is the only thing that moves. That turns a slogan into a curve and makes k a controlling quantity in the theory ledger's sense.
expected: k=0 is the collapsing reader: decided 1.000 and soundness equal to its accuracy, which is 0.000 interleaved. Soundness should rise steeply with k and decidedness fall, with the useful region at small k. I expect soundness to reach 1.000 by k=2 or 3 (there are three roles, so any misassignment is within a few swaps) and decidedness to be near 0 by then -- reproducing the vacuity result as the LIMIT of the curve rather than as a separate fact.
the_number_that_decides_it: whether any k has BOTH soundness near 1.000 and decidedness usefully above 0. If yes, the principle holds and bounded role ambiguity is usable after all, which would overturn the earlier vacuity finding. If no, the principle is narrower than I stated: it is not hypothesis SIZE that made the link case cheap but something about links specifically, and I should say so.
note: deliberately low. I stated the principle on one comparison and this is the experiment that can embarrass it.

verdict: MY OWN PRINCIPLE WAS WRONG, and the experiment I ran to test it said so
measured: k=0: soundness 0.433, decided 1.000. k=1: 0.867, 0.067. k=2: 0.867, 0.067. k=3: 1.000, 0.017. Decidedness COLLAPSES at the first step and soundness does not reach 1.000 until k=3 where 1.7% is decided. No useful middle anywhere on the curve.
what_i_claimed: 'ambiguity is cheap to carry when the hypothesis about it is small', stated at the end of the previous finding on ONE comparison whose two arms differed in claim KIND as well as bound. Confounded, and not earned. I gave the test 0.45 confidence and said it could embarrass the claim.
the_real_variable: DEPENDENCY, not hypothesis size. A spurious LINK is often inert because the network has other paths; a misassigned ROLE is never inert -- it moves the depot, the destination or the flooding, and the answer depends on all three.
the_instrument_already_knew: the audit's COLLISION COST, measured offline with no reader: 0.000 for bridge_on/link (nothing permutable) and 0.625 for depot+flooded+needs. Those exactly predict carrying being free vs vacuous. That is a SECOND USE for the audit -- it forecasts whether emit-rather-than-collapse will be usable on a given ambiguity -- and I had the number on disk without connecting it.
corrected_statement: carried ambiguity is cheap exactly when the ambiguous kind has LOW COLLISION COST, which is a measurable property of the domain rather than of how the hypothesis is phrased.
weakness_of_the_correction: it rests on TWO POINTS IN ONE DOMAIN, which is the same weakness that sank the first version. Scheduling and solvency audit at zero collisions so neither can test it. Labelled as such.

hypothesis: Setting up a third point for the corrected principle exposed an error IN the correction. I attributed 'carrying links is cheap' to the audit's COLLISION COST of 0.000 for bridge_on/link. That number measures PERMUTATION between two kinds and is 0.000 because their ROLE SIGNATURES DIFFER -- nothing is permutable. What the link policy actually carries is a SPURIOUS CLAIM, tested by DELETION. Two different quantities that coincided at zero, and I read the coincidence as a prediction.
the_right_variable: the dependency of the claim kind UNDER THE PERTURBATION BEING CARRIED. For links that is deletion: does removing one real link change the answer? For roles it is reassignment: does moving depot/needs/flooded change the answer? Those are what the enumerations actually explore.
expected: link DELETION dependency well below 1.0 -- often inert, because the network has other paths -- and role REASSIGNMENT dependency at or near 1.0, since every role the answer depends on moves. If so the corrected principle survives with the RIGHT number substituted, and the audit's collision cost is revealed as a different quantity that agreed by accident.
also_expected: solvency's owns has measured deletion dependency of exactly ZERO (0/60 verdicts change, 0 members lost), so it is the low-dependency point in a SECOND domain that the last finding said was missing.
would_change_my_mind: link deletion dependency near 1.0 would mean carrying spurious links should have been vacuous and was not, so something else entirely explains the free ride -- most likely that the phantom edge is usually redundant with an existing path rather than that links are individually inert.

verdict: right, and it corrects MY OWN CORRECTION from the previous turn
measured: dependency under the perturbation actually carried -- flood link DELETION 0.138 (carried free), flood role REASSIGNMENT 0.467 (carried vacuous), solvency owns DELETION exactly 0.000 (inert, nothing to carry). Separation 3.4x in the right direction.
the_error_being_corrected: I had replaced the failed hypothesis-size principle with 'cheap when COLLISION COST is low', citing 0.000 for bridge_on/link. Collision cost measures PERMUTATION between kinds and is 0.000 there because their ROLE SIGNATURES DIFFER so nothing is permutable. What the link policy carries is a SPURIOUS CLAIM, explored by DELETION. Two different quantities, both low for unrelated reasons, and I read the coincidence as a prediction.
also_wrong_in_my_explanation: I said a misassigned role is NEVER inert. It is 0.467, not 1.0. The link is inert three times as often, which is the real contrast.
what_is_still_not_established: any functional form. Two real carrying measurements only; owns adds an extreme point with nothing to carry, anchoring the variable without testing the relationship. Same thinness that sank both previous versions, stated up front this time.
the_guard: collision_cost and deletion_dependency now sit beside each other in audit.py, each documenting that they are NOT the same number with the bridge_on/link case as the worked example, and a test asserts both (permutable 0, deletion dependency in (0, 0.4)).
how_it_was_caught: not by a control or a refuter -- by building the NEXT experiment on top of the claim and noticing mid-write that the cited quantity was not the carried one. An argument for building promptly rather than polishing.

hypothesis: Three formulations of 'when is carried ambiguity cheap' have now failed or been thinned. The honest gap is that no FUNCTIONAL FORM is established, on two carrying measurements. There is a derivation available instead of a fourth slogan. Carrying at-most-one-spurious-of-kind-K decides exactly when NO SINGLE DELETION of a K claim changes the answer. If d is the per-deletion dependency and n the number of K claims, independence gives decided = (1-d)^n, with NO FREE PARAMETER -- d and n are both measured.
status_of_the_form: this is an exact identity given independence, so the experiment is a test OF INDEPENDENCE, not of a fitted model. That is the useful kind: the residual has a meaning.
expected: the model UNDER-predicts decidedness, because deletions of the same kind are positively correlated -- the structural redundancy that makes one link inert makes several inert at once, so P(all inert) exceeds the product of marginals. I expect the gap to be largest for kinds with many claims (link) and smallest for singleton kinds (depot, needs, demand) where n=1 makes the model exact by construction.
what_it_buys: six-ish points in one domain instead of two, an explicit derivation, and a residual that means something -- correlation between deletions -- rather than a slogan. Still ONE domain, which stays the stated weakness.
would_change_my_mind: the model over-predicting would mean deletions are ANTI-correlated, which would be surprising and would need a mechanism before I believed it.

verdict: the form holds; MY PREDICTION ABOUT THE RESIDUAL WAS AN ARTEFACT OF POOLING
measured: non-empty population, nine kinds: mean absolute residual 0.036 against decided = (1-d)^n with no free parameter, signs both ways, six multi-claim rows at +0.006 mean signed. Independence HOLDS.
what_i_predicted: independence FAILS with positive correlation from structural redundancy, making (1-d)^n a lower bound. That is exactly what the POOLED numbers say (+0.131) and it is an artefact of the case mix -- on an already-empty answer almost every deletion is inert, so decidedness floors at the empty-answer share.
the_tell: five kinds reading EXACTLY 0.433 -- flood's empty share -- with different n and different d. No real mechanism produces that.
re_checked_the_previous_finding: 'carrying links gave up nothing, 0.383 decided' was also pooled. Split: empty 0.115/0.115, non-empty 0.588/0.588. The decided==correct identity holds WITHIN each population and pooling UNDERSTATED the rate. The check was worth running and the answer went the other way.
scope_stated: measured on TRUE worlds, so it characterises the DOMAIN rather than a reader. A real policy enumerates over the READ world whose d and n differ -- true-world link 0.059 vs read-world carrying 0.588 -- and comparing those directly would be the next mistake on this thread.
status: controlling variable identified, functional form derived and unfitted, error 0.036 over six non-trivial kinds. Still ONE domain.

hypothesis: I recorded that the (1-d)^n law rests on one domain because 'scheduling and solvency cannot test it -- neither has an ambiguity worth carrying'. That is WRONG and I am correcting it before building on it. The law is about DELETION DEPENDENCY OF A CLAIM KIND, which every domain has and which needs no reader. Solvency's revenue and scheduling's duration/capacity/capabilities are all deletable.
the_sharper_form: the identity is PER CASE -- decided = E_case[(1-d_case)^n_case]. Plugging a POOLED MEAN d into (1-d)^n is an approximation that fails under heterogeneity by Jensen, and that is exactly what the flood pooled failure was: an empty-answer subpopulation with d near 0 mixed with a non-empty one with d high. So the per-case form should hold on BOTH populations while the mean-d form fails on the pooled one.
expected: per-case form accurate (mean absolute residual under ~0.05) on all three domains and on the pooled population as well as the non-empty one; mean-d form failing on pooled flood by roughly the +0.131 already measured. If so the law is cross-domain, has no free parameter, and its one previous failure is explained rather than excluded by a population rule.
would_change_my_mind: the per-case form failing on solvency or scheduling would mean deletions there are genuinely correlated in a way flood's are not -- worth knowing, and it would make the law domain-specific rather than general.

verdict: the law generalises to three domains; my prediction about WHICH estimator wins was half wrong
measured: non-degenerate population, three domains, twelve claim kinds: (1-dbar)^nbar tracks observed decidedness to 0.033 mean absolute error with signed bias +0.005, no free parameter. Extremes show the mechanism: solvency revenue decides 0.000 (every filing moves the sum) and solvency owns decides 1.000 (recoverable from the filings), same law, opposite ends.
corrected_my_scope_note: I had written that scheduling and solvency could not test the law. Wrong -- it is about DELETION DEPENDENCY OF A CLAIM KIND, which every domain has and which needs no reader; only the POLICY needs one.
the_swap_i_did_not_predict: per-case E[(1-d)^n] wins ONLY when pooling (0.040 vs 0.183) and LOSES on the clean population (0.051 vs 0.033). I predicted it would win everywhere.
why_per_case_wins_pooled: Jensen. Averaging d before exponentiating over a bimodal case mix. That -- not correlation between deletions -- is what the previous finding's +0.131 was. My earlier 'structural redundancy makes several claims inert at once' was a mechanism invented to fit a number with a simpler cause.
why_per_case_loses_clean: it SMOOTHS A DETERMINISTIC OUTCOME. Within a case d is measured from the very deletions being tested, so with k of n load-bearing the truth is 0 for any k>=1 while (1-k/n)^n stays positive. Systematic over-prediction, visible as negative signed error in both populations, and a property of the ESTIMATOR not the domain.
usable_rule: mean-d on a homogeneous population, per-case only if you must pool.
still_not_established: that this predicts a READER's decidedness. The law characterises the domain; a policy enumerates over the READ world whose d and n differ.

hypothesis: The programme's north star is $ per solved episode, and the honest milestone reports the collapsing reader at 0.500 accuracy with no abstention. The carrying policy reaches soundness 1.000 -- never wrong when it answers -- but it runs k+1 solves per case where the collapsing reader runs one. Soundness is NOT free, and the north-star metric is exactly the place that should show its price. It currently does not, because abstention has never been priced through cost.py's framing.
expected: the carrying policy costs roughly the candidate count -- median 16 on flood -- times the collapsing reader's spend, while answering on only the decided share. So $ per CORRECT answer should rise by about 16 / (decided share) relative to the collapsing reader's $ per correct, i.e. somewhere near an order of magnitude. My estimate: 10-20x.
what_makes_it_worth_measuring: the number IS the trade. A pipeline arguing its reasoning is inspectable rather than inferred has to be able to say what inspectability costs, and 'soundness 1.000' quoted without a price is the same error as 'grounded 1.000' quoted without a scope -- both of which this thread has already made.
would_change_my_mind: a much smaller multiple would mean most candidate solves are cheap because the flow short-circuits on the deletions, which would make soundness far more affordable than the candidate count suggests -- and would be the better outcome.

verdict: in range, and one property was better than expected
measured: 34 non-empty cases. Collapse answers 34, right 20, $1.35e-08 per correct. Carry answers 20, right 20, soundness 1.000, $2.11e-07 per correct -- 15.6x. Early exit 13.4x, mean solves 16.0 -> 13.7. I predicted 10-20x.
the_property_i_did_not_predict: it discards ONLY WRONG ANSWERS. Collapse right 20/34, carry right 20/20 -- the SAME twenty. Every refused case is one the collapsing reader would have got wrong, so the $/correct multiple equals the compute multiple exactly because the numerator does not move. Stronger than the usual 'sound at some coverage cost' shape, and measured rather than proven -- the test names it as the fragile half.
early_exit_disappointed: exact (decided set unchanged, asserted by test) but only 14% saving, not the near-halving the 14/34 undecided share suggests. On an undecided case the disagreement appears LATE: deletion dependency is 0.243, so the enumeration works through many inert candidates before the one that matters. The load-bearing claim is a needle.
next_optimisation: order candidates by measured deletion_dependency, which the audit already computes. Untried, and it would help exactly to the extent dependency is unevenly spread within a kind.
why_it_matters: a system arguing its reasoning is inspectable rather than inferred should be able to say what inspectability costs. 13.4x per correct answer, buying the ability never to be wrong when it speaks, on a surface where the alternative is right half the time with no signal.

hypothesis: The last finding named 'order candidates by measured deletion_dependency' as the next optimisation. That is WRONG AS STATED and I am correcting it before building: deletion_dependency is measured PER KIND, and every candidate in the link policy is the same kind. Within a kind, which claim is load-bearing varies case by case, so a kind-level number cannot order anything.
what_is_needed: a PER-CLAIM proxy for load-bearing-ness, computable WITHOUT solving. For links there is an obvious one: does removing this edge disconnect the depot from the delivery site in the read world's graph? That is an O(V+E) reachability check against a full datalog+ASP+SMT flow solve, so it is free by comparison.
why_ordering_is_safe: early exit is EXACT whatever the order -- one disagreement settles the case as undecided. Ordering changes only HOW SOON the disagreement is found, never which cases are decided. So a heuristic here cannot cost soundness, which is the property that makes it worth doing at all.
expected: mean solves fall from 13.7 toward 6-9, taking the price of soundness from 13.4x to roughly 6-9x. The load-bearing deletion is a needle -- deletion dependency 0.243 -- and a disconnection test should find it near-immediately when one exists.
would_change_my_mind: little saving would mean the answer-changing deletions are NOT the disconnecting ones -- more likely they act through load limits or flooding interactions, in which case connectivity is the wrong proxy and the right one is more expensive.

verdict: the proxy failed completely, and the direction was capped before I started
measured: disconnect-first ordering saves 0.0% -- mean solves 13.7 both ways, decided set identical. Not a mis-ranking: 0 of 270 candidate deletions disconnect depot->site, because the read graph carries extra links (bridges from crossings, phantom, distractor) and is redundant. Answer-changing deletions are 3.7% of candidates and act through LOAD LIMITS, not reachability.
the_bound_i_should_have_computed_first: an oracle ordering runs EVERY candidate on a decided case -- agreement must be PROVEN -- and two on an undecided one. Directly from per-case data: 13.7 -> 10.2 mean solves, so ANY ordering saves at most 25%, taking 13.4x to 10.0x at best. Early exit only helps undecided cases and they are the minority, 14 of 34.
the_real_conclusion: ordering is not where the cost is. THE COST IS THAT PROVING AGREEMENT REQUIRES EXHAUSTING THE CANDIDATES. Going below the ceiling needs a CERTIFICATE that no single deletion can change the answer, not an enumeration that checks each one -- and symbolic_ai_core/runtime/certificate.py already carries Sensitivity and slack machinery for exactly that question. Untried, and it could take a decided case from sixteen solves to one.
also_corrected: the previous finding named 'order by deletion_dependency', which is per KIND while every candidate here is the same kind. A kind-level number cannot order within a kind.
lesson: compute the ceiling of an optimisation before optimising. The bound was cheap and would have capped this at 25% before any proxy was written.

hypothesis: Enumeration is the wrong shape: proving agreement costs sixteen solves because every candidate must be checked. A CERTIFICATE can do it in one, and flood has a clean one because DELETING A LINK IS MONOTONE -- it removes routes, never creates them.
the_certificate: a vehicle qualifies iff capacity >= demand and some non-flooded route has min bridge limit >= mass + demand. Under deletion: a NON-qualifying vehicle can never start qualifying (monotone, free), and a qualifying one stops only if every admissible route used the deleted edge. So the sufficient condition is that for every qualifying vehicle, depot and site stay connected in that vehicle's admissible subgraph after removing ANY single edge -- 2-edge-connectivity, one DFS per edge, O(V+E) each, against a full datalog+ASP+SMT solve sixteen times.
expected: the certificate fires on most decided cases -- I estimate 60-90% -- taking mean solves from 13.7 toward 4-7 and the price of soundness from 13.4x toward 4-7x. It is SUFFICIENT not necessary, so cases where it does not fire still enumerate; that costs nothing but the certificate check.
the_check_that_matters: SOUNDNESS AGAINST THE ACTUAL FLOW, not against my reasoning. The flow enumerates routes through ASP with a max_routes cap, so its answer may not equal the graph-theoretic truth my certificate reasons about. If the certificate ever says invariant where enumeration says undecided, it is unsound as implemented and that must be reported rather than explained away.
would_change_my_mind: any soundness violation kills it as a shortcut -- a certificate that is sometimes wrong is worse than an enumeration that is slow, because the whole point of the policy is never being wrong when it answers.

verdict: better than predicted -- sound AND apparently exact
measured: 95 non-empty cases over 150 seeds: 50 decided, certificate fires 50, 0 unsound, 0 incomplete. Mean solves 16.0 -> 7.2 trusting only the proved direction, -> 1.0 trusting the measured converse. Price of soundness 13.4x -> 6.0x proved -> 1.0x exact.
i_predicted: fires on 60-90% of decided cases, price toward 4-7x. It fires on 100% and is exact, which I did not predict.
the_argument: SUFFICIENCY IS PROVED by monotonicity -- deleting a link removes routes and never creates them, so a vehicle that cannot qualify cannot be made to qualify, and only qualifying vehicles need proving. NECESSITY is measured exact and argued: if the certificate fails, some qualifying vehicle has a cut edge whose deletion disconnects it from the site, so it drops out and the answer changes. One assumption -- the flow's answer coinciding with the graph condition, which ASP's route cap could break and empirically does not.
the_headline: SOUNDNESS BECOMES FREE. One solve for the answer plus a DFS to decide whether to give it is exactly what the collapsing reader spends, for the same twenty correct answers, so $/correct is unchanged. The difference between 13.4x and 1.0x is the difference between CHECKING every candidate and PROVING none of them matters.
generality: needs a MONOTONE perturbation (so half the objects are free) and a STRUCTURAL INVARIANT standing in for the expensive computation (here 2-edge-connectivity for 'a route survives'). Not flood-specific, but the certificate as built covers DELETIONS only -- corrupting a limit is not monotone and the free half disappears.

hypothesis: I claimed the certificate pattern is 'not flood-specific' on ONE instance. That is the generality-from-one-case error this thread has already made three times, so it gets tested. The pattern needs two ingredients and scheduling separates them cleanly: it HAS monotonicity -- deleting a has_capability claim can only make an instance infeasible, never feasible -- but its decision is NP-hard, so it may LACK the cheap structural invariant that 2-edge-connectivity provided for flood.
expected: the monotone half alone pays: an INFEASIBLE instance is safe for free, exactly as flood's non-qualifying vehicles were, so at roughly half feasible on this generator the mean solves should fall by about half. The other half -- FEASIBLE instances -- should still need enumeration, because there is no polynomial structural characterisation of 'a feasible assignment survives deleting any one capability claim' the way reachability characterises 'a route survives'.
the_general_statement_being_tested: a certificate replaces enumeration where the kernel's decision has a cheap structural characterisation, and only the monotone half transfers where it does not. If that is right, the pattern's reach is set by the COMPLEXITY OF THE UNDERLYING DECISION rather than by anything about readers or ambiguity.
would_change_my_mind: finding a cheap sufficient invariant for scheduling feasibility -- something like 'every job has two capable machines with slack' -- that fires often enough to matter would mean NP-hardness does not block the pattern, only makes the invariant weaker. That would be the better outcome and I have not found one.

verdict: exactly as predicted, and the failing half failed hard
measured: 60 scheduling instances, delete one has_capability. Monotone certificate (infeasible is safe) fires 43, UNSOUND 0, worth 57% on its own (6.6 -> 2.9 mean solves). Structural attempt ('every job has two capable machines with room') fires on 9 feasible instances and is UNSOUND ON 8 of them.
the_general_statement: the certificate pattern's reach is set by the COMPLEXITY OF THE UNDERLYING DECISION, not by anything about readers or ambiguity. Reachability characterises 'a route survives' in polynomial time so flood gets a complete certificate and soundness becomes free; nothing characterises 'a feasible packing survives' without solving it, so scheduling gets only the monotone half.
why_the_structural_half_fails: two capable machines guarantee the CAPABILITY survives a deletion and say nothing about whether the PACKING still fits. That is where bin-packing bites.
the_free_half: the safe side of a monotone perturbation costs ZERO and needs nothing from the domain -- a vehicle that cannot qualify, an instance already infeasible, neither can be flipped by a perturbation that only removes. Any pipeline carrying a deletion-shaped ambiguity gets that half without a structural insight.
presentation_fix: the combined row reads 1.8 solves and 73% and is WRONG. Relabelled in place as not-a-saving, because an unsound certificate looks like the best row in the table and the number must not be liftable out of context.
how_to_use_it: in a new domain, ask whether the kernel's decision has a polynomial structural characterisation. If yes, expect a free certificate; if no, expect the monotone half and budget enumeration for the rest.

hypothesis: Both certificates so far cover DELETIONS, which are monotone -- and monotonicity is what makes half the objects free. The stated limit is that a MISREAD NUMBER is not monotone: a corrupted bridge limit can push either way, so nothing is safe by direction. That is a real failure mode here, since the load-limit sentence carries two numbers ('was rated at OLD kg ... it is now rated for NEW kg'), the reader takes the last, and the audit priced the capacity/load_limit collision at 0.550.
the_candidate_certificate: MARGIN rather than structure. A misreading only matters if it moves a limit ACROSS a vehicle's threshold. So: for every limit claim e with alternative value L', and every vehicle v with threshold t = mass+demand, if (L_e >= t) == (L'_e >= t) then no misreading changes any edge's admissibility for any vehicle, and the answer is invariant. O(E x V) comparisons, no graph work at all, and clearly sound.
expected: the certificate fires but LESS often than the structural one, because it needs the actual numbers to stay on one side of a threshold and the generator picks superseded values 500-2500 kg away -- enough to cross sometimes. I expect it to fire on 50-80% of decided cases. The FREE HALF IS GONE: no vehicle is safe by direction, so every one must be checked, though checking is arithmetic rather than search.
the_general_point_being_tested: whether cheap certification survives the loss of monotonicity. If margin substitutes for direction, the pattern is broader than the deletion case and the requirement is a CHEAP INVARIANT of any shape, not monotonicity specifically. If it does not fire often enough to matter, monotonicity was doing the real work and non-monotone ambiguity is genuinely more expensive.
would_change_my_mind: the certificate firing on essentially every decided case would mean margin is as good as direction and the monotonicity emphasis in the last two findings was overstated.

verdict: margin works but is incomplete; chasing WHY produced a much larger finding about the benchmark
measured: margin certificate for a misread bridge limit: fires 19, UNSOUND 0, misses 9 of 28 decided, 37% saving. Adding a relevance test (ignore edges on no depot->site path) changed NOTHING -- 19 fires and 9 missed either way, because every bridge edge is already on some path. My explanation for the misses was wrong.
the_larger_finding: the misses needed ROUTE-LEVEL reasoning, which is a WIDEST-PATH computation -- and a max-min Dijkstra reproduces the full datalog+ASP+SMT answer on 200 OF 200 CASES. FLOOD'S DECISION IS IN P and its kernel stack is exponential machinery on it.
what_it_reframes: 'a certificate makes soundness free' is true but the mechanism is not the elegant one I gave -- the certificate is exact because it IS the decision, and a polynomial restatement can of course settle insensitivity in one pass. And flood's cost figures measure THE PIPELINE, not THE TASK: real costs of the system built, but not evidence that heterogeneous kernels are needed here.
what_it_leaves_standing: everything about READING -- the reader arms, the audit, the closure result, the decidedness law, the honest milestone's decomposition -- none of which depends on how the answer is computed once the world is known. And scheduling, whose feasibility is genuinely NP-hard, which is exactly why the previous finding measured the structural half failing there.
the_control: an equivalence could hold because both sides ignore the hard parts, so a test asserts that removing flooding changes the bottleneck on some case and likewise for limits. Both fire.
lesson: before pricing an expensive computation, ask what the decision actually requires. The check cost twenty lines and should have come first.

hypothesis: Flood's decision turned out to be in P despite three kernels. Solvency's is openly polynomial -- sum the latest figure per member, compare to a threshold. I asserted scheduling is the genuinely hard one because feasibility is bin-packing with capability constraints. But NP-hard IN PRINCIPLE is not the same as hard ON THIS GENERATOR'S DISTRIBUTION, and I have not checked.
the_test: a two-sided POLYNOMIAL procedure: the capacity gate proves infeasible when total demand exceeds total capacity, and a greedy placement (longest job first onto the capable machine with most room) proves feasible when it succeeds. Neither can be wrong; together they are inconclusive only in the middle. Measure what share of the generator's instances they settle, across slack.
expected: at the default slack=0.15 the pair settles the large majority -- I estimate 85-95% -- because loose instances are greedily packable and tight ones fail the capacity bound. The inconclusive band should be narrow and centred near slack 0. If so, the honest statement is that the benchmark suite exercises search on a small minority of its instances, and NO domain here supports 'heterogeneous kernels are necessary' on its own distribution.
why_it_matters: this is the programme-level version of the flood finding. If the instances that need search are rare, then the cost figures across all three domains are measuring machinery against tasks that mostly do not require it, and the benchmark needs a hard regime rather than the kernels needing a defence.
would_change_my_mind: a large inconclusive band at the default settings would mean scheduling genuinely exercises search and the suite has one honest hard domain, which is the better outcome.

verdict: WRONG, in the better direction, and the shape of the answer is the finding
measured: a two-sided polynomial procedure (capacity gate proves infeasible, greedy placement proves feasible; both one-sided sound, both asserted by tests) settles only 26.7% at the default 6x3/slack 0.15 and 45.6% averaged over a grid of three shapes x seven slacks. I predicted 85-95% settled.
so_the_suite_has_one_hard_domain: scheduling genuinely exercises search, unlike flood (widest path) and solvency (sum vs threshold). Two of three domains are decorative with respect to kernel necessity; the third is not.
the_sharper_finding: ONLY 15.5% OF THE INCONCLUSIVE BAND IS FEASIBLE. At 6x3/0.15, 0.28 of instances are feasible and greedy proves 0.27 of them -- it exhibits an assignment for nearly every instance that has one. What nothing polynomial provides is a CERTIFICATE THAT NO ASSIGNMENT EXISTS. THE KERNELS EARN THEIR KEEP PROVING NEGATIVES.
unifies_three_earlier_results: ASP's UNSAT side being the expensive one (a negative needs exhaustion, a positive needs one witness); capacity_gate removing 87.7% of solver time by proving infeasibility cheaply; and the certificate work's monotone half making INFEASIBLE instances free in scheduling and NON-QUALIFYING vehicles free in flood. Same asymmetry three times.
where_to_sample: the band is widest JUST ABOVE SLACK 0 -- 100% at 6x3/+0.02, 98% at 20x5/+0.02 -- where capacity is sufficient but capabilities do not line up. That is the regime for studying search, and it is not the default.
not_refutable_by_a_better_heuristic: a stronger packer would prove more instances feasible but cannot prove any infeasible, so the 84.5% of the band that is infeasible is untouchable by that route. Only a polynomial INFEASIBILITY certificate stronger than the capacity bound would shrink it.

hypothesis: The suite's only genuinely hard domain is scheduling, and it is hard ASYMMETRICALLY -- on the infeasible side, where nothing polynomial certifies that no assignment exists. The inconclusive band is widest JUST ABOVE SLACK 0 (100% at 6x3/+0.02) and the generator's default sits at slack 0.15, where a polynomial pair already settles 27%. So every scheduling number this repo has measured comes from the easy band.
the_work: make the hard regime available additively -- default unchanged, since published numbers depend on it -- and price what proving a negative costs there against the default.
expected: ASP cost per instance several times higher in the band than at the default, with a larger share hitting any budget, because the band is exactly the barely-infeasible region where the solver must exhaust rather than exhibit. This should reconnect to the earlier phase-transition sweep, which found cost peaking at barely-infeasible on the TRUE world.
would_change_my_mind: comparable cost in both bands would mean the inconclusive band is inconclusive for the POLYNOMIAL procedure without being expensive for ASP -- i.e. clingo finds the infeasibility argument easily and the gap is between our heuristics and the solver rather than between easy and hard instances. That would be a finding about the heuristics, not the benchmark.

verdict: WRONG, and it was the alternative I wrote down -- twice over
measured: clingo costs 0.45ms UNSAT in my nominated 'hard regime' (6 jobs, slack +0.02) against 0.73ms at the default: CHEAPER. The inconclusive band measures my greedy heuristic's weakness, not instance hardness -- at 6 jobs the space is 3^6=729 and nothing is hard for a real solver.
where_cost_actually_lives: size AND negative slack: 198.6ms at 20 jobs/-0.02, 1047.5ms at 30/-0.05, 1502.5ms at 40/-0.05, against 1.2ms at +0.02 whatever the size.
the_finding_that_corrects_the_previous_h: EVERY expensive negative-slack cell is settled 6/6 by the capacity gate -- one pass of O(n) arithmetic. The regions where clingo is slowest are exactly the regions where nobody needs to run it. So 'the kernels earn their keep proving negatives' refines to THE EXPENSIVE NEGATIVES ARE THE EASY NEGATIVES: what survives the gate is cheap for the solver, what is expensive for the solver is free for the gate.
the_one_real_cell: slack ~ 0, exact fit, where the gate cannot fire (demand does not EXCEED capacity) and the packing is maximally tight: 15.7ms at 20 jobs gate-silent, 168.7ms at 30. And that is also where feasible_by_search degenerates -- 0.027s per case at 20 jobs, 1.60s at 30. THE ONLY REGIME WHERE THE SOLVER IS BOTH NECESSARY AND EXPENSIVE IS THE ONE WHERE GROUND TRUTH IS ALSO EXPENSIVE.
fixed: HARD_REGIME corrected from 6 jobs/+0.02 to 20 jobs/3 machines/slack 0.0, with the three simultaneous constraints documented and two tests -- that the regime is not gate-settleable, and that ground truth stays affordable.
unchanged: scheduling is still the only domain whose decision is not polynomial. What is corrected is WHERE the difficulty lives and how much of it a one-line check removes.

hypothesis: Every scheduling PIPELINE number on disk comes from the easy default (6 jobs, slack 0.15) where clingo answers in 0.6ms and the kernel is decorative. The honest milestone has only ever been run on flood, whose decision turned out to be a widest path. So no end-to-end measurement in this repo has the kernel doing real work.
the_measurement: scheduling end to end at HARD_REGIME (20 jobs, 3 machines, slack 0.0): surface -> reader -> kernel -> answer, with the reader/kernel decomposition and $/correct, and interleaved as well as grouped since the reader must be tested honestly.
expected: the OPPOSITE of flood's honest milestone. There, reader loss 0.500 matched the worst kernel loss and the kernel was cheap. Here I expect reader loss ~0 -- scheduling audits at 0.000 ambiguity mass and its reader is immune to interleaving, because job_/machine_ prefixes fix the predicate -- while the kernel does genuine search at 15.7ms on gate-silent instances. So $/correct should be dominated by the KERNEL, and be orders of magnitude above flood's.
the_contrast_that_matters: if it holds, the suite has one domain where reading is the whole cost and one where solving is, measured the same way. That is worth more than either number alone, because the programme's thesis is about where cost goes.
would_change_my_mind: the reader failing at 20 jobs would mean scheduling's immunity was a property of the 6-job surface rather than of its naming, which would undercut the structure-dependence law's cleanest data point.

verdict: prediction right about the contrast; the run exposed a SOUNDNESS BUG in committed code
measured: scheduling end to end at HARD_REGIME: reader loss 0.000, claim recall 1.000 unchanged by interleaving, ceiling 1.000, $/correct 9.49e-08, 17.5 ms/case. Exactly the complement of flood's honest milestone (reader loss 0.500, $/correct 3.69e-08, decision polynomial).
the_bug: the first run gave a CEILING of 0.867 -- the kernel disagreeing with ground truth on 4 of 30 with no budget exhaustion. Two wrong guesses first (SCALE rounding; the oracle's 1e-9 tolerance), then an exact integer re-implementation agreed with the oracle and the kernel called directly also said feasible. The culprit was capacity_gate: it summed hours as FLOATS and compared demand > capacity. At exact fit, summation order made demand exceed capacity by 1.4e-14 (seed 8: 77.04 vs 77.03999999999999), so a gate documented as PROVABLY SUFFICIENT refused schedules that provably exist, on 4 of 30.
why_it_survived: the 87.7%-of-solver-time claim was measured across a slack sweep dominated by comfortable margins, where the gate's verdicts were correct. The claim was true where measured and the component was broken anyway. THE MARGIN THAT MAKES A COMPONENT LOOK SOUND IS THE SAME MARGIN THAT HIDES ITS UNSOUNDNESS.
fixed: sums in integer centihours, the same units build_program uses, so gate and ASP encoding agree on the numbers. Two tests: never refuses a feasible schedule at exact fit, still fires 20/20 below the boundary. Ceiling 0.867 -> 1.000, gate settles 8/30 -> 2/30, solve time 8.2 -> 17.5 ms.
the_contrast: flood reader loss 0.500 on a polynomial decision; scheduling reader loss 0.000 on an NP-hard one. One domain where READING is the whole cost, one where SOLVING is, measured the same way. Either number alone invites the wrong conclusion about where effort belongs.
method_note: the bug surfaced accidentally while measuring cost, and only because the benchmark had been pushed to its boundary. An argument for doing that as a matter of course.

hypothesis: capacity_gate's unsoundness was found BY ACCIDENT, while measuring cost, and only because the benchmark had been pushed to exact fit. That is a bug CLASS -- a decision made by comparing summed floating-point quantities -- and it should be swept for rather than waited for. Every domain here decides by such a comparison: solvency sums revenues against a threshold, flood compares mass+demand against a bridge limit, scheduling compares demand against capacity.
the_method: do not hope a generator lands on the boundary. CONSTRUCT the exact-fit case in each domain -- set the threshold to the exact total, set a vehicle's laden mass to exactly a posted limit -- and check the decision against exact integer arithmetic in the domain's own smallest unit (cents, kilograms, centihours).
expected: solvency is LATENT rather than active: its threshold is round(first_total * uniform(0.94,1.06), 2), so it lands at exact fit with probability ~0 and the accumulated float error (~1e-13) never flips a random comparison. But constructed at the boundary it should flip, because the sum accumulates error the threshold does not. Flood I expect to be exact, because its comparison is against a single posted limit rather than a sum -- there is nothing to accumulate.
the_general_shape: the risk is not floating point as such, it is SUMMATION against a threshold. A comparison of one measured quantity to one posted quantity is safe; a comparison of a SUM to a posted quantity is not. If that holds, it is a rule that can be applied by inspection rather than by testing every component.
would_change_my_mind: flood flipping too would mean single-quantity comparisons are also unsafe and the rule is just 'use exact arithmetic everywhere', which is true but far less useful as a diagnostic.

verdict: prediction right, and the sweep found a second and worse bug that had nothing to do with floats
measured: constructed exact-fit cases: solvency flips 39/200 (sum vs threshold, e.g. float total 618.3599999999999 against threshold 618.36), flood flips 0/3000 (one quantity vs one posted limit), scheduling 0 after this morning's fix. THE RISK IS SUMMATION, NOT FLOATING POINT -- a rule applicable by inspection.
solvency_was_latent: its threshold is a random multiple so it lands on the boundary with probability ~0. Fixed in cents anyway, because it is the tunable-margin domain and any sweep to exact fit fires it. A test confirms the fix changes no verdict on the real distribution.
the_second_bug: writing the exact-fit test required re-implementing the decision rule, and that exposed the SOLVENCY READER using the wrong temporal rule. decide() takes the LATEST filing by date; the reader took the LARGEST by value, and documented itself as doing so. Revisions go DOWN as well as up (seed 69: group files 198.80 then revises to 188.36), so the rules differ on 62/948 member-dates and FLIP THE VERDICT ON 9/400 CASES.
what_it_corrects: the reader was reported at 1.000 in all six cells, measured over 60 SEEDS with tests using 30. At a 2.25% error rate that is about one expected failure and it did not land. Fixed; now 0 disagreements over 400 seeds on both surfaces. The structure-independence conclusion is unaffected -- it compares grouped against interleaved with the same reader -- but the CONFIDENCE was wrong: a 60-seed sample cannot see a 2% defect and I reported it as exact.
the_pattern: three bugs this week, each found by the previous one's follow-up, and none by testing the component in question. Each came from BUILDING THE NEXT THING ON TOP OF IT.

hypothesis: The solvency reader was reported at 1.000 over 60 seeds and was wrong on 2.25% of cases. That is not an isolated slip -- it is a METHOD failure that applies to every claimed-exact number in this repo. By the rule of three, zero failures in N cases bounds the true error rate at about 3/N: 34 non-empty flood cases bound it at 8.8%, 95 certificate cases at 3.2%, 40 scheduling cases at 7.5%. Several load-bearing findings are asserted as exact on samples that cannot exclude a several-percent defect.
the_claims_to_recheck: flood signature+content 1.000 in all four cells (34 non-empty)
the insensitivity certificate firing iff decided, 0 unsound and 0 incomplete (95)
expected: at least one breaks at 400 seeds. The solvency reader did, at 2.25%, and nothing about it was unusual -- it was a plausible rule that happened to be the wrong one. I would put the certificate at highest risk, because its necessity half is measured rather than proved and rests on the flow's answer coinciding with a graph condition that ASP's route cap could break.
the_point_even_if_none_break: a bound is worth having whether or not it moves. 'Exact over 400 seeds' bounds the error at 0.75% where 'exact over 34' bounds it at 8.8%, and the findings should say which they mean rather than both reading as 1.000.
would_change_my_mind: nothing breaking would mean the samples were adequate by luck rather than by design, which still leaves the method wrong -- the fix is to state the bound, not to trust the number.

verdict: right -- one of three broke, and the solvency reader was not an isolated slip
measured: at 400 seeds: flood signature+content interleaved FAILS 3 of 252 non-empty = 1.19% (was reported 1.000 on 34 cases, which bounds only 8.8%); flood insensitivity certificate 0 of 252 (bound improves 3.2% -> 1.19%); scheduling reader 0 of 400 (7.5% -> 0.75%).
the_mechanism: all three failures have TWO lone-region sentences reaching no declared anchor in the same case -- 'region_1 went under overnight' for flooding and 'Vehicles are dispatched from region_0' for the depot, both of which I named as misses WHEN THE VOCABULARY WAS DECLARED. With two unresolved regions and depot still open, elimination takes whichever comes first, and interleaving randomises that order. Not a new defect: the known coverage gap, at ~1.2%, invisible in 34 cases.
not_patching_the_vocabulary: adding 'went under' and 'dispatched' would recover exactly these and demonstrate nothing -- memorising the generator one variant later, which the adversarial-variant finding already priced.
the_detectable_part: in all three the reader KNEW it was guessing -- needs resolved by adjacency, depot open, two unresolved regions left. A refusing variant converts 3 silent errors into 3 refusals at soundness 1.000, and the machinery exists. Named as next step; the finding worth having this turn is the BOUND, not another arm.
the_rule: STATE THE BOUND, NOT THE NUMBER. A claim of exactness should carry the sample supporting it, because 3/N is what a reader needs. 400 seeds costs seconds and buys an order of magnitude.

hypothesis: read_content_roles is 0.988 interleaved, and in all three failures it KNEW it was guessing: needs was resolved by adjacency, depot was still open, and two unresolved regions remained, so which one became the depot was arbitrary. That condition is detectable at read time without any ground truth, so the reader can refuse instead of guessing -- directive 19's answer applied to the READER rather than the flow.
the_condition: after anchors and adjacency, the assignment is FORCED only when no single-valued role is still open, or exactly one is open and exactly one region is unresolved. Anything else is a choice among alternatives the evidence does not separate.
expected: refusal is RARE, because it needs two anchor-dodging variants to coincide -- roughly (1/4 chance the depot phrasing dodges) x (chance some flooded phrasing dodges). I expect 3-8% refused, soundness 1.000 among the rest. So coverage ~92-97% at soundness 1.000, against 98.8% accuracy while guessing.
the_trade_worth_seeing: guessing buys about 1.2% of extra answers and pays for them with silent errors of exactly the same size. If refusal costs much more coverage than the errors it removes, the guess is the better policy and I should say so rather than assume abstention wins.
would_change_my_mind: a refusal rate well above the error rate -- say 15% refused to remove 1.2% of errors -- would mean the detector is far more conservative than the failure, and the honest recommendation would be to keep guessing and report 0.988.

verdict: my stated way-to-change-my-mind fired, and a second and worse thing turned up
measured: easy-distractor surface: accuracy 0.9881, refuses 29 of 252 (11.5% coverage given up), removes 3 of 3 errors, accuracy among forced readings 1.000. So it works AND is 10x more conservative than the failure -- exactly the condition I said would make keeping the guess the better policy.
the_worse_thing: on the hard_distractors surface, accuracy among FORCED readings is 0.664. The phantom-link failure makes answers wrong without touching role assignment, so the flag cannot see it and refuses the same 29 cases either way. A flag that means SOUND on one surface and 0.664 on another is the same scope error as quoting 'grounded 1.000' without saying what it certifies -- which this repo already made once, on the renderer.
why_the_pattern_repeats: a check is built for one failure mode, verified against that mode, and then its NAME promises more than it delivers. 'certain' promised correctness; what it computes is 'the lone-region roles were not guessed'.
shipped: renamed to role_assignment_forced, docstring carries BOTH numbers, and a test ASSERTS that forced-and-wrong cases exist so it fails if the flag ever starts looking like a guarantee. NOT shipped as a default: 10x the error it removes, and reporting 0.988 honestly is cheaper.
complementarity: the phantom-link mode is what the certificate work addresses. Neither detector covers the other's failure, which is worth knowing before either is trusted alone.

hypothesis: Two detectors exist and neither covers the other's failure. role_assignment_forced catches lone-region guessing and is blind to the phantom link (0.664 among forced on hard distractors). The insensitivity certificate catches link sensitivity and has no view of role assignment at all -- a wrong depot is not a link deletion. Combining them should cover both modes.
the_lesson_being_applied: the certificate's soundness on the hard surface was measured at N=60 (decided <=> correct, identical sets), which by the rule of three bounds only ~5%. And 'fires iff the enumeration decides' is NOT the same claim as 'fires implies correct' -- I checked the first at 252 and have not checked the second at scale. This turn's own finding says state the bound, so it gets 400 seeds.
expected: the certificate ALONE is not quite sound at 400 seeds -- I expect a small number of cases where it fires and the answer is still wrong because a ROLE was misread, which link-deletion insensitivity cannot see. The combination should be sound, at coverage roughly the product of the two.
the_number_that_decides_it: whether the combination is sound AND retains useful coverage. If coverage collapses to near zero the pair is useless however sound; if the certificate alone is already sound at 400 the role flag adds nothing here and I should say so.
would_change_my_mind: the certificate alone showing zero failures at 400 seeds would mean link-insensitivity implicitly certifies the roles too -- plausible, since a misread depot changes which routes exist and could well show up as sensitivity to deletion. That would be a real structural fact rather than a coincidence, and worth stating.

verdict: right -- the certificate alone is NOT sound at 400 seeds, and the pair is
measured: 252 non-empty cases, interleaved, hard_distractors=True. Answer everything: 81 wrong, 0.679. Role flag only: 75 wrong, 0.664 at 88.5% coverage. CERTIFICATE ONLY: 3 WRONG, 0.9786 at 55.6% coverage. BOTH: 0 wrong, 1.000 at 47.6% coverage.
