the_mechanism_confirmed_exactly: the certificate's three failures are seeds 64, 83, 92 -- THE SAME THREE that broke the exactness audit. All have role_assignment_forced=False and all read the DEPOT AS A FLOODED REGION. A misread role is not a link deletion, so link-insensitivity cannot see it. The certificate's entire failure set is the role flag's entire catch set: complementarity demonstrated exactly rather than statistically.
what_it_corrects: 'refusing to collapse... soundness 1.000' was measured at N=60, which bounds the error at 5%. It is 0.9786 at 400. The finding's structure holds -- carrying discards only wrong answers on the population it measured -- but the sample could not distinguish 1.000 from 0.98, which is the very failure its successors kept finding.
the_bound_stated: 0 wrong in 120 bounds the error at 2.5%, NOT zero. Coverage 47.6% is roughly the product of the two conditions, so they are close to independent.
the_cost: against answering everything at 0.679, the pair converts 32% silent error into 52% refusal. Whether that trade is worth taking is the caller's, not the reader's.

hypothesis: The role flag refuses whenever the lone-region assignment is unforced -- 29 of 252 -- but only 3 of those are actually wrong. It is TEN TIMES more conservative than the failure, which the last finding named as the thing to fix. The fix is to stop treating unforced as unsafe and instead ENUMERATE the candidate assignments and check whether they agree on the ANSWER: refuse only when the ambiguity matters.
why_this_is_not_the_vacuous_case: an earlier arm bounded ROLE ambiguity and found decidedness collapsing to 0.067 -- but that enumerated all canonical assignments within k swaps on a reader that had discarded the candidates. Here the unresolved set is what the reader actually could not resolve, typically TWO regions, so the candidate count is 2 rather than combinatorial and the enumeration is 2 solves on 11.5% of cases.
expected: most of the 29 unforced cases have both assignments agreeing -- the ambiguity is real but inert -- so coverage should recover from 88.5% toward 95-98% while keeping every genuine error refused. Paired with the certificate I expect coverage well above the 47.6% the flag version gave, at the same 0 wrong.
would_change_my_mind: the assignments disagreeing on most of the 29 would mean the ambiguity nearly always matters, the flag was right to refuse, and there is no cheaper detector -- which would close the direction rather than improve it.

verdict: the improvement works on coverage and BREAKS soundness, for a structural reason
measured: 48% of unforced assignments are inert, so enumeration recovers coverage: 0.885 -> 0.940 alone, 0.476 -> 0.516 paired with the certificate, at 1.19 solves per case. But the pair goes from 0 wrong to 1 wrong.
the_mechanism: seed 83 -- needs is read correctly, the TRUE assignment IS among the candidates, and all three agree on a wrong answer because the error is the PHANTOM LINK which every candidate shares. The certificate should catch that and returned True, because it was computed on the collapsed world where depot=region_1. certifies_insensitive READS THE ROLES TO BUILD ITS GRAPH -- with the wrong depot it answers about the wrong graph.
the_correction: the two detectors are NOT independent, which is what I said last turn ('coverage is roughly the product, so close to independent'). The NUMBERS multiply (0.885 x 0.556 = 0.492 vs 0.476 observed); the LOGIC does not. The role flag's over-conservatism is exactly what guarantees the certificate is asked about the right graph -- it is a PRECONDITION, not a second opinion.
the_general_rule: A CHECK THAT READS PART OF THE WORLD INHERITS THAT PART'S ERRORS. The certificate consumes the roles so it cannot validate them. Same shape as the grounding scope result (ungrounded builds admissible edges from the flow's own output, so it cannot catch reader errors) -- third time this pipeline has produced it, and worth stating as a property of layered checks rather than three separate surprises.
decision: enumeration measured and REJECTED. Keeping the flag costs 4 points of coverage and buys the property the policy exists for. The version worth building if coverage ever matters more: a certificate that does not consume the roles, arguing insensitivity over ALL role assignments at once.

hypothesis: certifies_insensitive READS THE ROLES to build its graph, so on a world whose depot is wrong it certifies the wrong question -- which is why role enumeration broke the pair's soundness. The fix the last finding named: a certificate that does NOT consume the roles, by requiring insensitivity to hold for EVERY candidate role assignment rather than for one arbitrary collapse.
the_construction: for each candidate assignment emitted by read_content_roles_worlds, run the DFS certificate AND solve. Certify only if every candidate certifies and all candidates agree on the answer. Cost is k DFS plus k solves with k typically 1-3, not k times sixteen, because the certificate is the cheap half.
the_test_case: seed 83 is the one that broke enumeration -- all candidates agree on a wrong answer and the collapsed world certified. If the TRUE-depot candidate fails to certify, requiring ALL to certify refuses it and soundness returns. If every candidate certifies, then the phantom link is invisible to the certificate under every reading and this construction cannot help.
expected: soundness restored (0 wrong) at coverage between the flag pair's 0.476 and enumeration's 0.516 -- I would guess around 0.49-0.51. It should also be conceptually cleaner: a certificate that assumes nothing the reader guessed.
would_change_my_mind: every candidate certifying on seed 83 would mean the phantom link is invisible to link-insensitivity under all readings, which would say the certificate does not actually cover the phantom-link mode at all and the pair's soundness came from the role flag alone.

verdict: works, sound, and the coverage gain is marginal -- the value is structural
measured: 252 non-empty cases, 400 seeds, interleaved, hard_distractors=True. Role-independent certificate: 0 wrong at 48.8% coverage (123 answers, bounding the error at 2.44%), against flag+certificate 0 wrong at 47.6% and enumeration+certificate 1 wrong at 51.6%. Mean 1.19 candidate worlds.
the_mechanism_on_seed_83: three candidates, all agreeing on a WRONG answer. The two wrong-depot candidates CERTIFY and the TRUE-depot one does NOT, so requiring all of them refuses the case that agreement alone admits. A check that consumes no guess cannot be misled by one.
honest_about_the_gain: +1.2 points of coverage is marginal and is NOT the reason to prefer it. The reason is structural: flag+certificate works only because the flag is a PRECONDITION guaranteeing the certificate is asked about the right graph -- a composition that must be got right in order and cannot be checked locally. The role-independent form is ONE CHECK WITH NO PRECONDITION.
consolidated: the certificate had become load-bearing across four findings while living in scripts/. Moved to symbolic_ai_generators/flood/certificate.py with both forms; the script imports it. Three tests: soundness; refusal of seed 83 WHERE THE COLLAPSED FORM IS MISLED, asserted as a gap that must exist; and that the collapsed form's verdict changes when only the roles are swapped.
open: coverage is still under half -- both forms refuse whenever any qualifying vehicle's subgraph has a cut edge, and the deletion-dependency work suggests most such cuts are inert.

verdict: corrects an open item I published one turn earlier
measured: over 196 non-empty cases the certificate refuses-when-insensitive 0 times and fires-when-sensitive 0 times. It is TIGHT for single-link deletion.
what_it_corrects: the previous finding's open item said 'a sharper sufficient condition would recover more' coverage. FALSE -- there is no sharper condition. 48.8% is the fraction of cases whose answer is genuinely insensitive to losing one link, a property of the task and the perturbation model rather than of the check.
where_more_coverage_would_come_from: narrowing the HYPOTHESIS, not sharpening the check -- knowing WHICH link is suspect instead of treating all as candidates. That needs content, since the disused-track sentence carries exactly the link signature, which is the closure result.

hypothesis: Flood and scheduling both have an end-to-end milestone measured the same way -- reader claim recall, task accuracy, $/correct, grounding -- and they showed opposite corners: flood reader loss 0.500 on a polynomial decision, scheduling 0.000 on an NP-hard one. Solvency has a reader, a bitemporal renderer and grounding but has never had the row.
expected: the THIRD corner: neither reading nor solving is expensive. Reader loss 0.000 (the domain audits at 0.000 ambiguity and its reader is exact over 400 seeds, unchanged by interleaving), and the decision is a sum against a threshold, so kernel cost is essentially nil. $/correct should be far below both other domains.
why_that_is_worth_having_rather_than_tri: a table with a domain where BOTH halves are cheap is what makes the other two rows readable. Flood's 3.69e-08 and scheduling's 9.49e-08 mean little without a floor showing what the pipeline costs when the task demands nothing of it. It also prices the SURROUNDING machinery -- reading, rendering, grounding -- separately from the kernel, which no row has done.
would_change_my_mind: a non-zero reader loss would contradict the 0/400 measurement and mean the milestone harness differs from the reader test in some way worth finding. Grounding below 1.000 would be a genuine defect in the bitemporal renderer, which has only ever been checked on the published surface.

verdict: the third corner as predicted, and it exposed a gap in the metric
measured: solvency end to end: filing recall 1.000, task accuracy 1.000, grounded 1.000, on all three surfaces including interleaved. Reader loss 0.000, bounded at 1.50% by n=200.
the_gap_it_exposed: solvency's reader takes 0.219 ms against a decision costing 0.0021 ms -- a factor of a hundred -- but the milestone's $/correct prices KERNEL ARTIFACTS ONLY. Measured across all three: read share of time is 1.9% (flood), 0.9% (scheduling), 96.1% (solvency). So $/correct captures 98% of flood's time, 99% of scheduling's, and 4% of solvency's.
why_it_matters: the omission is invisible where the kernel dominates and is the ENTIRE cost where it does not -- which is exactly the regime the programme's thesis is about, since the argument is that symbolic reasoning is cheap. If reasoning is cheap, reading is what you are paying for, and a metric pricing only reasoning reports the system as nearly free while missing 96% of its work.
the_two_axes: flood -- reading is 2% of time and ALL of the error. scheduling -- solving is 99% of time and all of the error. solvency -- reading is 96% of time and there is NO error. ERROR CONCENTRATES WHERE THE SIGNATURE IS AMBIGUOUS; TIME CONCENTRATES WHERE THE DECISION IS HARD. Both are predicted separately before measurement -- by the audit's ambiguity mass and by the complexity of the decision -- and neither predicts the other.
recommendation: the milestone should report reader time alongside kernel cost, not because 0.06-0.24 ms is expensive but because its SHARE is the diagnostic: a row showing 96% says the kernel is decorative.

hypothesis: CLAUDE.md states the rule: cost is charged to the SYSTEM, and an upstream component is in the ledger whether or not it exists yet. symbolic_ai_core/cost.py has System documented as existing precisely because 'sum is not optional'. And I have just measured that reading is 96.1% of solvency's time and is priced at zero, because every milestone charges kernel artifacts only. That is a stated principle violated in the place the principle was written for.
the_work: build each domain's System from BOTH a reader component and a kernel component, priced from measured throughput, and report usd_per_solved_episode_above_floor with the reader in and out.
expected: flood and scheduling barely move -- reading is 1.9% and 0.9% of their time -- so their published cost figures survive with a small correction. Solvency moves by roughly 25x, because kernel-only prices 4% of what runs. The ordering of the three domains by cost should be unchanged, since flood and scheduling are dominated by kernels that solvency does not have.
the_point: not that the numbers move much, but that two of three barely moving is exactly why the omission survived. A metric is not validated by the cases where the missing term is negligible.
would_change_my_mind: the ordering changing would mean the reader term is large enough to reorder domains, which would make every published cross-domain cost comparison suspect rather than merely incomplete.

verdict: right on the numbers and on why it lasted
measured: charging both a reader and a kernel component: flood 8.480e-08 -> 8.684e-08 (1.02x), scheduling 4.048e-07 -> 4.089e-07 (1.01x), SOLVENCY 2.161e-11 -> 7.218e-10 (33.4x). Ordering unchanged both ways: solvency < flood < scheduling.
so_what_survives: flood and scheduling's published cost figures are 1-2% low, inside single-machine timing noise, and no conclusion drawn from them changes. Solvency's was 33x too low. Cross-domain comparisons are INCOMPLETE rather than WRONG.
why_it_lasted: two of three domains barely move. A METRIC IS NOT VALIDATED BY THE CASES WHERE ITS MISSING TERM IS NEGLIGIBLE -- and the case where it is not negligible is the one the thesis is about, since if symbolic reasoning is cheap then reading is what you are paying for.
the_durable_fix: cost.py's module docstring now carries the rule and the three numbers, because the omission was never a bug in that module but in every caller of it. System still CANNOT detect it -- sum is not optional over the components it is GIVEN, and nothing forces a caller to hand it all of them. Written down rather than assumed away.

verdict: guard built and behaves as designed
measured: Component gains a `stage` field and ledger() emits a note when a system declares stages and none is `read`. Fires on a declared kernel-only system, silent when a reader is priced, silent when nothing is declared. Pricing is unchanged by declaring a stage (asserted, since the field is metadata).
the_deliberate_limit: opt-in. A caller declaring no stages gets no check, because the alternative was a note every existing caller would receive and could not act on. System still cannot detect a component nobody handed it. Recorded in the test name and docstring rather than hidden.
the_lesson: a metric is not validated by the cases where its missing term is negligible -- flood and scheduling agreed with the kernel-only figure to 1-2%, which reads as confirmation and is not. The finding required a domain whose kernel does almost nothing, and the guard's second half is 'check a metric where its missing term DOMINATES'.

hypothesis: The lesson just written says to check a metric where its MISSING TERM DOMINATES, not where it is comfortable. Applying it immediately: the ledger now knows three stages -- read, solve, render -- and I have measured two. NO milestone has ever priced rendering, and the pipeline is read -> solve -> render with a grounded paragraph as the deliverable.
where_it_would_dominate: solvency again. Its solve is 0.002 ms and its read 0.061 ms, so a renderer costing even half a millisecond would be the largest term in the system. flood and scheduling have kernels at 8.6 ms and 26 ms, so rendering has to be enormous to matter there.
expected: rendering is a few tenths of a millisecond everywhere -- these are string-formatting routines over a handful of claims -- so it should be a small share for flood and scheduling and a LARGE share for solvency, plausibly comparable to or above its reader. If so the three-stage accounting shows solvency's cost is essentially all text handling and none of it reasoning.
what_makes_it_worth_running_rather_than_: the direction is predictable; the SHARE is not, and the share is the diagnostic. A renderer at 5% of solvency changes nothing; at 60% it means the domain's cost is dominated by explaining an answer that took no work to compute, which is a different statement about where symbolic pipelines spend.
would_change_my_mind: rendering being negligible everywhere would mean the read/solve split is the whole story and the third stage is bookkeeping -- worth knowing, and it would close the stage accounting rather than open it.

verdict: wrong in the direction that CLOSES the question
measured: render share of pipeline time: flood 0.2%, scheduling 0.1%, solvency 9.4%. I predicted it would be comparable to reading in solvency; it is about a tenth of it. Rendering is MINOR EVERYWHERE and the stage accounting is complete.
the_number_worth_keeping: solvency's renderer costs 0.006 ms against a solver at 0.002 ms -- three times more spent EXPLAINING the answer than COMPUTING it. With the rest of the row: 97.2% of that pipeline is text handling (87.8% read, 9.4% render) and 2.8% is reasoning. That is the sharpest statement of what a symbolic pipeline costs when the reasoning is genuinely cheap, which is the regime the thesis describes.
why_worth_running: the direction was predictable but the SHARE was not, and the share is the diagnostic -- a renderer at 60% would have meant solvency's cost is dominated by explanation rather than parsing, a different claim. It also forecloses a 'we never priced rendering' surprise of the kind that produced the last two findings.
caveat: these renderers emit a few sentences from a handful of claims. One that had to SELECT what to say -- ranking, summarising, choosing among many true statements -- would not be a string-formatting routine and this would not transfer.

hypothesis: Every renderer in this repo formats a FIXED TEMPLATE from a handful of claims, so nothing is ever omitted by choice and the grounding check has never had to face omission. A renderer that must SELECT what to say -- the case the last finding flagged as not transferring -- makes omission possible for the first time.
the_claim: ungrounded() verifies that everything ASSERTED is supported: tokens appear in the world or the flow's outputs, route hops are real edges, the paragraph does not contradict the structured answer. Every one of those is a property of what is PRESENT. None of them can see a true statement that leaves out the fact the decision turned on.
expected: a selecting renderer under a citation budget produces paragraphs that are grounded 1.000 at EVERY budget while being decision-incomplete at small budgets -- a reader of the paragraph alone cannot reconstruct the answer, because the binding bridge limit or the flooded region was not cited. Grounding should be flat in the budget and completeness should rise with it, which is the whole point: the two are independent.
why_it_matters: the pipeline's argument is that its reasoning is INSPECTABLE. A paragraph that is fully grounded and materially incomplete is inspectable in the letter and not in substance, and this repo has already made the mistake of quoting a check's name for more than it certifies -- twice, with 'grounded 1.000' and with a flag that meant 0.664 on another surface.
would_change_my_mind: completeness tracking grounding would mean the existing check already implies it, which would be surprising given that ungrounded never inspects what the flow used to DECIDE, only what the paragraph mentions.

verdict: right, and it turned out to be about SHIPPED code rather than a hypothetical renderer
measured: under a citation budget, grounding is FLAT at 1.000 across every budget (measured with the real ungrounded() on real paragraphs, after I first asserted it and corrected that) while decision-completeness runs 0.000 at 4 cited facts, 0.529 at 16, 1.000 at all 28.5. Independent axes by construction: ungrounded inspects what is PRESENT and omission is a property of what is ABSENT.
the_stronger_finding: the SHIPPED template renderer cites 2.0 of 28.5 claims, is grounded 1.000, and is decision-complete 0.000. Every 'grounded 1.000' figure in this repo describes a paragraph citing 7% of the claims from which the answer cannot be rebuilt.
fair_framing: NOT a defect in the renderer -- it is a summary and was never meant to be reconstructible; reciting 28 facts would be worse output. The defect is in what the number was taken to mean.
shipped: incomplete(answer, case) rebuilds a world from the cited claims, re-solves, and reports the kinds whose absence changes the answer. Two tests: the shipped renderer is grounded on every case and complete on none; and the check is satisfiable by citing everything, so it measures something rather than always failing.
the_pattern_now_three_times: ungrounded certifies consistency with the world AS READ not truth; role_assignment_forced means roles were not guessed not that the answer is right; ungrounded certifies nothing false was SAID not that enough was. Each time the check was correct and its NAME promised more.

hypothesis: Decision-completeness as defined demands the answer be REBUILDABLE from the paragraph, which no human explanation meets -- the shipped renderer scores 0.000 and a paragraph reciting 28 facts would be worse output. The forgiving version the finding named: does the paragraph cite every claim WHOSE DELETION CHANGES THE ANSWER? That is the load-bearing set, and deletion_dependency already computes it.
expected: the load-bearing set is SMALL -- flood's per-kind deletion dependencies are 0.243 for link and near 1.0 for depot/needs/demand, so I expect roughly 4-8 claims per case out of 28.5. The shipped renderer cites 2.0 claims and I expect it to cover almost none of the load-bearing ones, because what it cites is the demand and the site rather than the constraints that bind. A renderer that cited the load-bearing set would be both grounded AND complete in this weaker sense, at a paragraph length a person would actually read.
why_this_is_the_useful_version: strict completeness is a diagnostic and cannot be an objective -- nothing can satisfy it without reciting the world. Load-bearing completeness is achievable, and it is the honest target for an explanation: cite what the decision turned on.
would_change_my_mind: a load-bearing set as large as the world would mean flood's answers depend on nearly everything, so no short explanation can be complete in any sense and the diagnostic is all that is available.

verdict: target confirmed reachable, and the cheap version works after two corrections of the SAME mistake
measured: load-bearing is 10.8 of 28.4 claims (38%); the shipped renderer covers 9% and is complete on 0 of 18. Finding the set exhaustively costs 235 ms/case against a 9.1 ms answer -- 25.5x. The cheap per-kind version over 73 non-empty cases: 0.22 ms/case, RECALL 1.000, precision 0.881, 1140x faster. Only over-claim is flooded (1.4/case), which is the safe direction.
two_corrections_same_mistake: first version tested links by CONNECTIVITY and missed 0.83 load-bearing links per case -- a link matters by lowering the BOTTLENECK, not by disconnecting. That is the identical wrong proxy that fired 0 of 270 times when tried for ordering candidate deletions several findings ago. Second version tested limits by arithmetic on the largest threshold and missed 0.33 of each limit kind, for the same reason: a limit binds for a PARTICULAR vehicle on a PARTICULAR route. Both fixed by recomputing the bottleneck without the claim.
what_it_closes: INSPECTABILITY COST 25.5x AND NOW COSTS 1.03x. Same arc as soundness (13.4x by enumeration -> 1.0x by certificate): both times the expensive version was a per-item enumeration and the cheap version a structural argument over the quantity the kernel already computes.
bound: recall 1.000 over 73 cases bounds the miss rate at 4.1%, not zero. The test checks EVERY claim of every case rather than sampling.
not_done: the renderer is not yet complete -- that is a separate change, and this supplies the set it would need to cite.

hypothesis: The load-bearing set is now computable at 1.03x the answer, and the shipped renderer cites 9% of it. Building a renderer that cites all of it closes the output half: the first explanation in this repo that is complete in the sense that matters.
one_thing_to_get_right: incomplete() is the STRICT check -- rebuild a world from the cited claims and re-solve -- and citing the load-bearing set will NOT satisfy it, because 38% of claims is not enough to reconstruct a world. The achievable objective needs its own check, omits_load_bearing(), or I would be measuring the new renderer against a bar I already showed nothing can meet.
expected: grounded 1.000 (every cited token comes from a claim, so there is nothing false to assert), omits-nothing 1.000, and the paragraph grows from about 2 cited facts to about 11. Strict completeness should stay 0.000, which is the honest result rather than a failure -- it was never the target.
would_change_my_mind: grounding falling below 1.000 would mean citing more facts introduces assertions the check rejects -- most likely a number formatted differently from the claim it came from, which would be a real defect in how the paragraph renders quantities rather than in the selection.

verdict: works, and one prediction was wrong in the useful direction
measured: template renderer: grounded 1.000, omits-nothing 0.000, 79 words. Complete renderer: grounded 1.000, OMITS-NOTHING 1.000, 108 words. Complete coverage for +37% length -- a paragraph, not a recitation.
the_wrong_prediction: I expected STRICT rebuildability to stay at 0.000 for the complete renderer since the load-bearing set is 38% of claims. It reaches 0.727 -- the claims that MATTER are nearly the claims you NEED. A fact about this domain rather than a general one; the remaining 27% fail because reconstruction also wants network structure no single deletion touches.
two_checks_kept_distinct: incomplete() is the DIAGNOSTIC (rebuildable, unmeetable by anything readable) and omits_load_bearing() is the OBJECTIVE (cites every claim whose deletion changes the answer, reachable and now met). Measuring the new renderer against the strict bar would have been measuring it against something already shown unmeetable.
the_arc_closed: soundness 13.4x by enumeration -> 1.0x by structural argument; inspectability 25.5x -> 1.03x. Both halves of 'reasoning you can check' started as per-item enumerations over the kernel and ended as arguments over the quantity the kernel already computes. The renderer is the first place that arc produces OUTPUT A READER SEES rather than a number in a table.
inherited_risk: omits_load_bearing inherits load_bearing_cheap's recall -- 1.000 over 73 cases, bounded at 4.1%. A missed claim there is an explanation that omits something material while reporting that it does not.

hypothesis: The complete renderer costs +37% length on flood because only 38% of claims are load-bearing -- the road network is redundant, so most single deletions change nothing. That is flood's number and the finding flagged it as such. Whether a SHORT honest explanation exists should be a property of the DECISION, not of the renderer.
the_structural_prediction: flood's answer is a max-min over paths, which has redundancy: alternative routes mean most links do not matter. Solvency's answer is a SUM against a threshold, and a sum has no redundancy -- though only the LATEST filing per member enters, so superseded revisions and the zero-dependency `owns` claims should be inert. Scheduling at HARD_REGIME sits at exact fit, where by construction every hour is spoken for, so nearly everything should matter.
expected: flood 38%, solvency somewhere near the share of claims that are latest-filings (I would guess 30-45%, since owns is measured at exactly zero dependency and superseded revisions are inert), scheduling HIGH -- 70%+ at exact fit. If so, scheduling is the domain that does not admit a short honest explanation, and the reason is that its regime was chosen to have no slack.
why_it_matters: it converts 'the renderer is complete' from a property of one implementation into a statement about which tasks can be explained briefly at all. A task with no redundancy cannot have a short complete explanation, and that is worth knowing before anyone tries to build one.
would_change_my_mind: solvency coming out HIGH would mean a sum really does make every term load-bearing and my expectation that superseded filings are inert is wrong -- easy to check, since deleting a superseded revision should not move a latest-filing total at all.

verdict: BOTH structural predictions wrong; the data shows something flatter and duller
measured: load-bearing claims: flood 11.2 of 28.5 (39%), solvency 5.0 of 11.1 (45%), scheduling 12.4 of 48.9 (25%). Explanations run 5-12 facts (2.5x spread) across worlds of 11-49 claims (4.4x spread).
first_wrong_prediction: exact fit means no slack means everything matters, so scheduling should need the MOST. It needs the LEAST by share, 25%.
second_wrong_prediction: then the small share must mean a small local witness -- a few conflicting jobs. It touches 10 of 20 jobs. Not local either.
what_actually_drives_it: the DENOMINATOR. Scheduling has 48.9 claims, mostly has_capability facts that are individually inert, and its explanation is 12.4 facts -- the LARGEST of the three in absolute terms. The share was telling a story about the generator's verbosity, not about the decision.
what_is_worth_carrying: every domain admits a complete explanation of about a dozen facts, so the complete renderer is not a flood-specific trick. And EXPLANATION LENGTH DOES NOT TRACK DECISION DIFFICULTY -- scheduling is NP-hard and explains in the same space as flood's widest path. Third axis, independent of the two already measured (error where the signature is ambiguous, time where the decision is hard).
recorded_as: a description, not a law. Three points, two dead hypotheses, three generators by the same hand with worlds under fifty claims. Single-claim deletion only, so every number is a lower bound.

hypothesis: load_bearing and omits_load_bearing both test SINGLE-claim deletion. A pair whose joint removal changes the answer while neither alone does is invisible to them, which would make the 'complete' renderer incomplete and the objective I shipped last turn unsound as stated.
why_i_expect_them_to_exist: the very redundancy that makes flood's explanations short is PARALLEL ROUTES. Two links where deleting either leaves the other usable, but deleting both disconnects, is precisely a joint dependency and is exactly what a redundant network is made of. The property that buys brevity is the property that creates the blind spot.
expected: joint pairs exist in flood and are concentrated in `link` claims. Solvency should have far fewer -- its answer is a sum over latest filings, and each of those is already individually load-bearing, so there is little that is jointly-but-not-singly critical. If so, `omits_load_bearing` is a LOWER BOUND and its name promises more than it delivers, which would be the FOURTH instance of that pattern in this repo.
the_honest_consequence: if pairs exist the shipped check is not wrong about what it computes, it is wrong about what it was called. The fix is the same as the previous three: rename for the thing computed, carry the counter-example, and assert the gap in a test.
would_change_my_mind: no joint pairs anywhere would mean single-claim sensitivity captures the whole dependency structure of these domains, which would be surprising for a graph with alternative paths and would deserve its own explanation.

verdict: pairs exist -- the shipped objective is a lower bound -- and I corrected myself mid-run on a small sample
measured: flood 30 joint pairs over 12 cases (2.50 per case) that change the answer together while neither changes it alone; solvency 0 over 24. Commonest kind link+link (10 of 30): parallel routes.
the_consequence: omits_load_bearing is a LOWER BOUND, not a guarantee -- a paragraph can cite every singly-load-bearing claim and still omit a pair the answer depends on. Fourth check in this repo whose name promised more than it computes; now documented on the function and asserted by a test that requires such a pair to EXIST.
the_mechanism: the commonest joint pair is two parallel links, which is exactly the redundancy that makes flood's explanations short (only 39% singly load-bearing BECAUSE alternatives exist). THE PROPERTY THAT BUYS BREVITY IS THE PROPERTY THAT CREATES THE BLIND SPOT. Solvency has zero, which a sum predicts.
self_correction_inside_the_run: a first pass over 6 cases found 2 pairs, reported them concentrated in `flooded` with links not involved, and I wrote that into the verdict. At 12 cases it is 30 pairs and link+link is the largest group -- my ORIGINAL prediction, which the small sample had talked me out of. Two data points and a mechanism story, wrong.
not_doing: extending the check to pairs -- O(n^2) solves, 400 combinations against 28, and load_bearing_cheap has no pairwise analogue. Name the bound, carry the counter-example, assert the gap.

what: the test written for this finding FAILED and I committed anyway, which breaks the standing rule. Fixed in the following commit rather than left.
the_cause_was_also_a_finding: the test scanned seeds 0-5 and found no jointly-critical pair. Joint dependencies are CONCENTRATED, not spread: only 5 of 14 non-empty flood cases have any (seeds 6, 11, 13, 19, 23), and the affected ones have up to ten each. '2.50 per case' is an average over a skewed distribution and describes no typical case.
corrected_in: the test (now scans 24 seeds and says why), the finding, and the shipped docstring on omits_load_bearing.

hypothesis: state.yml records the neural comparison as BLOCKED on paid credentials. That blocks measuring a language model's ACCURACY; it does not block its PRICE, which is published, and cost.py has api_component for exactly that. So the question that can be asked without credentials is the break-even one: AT WHAT ACCURACY WOULD A LANGUAGE MODEL MATCH OUR $/SOLVED? Accuracy is bounded above by 1, so if break-even exceeds 1 the answer is that no accuracy closes the gap.
expected: break-even accuracy far above 1 for all three domains -- our systems cost 7.2e-10 to 4.1e-07 per solved answer while an episode of ~150-360 tokens at published rates is 1e-05 to 1e-03 per ATTEMPT. That is three to six orders of magnitude, and no accuracy can recover it.
the_caveat_that_matters_more_than_the_nu: this is not the whole comparison and I should not report it as though it were. Our system works because a reader was HAND-WRITTEN for this surface, and the language model needs no such engineering. Charging the reader's runtime -- which the ledger now does -- is not the same as charging its DEVELOPMENT, and the repo's own rule says cost is charged to the system. A per-answer figure that ignores the engineering is a true number answering a narrower question than it appears to.
would_change_my_mind: a break-even below 1 for any domain would mean the symbolic pipeline is not cheap enough to win on price alone there, which would be the more interesting result and would point at which domain to defend on other grounds.

verdict: as predicted, and the caveat is the deliverable
measured: break-even accuracy -- what a model would need to match our $/solved -- is 1,109 (flood), 337 (scheduling), 66,742 (solvency) against a $0.15/Mtok hosted model, and 22,174 / 6,748 / 1,334,849 against a $3/Mtok frontier one. Accuracy cannot exceed 1, so no accuracy closes the gap, and the comparison is decided without measuring the model.
insensitive_to_our_accuracy: quoted on the PUBLISHED surface at 1.000; on the honest surface flood is 0.500, which halves its break-even to ~554 and changes nothing. Two orders of margin absorb any accuracy assumption.
the_narrow_claim: per answer, at inference time, on a task a reader ALREADY EXISTS FOR, the symbolic pipeline is 337x to 1.3M x cheaper at published rates. Every qualifier is load-bearing; strip one and the sentence is false or unsupported. It says nothing about a task nobody has written a reader for, which is what a general model is actually bought for.
the_missing_half: the ledger charges the reader's RUNTIME, not its DEVELOPMENT, and the repo's rule is that cost is charged to the system. At 337x minimum a great deal of engineering amortises, and the break-even EPISODE COUNT is development cost divided by per-answer saving. That number is not computed because development cost is measured nowhere here. It is the missing half of the argument, not a footnote.
conservative_directions: published not negotiated prices; input tokens only; whitespace words undercount against BPE by ~1.3x. All three understate the gap.

hypothesis: The break-even accuracy finding ends on the missing half: at 337x minimum a great deal of engineering amortises, and the break-even EPISODE COUNT is development cost divided by per-answer saving. Development cost is measured nowhere here, so the honest move is to leave it a PARAMETER and report the episode count across plausible engineering budgets rather than invent a single number.
expected: the counts are smaller than the 337x-1.3M x language suggests, because the SAVING per answer is tiny in absolute terms. Against a frontier model at $3/Mtok an episode of ~360 tokens costs about 1.1e-03, so $1,000 of engineering amortises in roughly a million episodes. Against a $0.15/Mtok model the saving is twenty times smaller and the count twenty times larger. So I expect 10^5 to 10^7 depending on price point and budget.
why_this_reframes_the_headline: '337x cheaper per answer' sounds decisive and 'pays back after a million episodes' sounds like a business constraint. Both are the same measurement. The second is the one that tells you whether to build the reader, and it is the form the argument has been missing.
would_change_my_mind: counts in the billions would mean the symbolic route never pays outside extreme volume and the per-answer multiple is a vanity number -- worth knowing, and it would change what this programme should be arguing.

verdict: in the predicted range, and the ranking inversion was not predicted
measured: break-even episodes at $1,000 of engineering: 0.9M-2.2M against a frontier model, 18M-44M against a cheap hosted one. Scaled by reader size against a frontier model: scheduling 1.0M (63 lines), solvency 3.1M (89), flood 9.7M (666).
the_inversion: solvency has the LARGEST per-answer multiple (1,334,849x) and needs the MOST episodes to pay back. Its saving is 150 tokens against a decision costing nothing, so the absolute gap is smallest. A BIG RATIO ON A TINY NUMBER IS STILL A TINY NUMBER -- the multiple and the amortisation threshold rank the domains OPPOSITELY, and only one of them decides whether to write the reader.
the_unification: scheduling pays back soonest because its reader is 63 lines, and it is 63 lines because job_/machine_ prefixes fix the predicate -- which the signature-determinacy audit measures OFFLINE at 0.000 ambiguity mass before any reader exists. The instrument built to predict where READING is hard also predicts how expensive the READER is to write, and therefore how soon the route pays back. Same quantity in three places now: reader difficulty, error concentration, and a budget.
confound_stated_in_output: flood's file holds FIVE reader arms built for research where the others hold one. Read the ordering, not the multiple.
what_it_changes: '337x cheaper per answer' is hard to act on; 'pays back after about a million episodes against a frontier model' is a volume threshold. A million is not large for anything running continuously and is very large for a one-off analysis. That is the honest shape, and it took leaving the unknown as a PARAMETER to see it.
unpriced: maintenance. A reader that needs revising when the surface changes never finishes amortising, and this repo has changed its surfaces repeatedly.

hypothesis: Maintenance is the last unpriced term, and this repo has the data. Every surface transform built this session -- drop headings, shuffle paragraphs, interleave, paraphrase at V=4 -- is a maintenance EVENT, and whether each domain's reader survived it is measurable now.
expected: flood breaks on most of them and the other two on none. flood's reader broke on shuffling (read_signature 1.000 -> 0.000), again on interleaving (read_signature_roles 1.000 -> 0.000), again on hard distractors (read_content_roles 1.000 -> 0.367), and the rules arm broke on paraphrase. Scheduling and solvency audited at 0.000 ambiguity mass and survived interleaving unchanged, so I expect 0 breakages each.
the_unification_if_it_holds: maintenance would be the FOURTH thing the signature-determinacy audit predicts, after reader difficulty, error concentration and payback. A domain whose signatures fix their predicates has a reader that survives surface change because it never depended on the surface; a domain that needs arrangement breaks whenever arrangement moves.
would_change_my_mind: scheduling or solvency breaking on any transform would mean 0.000 ambiguity mass does not buy maintenance immunity, and the four-way unification would be a three-way one.

verdict: prediction right, but only after catching a measurement that would have said the opposite
measured: testing each domain with the reader that EXISTED FIRST, against four surface events: flood breaks on 2 of 4 (shuffle paragraphs 1.000->0.000, interleave sentences 1.000->0.000) and survives drop-headings and paraphrase; scheduling and solvency break on NONE.
the_mistake_i_nearly_published: a first version tested read_content_roles for flood and reported ZERO breakages everywhere -- maintenance free in all three domains. That reader was BUILT to survive interleaving and paraphrase, so testing it measures the repair and reports the damage as zero. Scheduling and solvency have only ever had one reader each, so their rows were already historical, which is why the flat 1.000 table looked plausible instead of suspicious.
the_unification: flood breaks on the two events that move ARRANGEMENT and neither that moves wording -- it survives paraphrase because its reader is signature-based and dies when rearranged because its signatures do not fix their predicates. The audit measures that offline at 0.161 against 0.000. So one offline number now predicts FOUR things: reader difficulty, where error concentrates, how soon the route pays back, and how often it needs repairing.
why_it_matters_for_amortisation: maintenance is a RECURRING cost, which is what stops it amortising -- the amortisation finding assumed a reader is written once.
limits: four events, all invented in one session, all arrangement-or-wording. A change in the underlying TASK would break every reader here and the audit says nothing about that. And two domains at exactly 0.000 mass is a thin basis for a four-way claim.

hypothesis: The audit predicts robustness to SURFACE change and says nothing about TASK change. Simulating one -- a new claim kind the reader has never seen, a curfew closing a region to all traffic -- should break every reader in the suite. The interesting question is not whether but HOW: silently or loudly.
expected_mechanism: the reader types sentences by signature and simply has no branch for the new kind, so it DROPS the sentence and answers as if the region were open. Silent, and wrong. And no existing check catches it: role_assignment_forced, certifies_role_independent and omits_load_bearing all inspect the READ WORLD, and a claim kind that never entered the world is invisible in it -- the same 'a check that reads part of the world inherits that part's errors' lesson, one level up at the task.
the_signal_nobody_has_used: INPUT COVERAGE. The text still contains the sentence even though the world does not. A reader that accounted for every sentence -- rather than every claim it managed to produce -- would notice a sentence it could not type. That is a cheap detector for task drift and nothing in this repo computes it.
expected: answers wrong on the cases where the curfew binds, all existing checks silent, and an input-coverage check catching it on 100% of affected cases because the sentence is simply never consumed.
would_change_my_mind: an existing check firing would mean the soundness apparatus generalises beyond what it was designed for, which would be a much stronger safety property than advertised and worth knowing.

verdict: prediction right, after FOUR measurement traps in one experiment
measured: a weight restriction the world cannot express: answers wrong 22/22; caught by role_assignment_forced 0/22, the role-independent certificate 0/22, omits_load_bearing 0/22, and UNCONSUMED SENTENCES 22/22. Catches counted only where the check is silent without the drift.
the_four_traps: (1) the first 'task change' was a curfew, which has the same signature as flooding and the same semantics, so elimination landed on the right answer by accident -- 0/16 wrong, no task change at all. (2) firing counted as catching, on cases the system got RIGHT. (3) no baseline arm: omits_load_bearing 'caught' 22/22 while firing on every template paragraph regardless. (4) the detector compared a paragraph-structured read against sentence-joined variants, so nothing ever looked unconsumed and it reported 0/22 while working correctly.
the_mechanism: every world-level check inspects the READ WORLD, and a claim kind with no branch never enters it. Fourth appearance of 'a check that reads part of the world inherits that part's errors', now at the TASK level rather than the roles.
shipped: audit.unconsumed(text, reader) -- sentences whose removal leaves the read world unchanged. NOT entity familiarity (that version caught 0/22, because the restricted region is already known from link claims) and NOT a presence test (clean text has distractors that consume to nothing, so the signal is an INCREASE). Costs len(sentences) reads, cheaper than solving once.
scope_stated_in_the_docstring: it detects that the reader IGNORED something, not that the answer is wrong. A drift alarm, not a correctness oracle -- said explicitly after four checks whose names promised more than they computed.

question: When the declared vocabulary does NOT reach the wording -- the all-adversarial surface where read_content_roles falls 1.000 -> 0.618 -- does EMITTING the candidate role assignments (directive 19) recover the lost accuracy, or only convert it into refusal?
why_now: next_actions names (a2) 'let the reader EMIT CONSEQUENCES and the kernel BIND them' as the live edge, and the 0.382 gap is the measured target. Every earlier enumeration/certificate measurement was taken on the PUBLISHED V=4 surface where the anchors mostly fire, so the machinery has never been tested in the regime the lexical-generalisation argument is actually about.
predict: emitting recovers SOUNDNESS and very little ACCURACY. Candidate agreement on 40-55% of ambiguous cases (flood role-reassignment dependency is 0.467 and 48% of unforced assignments were inert on the published surface), so overall coverage 0.45-0.65 with 1-4 wrong from agreement-on-a-wrong-answer (the seed-83 mechanism); certificate on top -> 0 wrong at coverage 0.30-0.45. Honest statement expected: when the vocabulary fails you can know that you do not know, but you cannot answer.
would_refute: agreement recovering most of the 0.382 -- that would say the words the reader lacked were mostly deciding something INERT, and lexical generalisation is not the front after all.

verdict: prediction RIGHT on the direction and stronger than stated; wrong on two numbers
measured: 400 seeds, 252 non-empty, all-adversarial interleaved: collapse 0.710 accuracy answering everything; role flag coverage 0.000 (refuses EVERY case); emit-on-agreement 0 wrong at 0.361 coverage; emit+certificate 0 wrong at 0.056.
against_the_prediction: predicted 40-55% agreement -> got 36.1%, in range; predicted 1-4 wrong from agreement -> got ZERO, and predicted certificate coverage 0.30-0.45 -> got 0.056, badly over-called.
the_reason_it_is_zero_is_a_theorem: where the read world can differ from the true one ONLY in the role assignment, the true assignment and the collapsed one are BOTH among the candidates, so agreement implies correct and a wrong collapse implies disagreement. Sound AND complete detector, by construction. Empirical content is only the premise (true assignment enumerated), 504/504, bound 0.6%. Corollary: no certificate can improve emission on such a channel, it can only remove coverage -- which is exactly what 0.361 -> 0.056 is.
the_control_is_the_load_bearing_half: turn hard_distractors back on -- invented LINKS, a channel the enumeration does not cover -- and the same agreement arm is 40 wrong of 114, soundness 0.649. Premise fails, theorem goes. Certificate restores 1.000 at 0.127. GENERAL: soundness is a property of the pairing (channel, check), never of the check.
first_thing_the_audit_CANNOT_predict: audit_surface(prose=True) is IDENTICAL on both surfaces -- mass 0.640, same four prose signatures, same 280 flags -- while soundness differs 1.000 vs 0.649. The disused track carries the link signature on both; only the generator's ENDPOINTS decide whether admitting it is harmless. The audit predicts which channels are AMBIGUOUS, not which are ERRONEOUS.
correction: the published all-adversarial floor 0.618 was n=34. At 400 seeds it is 0.710 (grouped stable 0.765 -> 0.758). The measured case for lexical generalisation on the interleaved surface is 0.290, not 0.382 -- overstated by a third.

finding_that_prompted_it: scripts/adversarial_variants.py states two questions and says the SECOND matters more: 'whether a declared vocabulary can be worse than none, by MISFIRING'. Its _verify_adversarial asserts that no adversarial form contains a declared anchor, using t.startswith(w) over re.findall('[a-z]+', s.lower()) -- which is EXACTLY the predicate _anchor_role computes. So misfiring was excluded by construction and the arm reproduces the emptied-anchor arm CASE BY CASE, 252/252 at 400 seeds and 34/34 at 60, not 'to three decimals'. The published 'the anchors never MISFIRE, so its failure mode is silence rather than error' is implied by the verification, not measured.
experiment: phrasings that DO carry an anchor -- for the WRONG role, and exactly one role, so _anchor_role returns a confident wrong answer instead of silence. Verification asserts the misfire EXISTS rather than asserting it away.
predict: accuracy falls well BELOW the no-vocabulary floor (0.710 interleaved / 0.758 grouped at 400 seeds), to roughly 0.15-0.35. Mechanism: elimination only assigns into an OPEN role, so a flooded region misfiring as depot both takes the depot slot and pushes the true depot into flooded -- the code comment already names that as the failure that scored 0.000. A vocabulary is worse than none exactly when it is confident and wrong.
would_refute: landing at or above 0.710 -- which would mean elimination repairs a confident wrong role, and the whole 'silence rather than error' framing survives on merit rather than by construction.

question: A misfired role is invisible to every check measured today -- it reads as `forced`, enumerates to ONE world, and its sentence IS consumed. Is there anything that catches it? Candidate: the reader already has TWO INDEPENDENT signals for `needs` -- the lexical anchor, and POSITIONAL ADJACENCY to the bare demand quantity -- and it throws the second away whenever the first fired (`if not needs and adjacent ...`). Disagreement between them should be a sound misfire alarm.
predict: in the misfire arm the depot phrasings trip `require` -> needs, so the anchor names the DEPOT region while adjacency names the true needs site: contradiction on most cases where adjacency is available. Expect the check to fire on 60-85% of misfire cases (bounded by how often `adjacent` is populated) and on under 5% of clean ones. If so it is the first check that sees a misfire, at the cost of one comparison.
mechanism_if_it_fails: adjacency may be unavailable more often than I think, or `order[-1]` may already be the anchored region so both signals name the same thing and agree vacuously.
would_refute: a high false-alarm rate on the clean surface -- that would make it a redundancy detector rather than a contradiction detector.

verdict: prediction right on the depot direction, and the metric I proposed was the wrong one
measured: 400 seeds, 252 non-empty, interleaved, fire rate by which role misfires: published 0.000 at acc 0.988; evading 0.000 at 0.710; depot->needs 0.774 at 0.865; flooded->depot 0.000 at 0.655; needs->flooded 0.976 at 0.151; all three 1.000 at 0.421.
the_metric_was_wrong: I framed it as recall over WRONG answers and got 0.993 recall with 0.981 false alarm, which reads as useless. It is not a wrongness detector, it is a detector of the CONDITION -- an anchor fired on a sentence it was not written for -- and a misfire changes the answer only 58% of the time. Fire rate against the ARM is the honest column; precision against wrongness (0.582) is barely the base rate.
the_generalisation_that_was_needed: the first version compared only anchored-needs vs adjacent and scored 0.000 on the WORST arm (needs sentences tripping `water` -> flooded, accuracy 0.151, worse than all three misfiring at once) because that misfire does not steal the needs slot. Added the `reassigned` form -- the adjacent region anchored to some OTHER role -- and it goes 0.000 -> 0.976 with published still at 0.000.
the_blind_spot_is_the_finding: flooding misfiring onto depot costs 0.655 and fires NOTHING, because neither depot nor flooding has content-free corroboration. Constructive form of this morning's pairing law: to make a failure detectable, give the thing it corrupts a SECOND INDEPENDENT SIGNAL -- not a better check.
non_monotonicity: all three misfiring (0.421) is BETTER than needs alone (0.151). Misfires interact through elimination: a depot sentence stealing the needs slot stops the destination being marked impassable. Reader errors are not independent and multiplicative.

question: The misfire finding named a blind spot -- flooding sentences misfiring onto depot cost 0.655 accuracy and fire nothing, because depot has no second signal. But depot and needs are SINGLE-VALUED, and the reader silently takes the first claimant (`if role == 'depot' and not depot`). Two sentences claiming one single-valued role is a contradiction the domain's own arity supplies, needing no extra evidence.
predict: arity violation fires on flooded->depot at ~0.9+ (>=2 flooding sentences plus the true depot all claim depot) and on depot->needs at ~1.0, and is SILENT on needs->flooded (0.000) because `flooded` is multi-valued -- an extra flooded region violates no arity. Published surface 0.000. So arity and the adjacency contradiction are COMPLEMENTARY and together cover all three misfire directions.
would_refute: arity firing on the published surface (the generator would then be emitting two depot sentences), or arity subsuming adjacency, which would make the reassigned form dead weight.

verdict: right on the shape, one number badly over-called
measured: fire rate by form, 400 seeds, 252 non-empty: published 0.000/0.000/0.000 (stolen/reassigned/arity) at acc 0.988; flooded->depot 0.000/0.000/0.833 at 0.655 -- BLIND SPOT CLOSED, 0.000 -> 0.833; needs->flooded 0.000/0.976/0.000 at 0.151; depot->needs 0.774/0.000/0.492 at 0.865, ANY 0.988. All three misfire directions covered at zero false alarms, and the forms are COMPLEMENTARY not nested: on depot->needs neither stolen nor arity reaches what they reach together.
over_called: predicted arity ~1.0 on depot->needs, measured 0.492. Reason found by INSPECTION not inferred: arity needs the TRUE needs sentence to claim the role too, and only two of the four original needs phrasings trip an anchor at all ('There is an outstanding call from {w}' and '{w} is asking for resupply' -- `supply` does not reach `resupply`, a documented miss).
general_shape: three signals of three DIFFERENT KINDS -- positional (a quantity sits beside its site), cross-role (that site was given away), structural (the domain says this role holds one region). None is a stronger check; each reads a different fact. 'What else knows this?' is a cheaper question than 'what stronger check exists?', and it was answerable three times here without adding one word of vocabulary.

question: Does today's flood result generalise? Scheduling's distractors are DEFANGED the same way flood's disused track was: the withdrawn machine and cancelled job carry no capability and no quantity, and 'no machine is set up for anodising' names a capability OUTSIDE the vocabulary. Point one at a REAL entity with an IN-vocabulary capability and the reader must admit it.
structural_asymmetry_found_first: each job needs EXACTLY ONE capability (checked, seeds 0-2) while a machine has one to three. So a spurious needs_capability is an ARITY VIOLATION and detectable; a spurious has_capability is not. AND THE UNDETECTABLE ONE IS THE UNSOUND ONE -- an extra machine capability makes an INFEASIBLE instance read as feasible, where an extra job requirement makes a feasible one read as infeasible.
predict: machine-side distractor costs 0.10-0.30 accuracy, all in the false-FEASIBLE direction, with an arity check firing 0.000. Job-side costs more, 0.25-0.50, all false-INFEASIBLE, with arity firing ~1.000. Baseline 1.000 and arity 0.000.
why_it_matters: scheduling is the domain the audit scores at 0.000 ambiguity mass -- 'easiest to read'. If a misfiring/admitted distractor still costs this much, that is a SECOND thing the audit cannot predict: it measures ambiguity of the SIGNATURE, not fragility of the VOCABULARY.
would_refute: a small drop on both arms -- scheduling's redundancy (durations and capacities pinning the same entities) would then be doing work I have not credited.

verdict: direction right on both arms, magnitude wrong by 6x on one, and the headline is the inversion
measured: 200 cases, default regime (6x3, slack 0.15): default distractors acc 1.000, 0 errors, arity 0.000; MACHINE-side spurious has_capability acc 0.790 with ALL 42 errors FALSE-FEASIBLE and arity 0.000; JOB-side spurious needs_capability acc 0.965 (2 false-feasible, 5 false-infeasible) with arity 1.000; both 0.780.
against_the_prediction: predicted machine 0.10-0.30 -> measured 0.210, in range. Predicted job 0.25-0.50 -> measured 0.035, over-called 6x. My reasoning (an extra requirement makes a job harder to place) was wrong because machines hold several capabilities, so some machine usually has both.
headline: THE DAMAGING ERROR IS INVISIBLE AND THE VISIBLE ERROR IS HARMLESS. One admitted sentence costs 0.210, every failure UNSOUND, arity fires on NONE. The catchable side costs 0.035 and fires on EVERY case.
second_thing_the_audit_cannot_predict: scheduling is the 0.000-ambiguity-mass domain, credited with predicting reader difficulty, error concentration, payback and maintenance. One sentence takes it 1.000 -> 0.790 and the audit says the surface is clean. It measures ambiguity of the SIGNATURE, not fragility of the VOCABULARY: 'machine_0 was set up to paint' has the (machine, capability) signature unambiguously and is FALSE. Same shape as this morning's blind spot -- two in one day.
general: DETECTABILITY COMES FROM REDUNDANCY, REDUNDANCY IS A PROPERTY OF THE ROLE'S ARITY, AND ARITY HAS NOTHING TO DO WITH HOW MUCH DAMAGE AN ERROR THERE DOES. Lands the wrong way round in both domains: flood's undetectable direction costs 0.655, its most detectable one 0.865. A system built to catch its own reading errors catches the ones it could most afford to make.

question: Today's open unknown is a SECOND READING OF A MULTI-VALUED FACT -- flood's `flooded` and scheduling's `has_capability` are where the damage is and neither has arity to check. No other SOURCE knows those facts, so the only second reading available is of the SAME sentence: does it QUALIFY the claim it makes? Every real phrasing in both domains is present tense; every distractor is past tense with a cancelling clause ('A disused track ONCE ran', 'was set up to paint last shift, BEFORE the head came off', 'USED TO cut as well, UNTIL the drawing was revised', 'job_90 WAS CANCELLED').
the_discriminating_version: tense and cancellation are different signals and the generator has confounded them. Two gates, declared from linguistics and not tuned: TENSE (was/were/had/used to) and CANCELLATION (disused, former, no longer, used to, once, previously, struck, cancelled, withdrawn, before/until clause). Third arm: REAL claims rephrased in the PAST but still true ('machine_0 was fitted for paint work', 'region_0 was joined to region_3 by a surfaced road').
predict: both gates catch the hard distractors at ~1.000 with 0 false positives on the CURRENT phrasings. On past-tense-but-true real claims the TENSE gate rejects nearly all of them (accuracy collapses toward the no-claim floor) and the CANCELLATION gate rejects ~none. So the signal is CANCELLATION, not tense, and the coincidence that every distractor here is also past tense is a generator artefact.
would_refute: the cancellation gate also firing on past-tense-but-true claims -- meaning my cue list is really a tense detector wearing a different name; or the tense gate surviving, meaning tense IS the signal and the distinction I am drawing does not exist.

verdict: prediction right, and the failure mode found was better than the prediction
measured: scheduling (200 cases) no-gate/tense/cancellation -- clean 1.000/1.000/1.000; HARD 0.790/1.000/1.000; clean with real claims in the PAST 1.000/0.645/1.000. flood (400 seeds, 252 non-empty, interleaved) -- clean 0.988/0.881/0.933; HARD 0.679/0.659/0.933; clean PAST 0.988/0.317/0.933.
1_cancellation_not_tense: both gates repair the scheduling distractor so the catch decides nothing; the PAST arm decides it -- tense takes scheduling to 0.645 and flood to 0.317 on claims that are TRUE, cancellation does not move. And the flood distractor 'A disused track ONCE RAN' has no past auxiliary, so the tense gate misses it outright.
2_first_component_that_transfers_unchang: one closed-class domain-independent gate repairs the hardest channel in BOTH domains -- scheduling 0.790 -> 1.000, flood 0.679 -> 0.933 -- on the channel arity, adjacency and enumeration all miss. No per-domain word list.
3_the_failure_mode: it is NOT free: flood clean 0.988 -> 0.933 because it deletes a TRUE claim, 'Water rose through X and it is NO LONGER passable'. The gate cannot distinguish a sentence that WITHDRAWS its own claim from one ASSERTING SOMETHING WAS WITHDRAWN -- and flood's `flooded` predicate IS a cancellation. Property of the predicate, not of the cue list; no words fix it. Mild here (deleting a flooded claim merely fails to help, where a phantom link destroys the answer), so net on the honest surface is +0.254.
test_i_had_to_fix: I first wrote a test asserting NO real phrasing trips either gate, which I already knew was false. Rewrote it to ENUMERATE the exception and assert it is exactly ['flooded'] -- the blind spot documented rather than asserted away, which is this morning's lesson applied to my own test.

question: Third domain, same defect? Solvency's single distractor is 'A former subsidiary, sub_99, was divested before the period and does not consolidate' -- and sub_99 appears NOWHERE ELSE, exactly like flood's disused track drawing endpoints from outside the network and scheduling's withdrawn machine carrying no capability. It is inert TWICE over: one entity so it matches no branch, and no filings so it would sum to nothing anyway.
design: a divested subsidiary that DOES have filings (owns side, multi-valued -> no arity) and a withdrawn later figure (revenue side). Each written in a CUED form carrying a declared cancellation word and an UNCUED form carrying none -- 'sub_98 left the group in April', 'An unaudited memorandum from sub_0 on {d} shows {n} USD'. The uncued arm is the gate's honest floor and is the cell I cannot predict; writing only cued distractors would be this morning's constructed-to-pass trap.
predict: clean 1.000 unchanged. Cued hard distractors cost 0.15-0.40 and are REPAIRED to ~1.000 by the shared cancellation gate, making it 3-for-3 across domains with no per-domain words. Uncued hard distractors cost about the same and are NOT repaired -- gate fires 0.000 -- which is the honest ceiling. Arity and adjacency see nothing either way, because `owns` is multi-valued and revenue is keyed by date.
would_refute: the cued arm not being repaired (the cue list does not transfer), or the uncued arm being harmless (solvency's bitemporal rule already discards stale figures by date, which would make this domain structurally immune and the pattern two-for-three).

verdict: pattern confirmed for the third domain, magnitude badly under-called, and the mechanism was not what I predicted
measured: 200 cases, majority floor 0.550. clean 1.000 all four cells. HARD CUED: published 0.450, published+gate 0.485, consolidated 0.450, CONSOLIDATED+GATE 1.000. HARD UNCUED: 0.450 in all four. Predicted 0.15-0.40 damage repaired to ~1.000 by the gate ALONE; measured 0.550 damage and a STRICT CONJUNCTION.
the_bigger_find: read_signature enrols a member the moment it FILES (r.members.add(ents[0]) on the filing branch), so the entire ownership paragraph -- one of the domain's two claim kinds -- is DECORATIVE: deleting it changes 0 of 200 answers. Reported at 1.000 accuracy and 1.000 filing recall in all six cells of V x arrangement and none could see it, because the generator never files for a non-member. Third instance of inert-by-construction, now in the READER'S LOGIC rather than in a distractor.
conjunction: the divested filer is enrolled by EITHER its filing (only the reader fix removes that) OR its ownership sentence (only the gate removes that), so each fix alone leaves the other route open. Gate alone +0.035, reader alone +0.000, together +0.550.
honest_floor: the UNCUED arm is unrepairable at 0.450 -- 'sub_98 left the group in April' is semantically stale with no declared cue. Asserted by a test so the 1.000 cannot be read as a solution.
dose_response_is_U_SHAPED: 0.05 -> 0.630 (4 false-TRUE, 70 false-FALSE); 0.10 -> 0.665 (33/34); 0.25 -> 0.515 (97/0); 0.50 -> 0.450 (110/0). The withdrawn figure is dated the determination date so it REPLACES the real filing under latest-by-date: a small spurious figure LOWERS the sum, a large one raises it. Third instance of opposite-signed evidence in this repo. QUOTE THE INJECTION WITH THE NUMBER -- at 0.50 the reader answers True on all 200, which is why accuracy lands exactly on the 0.450 true share, and that is BELOW the 0.550 majority floor.

verdict: the direction was predictable; the gate's cost share was not, and one row changed KIND
measured: honest surface, every stage charged. flood 0.669 -> 0.915, gate 0.5% of time, $/above-floor 1.124e-07 -> 8.688e-08 (1.29x). scheduling 0.790 -> 1.000, gate 4.9%, 7.527e-08 -> 3.249e-08 (2.32x). solvency 0.450 -> 1.000, gate 44.0%, INF -> 1.306e-09.
one_row_changes_kind: solvency's honest reader is BELOW its own floor (0.450 vs 0.550), so its cost per unit of capability is infinite -- it bought nothing and the ledger says so. The checks take it to finite. Only qualitative move in the table and exactly what the above-floor denominator exists to produce.
the_floor_amplifies: scheduling's accuracy rises 1.27x and its $/above-floor improves 2.32x, because (1.000-0.645)/(0.790-0.645) = 2.45. Quoting $/correct would have shown 1.20x and understated the gain by half.
under_called: predicted the gate at ~29% of solvency's pipeline; measured 44.0%. Structural reason: filter_stale RE-SPLITS AND RE-SCANS the same sentences the reader is about to split and scan, paying tokenisation twice. Folding it into each reader's loop would bound it by cue matching alone -- NOT done, because the component's whole claim is that it transfers across domains UNCHANGED, and folding it in gives that up. Trade named rather than taken.

decision: NOT RUNNING IT, recorded instead. An insensitivity certificate for solvency's revenue channel would have near-zero coverage because the decision is a SUM and every term moves it -- and that number is already on disk as the decidedness law's extreme case (revenue decides 0.000, owns decides 1.000, computed on true worlds with no reader). Running it re-derives a number the law already gives.
the_synthesis_it_comes_from: there are exactly TWO responses to a corrupt channel and they are gated by different properties. (a) DETECTION -- read the fact twice; sound and complete; gated by EVIDENCE STRUCTURE (arity, companion sentences); measured 0.774/0.976/0.833/1.000 for single-valued roles and 0.000 for every multi-valued one across three domains. (b) ANSWER-INSENSITIVITY -- prove the answer does not depend on the claim; sound but LOSSY; gated by the shape of the DECISION. Available in inverse proportion to aggregation: reachability-with-redundancy free (0 wrong at 48.8%), NP-hard feasibility half (monotone yes, structural unsound on 8 of 9), a SUM not at all.
claim_recorded: solvency admits NEITHER response on its revenue channel -- no second reading and no insensitivity -- which is why the honest move there was to fix the READER (consolidated membership + staleness gate).
what_IS_worth_running_and_is_different: solvency's `owns` channel is multi-valued but membership is not a sum: dropping one member changes the total by that member's filing, which may or may not cross the threshold. Insensitivity THERE has an unknown answer.

question: The decision note named this as the one genuinely open version: solvency's `owns` channel is multi-valued (so DETECTION is impossible, measured 0.000) but membership is NOT a sum in the way revenue is -- dropping one member changes the total by that member's filing, which may or may not cross the threshold. So ANSWER-INSENSITIVITY is a real question there. Certificate: the verdict is unchanged under EVERY single-member deletion => insensitive to one spurious `owns`.
why_it_matters: the target is the UNCUED owns arm, which I declared unrepairable at 0.485 today. A certificate that fires soundly there would raise the floor everything else stopped at.
predict: coverage 20-40% with soundness ~1.000 on the one-spurious-member hypothesis. Driven entirely by the MARGIN: it fires exactly when no single member's filing straddles the threshold, so coverage is roughly P(|sum - threshold| > max member filing).
would_refute: near-zero coverage, which would mean the threshold sits close to the sum by construction and solvency admits neither response on EITHER channel -- the stronger version of the prediction I declined to run.

verdict: right, coverage slightly better than predicted, and the mechanism I proposed for it was WRONG
measured: clean 1.000 acc / 0.550 coverage / 1.000 acc|cert; hard owns UNCUED 0.485 acc / 0.485 coverage / 1.000 acc|cert / 0 WRONG; hard owns+filing UNCUED 0.450 acc / 0.935 coverage / 0.481 acc|cert / 97 wrong. Predicted 20-40% coverage; measured 48.5%.
it_rescues_the_declared_floor: on the arm nothing else could touch -- multi-valued role, no cue -- CERTIFIED <=> CORRECT exactly. 0.485 accuracy with 103 silent errors becomes 0.485 coverage with ZERO.
my_mechanism_was_wrong: I predicted coverage would be driven by the MARGIN, P(|sum-threshold| > max member filing). That statistic is 0.080 against a measured 0.550. The real driver is ONE-SIDEDNESS: removing a member can only LOWER the sum, so a False verdict survives every deletion for free. Fires on 1.000 of false verdicts and 0.000 of true ones, and clean coverage 0.550 IS the false-verdict share. FOURTH appearance of 'what is cheap to prove is the negative'.
the_warning_and_it_is_the_second_instanc: add a spurious FILING and coverage RISES 0.485 -> 0.935 while accuracy among certified falls to 0.481. Coverage rises BECAUSE the corruption is larger -- the spurious figure pushes the sum clear of the threshold so no member deletion flips it. Flood's certificate did the same this morning (0.056 clean -> 0.127 hard, phantom links adding 2-edge-connectivity). GENERAL: a certificate that asks 'would a small perturbation change the answer' READS A LARGE ERROR AS STABILITY; its coverage is not a measure of its reliability and comparing coverage across surfaces is a trap.

question: symbolic_ai_generators/staleness.py is the one component claimed to be DOMAIN-INDEPENDENT and closed-class, and every number for it comes from surfaces this repo generated with distractors I wrote. Does it behave on English nobody here wrote? data/sources/openalex-prose has 5,000 real scientific abstracts on disk.
predict: the cancellation gate fires on 5-15% of real sentences and MOST OF THOSE ARE FALSE POSITIVES, dominated by two cues used temporally rather than cancellingly: `once` ('once the sample was heated') and `before the` ('before the reaction'). `until the` is the same shape. The tense gate fires on 40-60%, because scientific abstracts narrate method in the past.
the_consequence_if_right: the declared cue list is bigger than the honest one, and the fix is REMOVAL on linguistic grounds rather than tuning: every synthetic distractor carries a second, genuinely cancelling cue (disused, came off, used to, former, withdrawn, struck), so dropping the temporal three should cost the domains NOTHING while cutting real-text firing. Verifying that afterwards is a check, not a fit -- removing cues can only reduce firing, so the synthetic numbers can only stay or fall.
would_refute: a firing rate near zero on real prose, which would mean the cue list is already precise and my worry about closed-class-does-not-mean-safe was unfounded; or the temporal cues NOT dominating, which would mean the false positives are somewhere I have not looked.

verdict: the worry was right and BOTH specific predictions were wrong; the real error was better than the one I guessed
measured: 36,223 sentences of real scientific abstracts (data/sources/openalex-prose). Cancellation gate fires on 2.29% (predicted 5-15%), tense gate on 13.5% (predicted 40-60%). Roughly 85% of the cancellation fires are FALSE.
what_I_got_wrong: I predicted the dominant false positives would be `once` and `before the` used temporally. They are 10.6% and 2.5%. The dominant one is `used to` at 53.5% -- 439 of 443 as the ONLY cue -- and it is the PASSIVE OF USE ('is used to obtain', 'have been widely used to examine'), not a temporal confusion at all but an ambiguity between two grammars. `previously` is second at 24.9%.
two_corrections_both_on_meaning: (1) habitual `used to` vs the passive separates on ONE OBSERVABLE -- the passive is preceded by a form of BE, usually with an adverb between; three tokens of lookback is what is available without a parser. (2) `once`, `previously`, `before the`, `until the` mark TEMPORAL ORDERING not withdrawal; dropped, kept as CANCELLING_V1 so earlier numbers reproduce.
result: real-prose firing 2.29% -> 0.34%, 6.8x. And EVERY generated-surface number is byte-identical (scheduling 1.000/1.000/1.000, flood 0.933 in all four cells). Removals can only reduce firing, so the domains could only have stayed or fallen -- they stayed, which is the evidence that what was removed was noise.
residual_needs_word_senses_not_words: 122 fires left. `no longer` 19% (sampled, genuine); `former` 18% of which 77% are 'the former' -- the CORRELATIVE PRONOUN paired with 'the latter', a different sense. Telling a pronoun from an attributive adjective is a part-of-speech question no cue list answers, and the available patch (suppress 'the former') would kill 'the former subsidiary', exactly the phrase the solvency domain uses. Recorded, not patched.

question: One corpus is not a measurement. Scientific abstracts over-represent the passive of `use` and contain almost no narrative past, which is exactly where the two corrections I made are least tested. Project Gutenberg narrative is the opposite draw: habitual `used to` GENUINELY occurs, `once` is everywhere, and the past tense is the default.
blocked_first: SEC EDGAR was the genre I wanted -- solvency imitates financial filings -- and it 403s without a contact EMAIL in the User-Agent. I will not send the user's personal address to an unrelated service without being asked, and I will not invent one. Blocker recorded; the user can unblock it in one line.
predict: tense gate 45-65% (narrative past is the default). Corrected cancellation gate 1-3% -- HIGHER than the 0.34% on abstracts, and mostly CORRECT fires, because habitual `used to` is genuinely frequent here. The V1 list would be far worse in this genre than in abstracts, since `once` and `previously` are narrative staples.
the_measurement_that_matters: the three-token lookback's FALSE NEGATIVE rate. In narrative, most `used to` are habitual; how many sit within three tokens of a be-form ('she was young and used to walk')? That is the cost of the approximation and it is unmeasured, because the abstract corpus has no narrative. Predict under 10% of habitual uses are lost.

verdict: the genre point is confirmed and STRONGER than stated; my false-negative prediction was wrong in an instructive way
measured: 75,555 sentences, 12 public-domain novels. Tense gate 0.451 (predicted 45-65%, right). Cancellation after the abstracts fix 0.0191 vs 0.0033 on abstracts. V1 list 0.0449.
the_finding: EACH GENRE SURFACED A DIFFERENT DOMINANT FALSE POSITIVE AND NEITHER WAS PREDICTABLE FROM THE OTHER. Abstracts: `used to` passive, 53.5%. Narrative: `struck` -- the verb STRIKE -- 29.9%, against TWO fires in 36,223 scientific sentences. Correction on meaning again: the cancelling sense carries a particle, `struck from` / `struck off`. Narrative firing 1.91% -> 1.35%, abstracts 0.34% -> 0.33%, generated surfaces byte-identical for the THIRD time.
my_false_negative_prediction_was_wrong: predicted the lookback would lose under 10% of habitual `used to`; measured 21%. But reading the sample, it is mostly NOT AN ERROR -- it is `be used to` meaning ACCUSTOMED ('had been used to look', 'has been used to her complaints'), a state that may still hold and correctly does not cancel. `used to` is THREE constructions, not two. The one genuine loss was the window crossing a comma into another clause; bounding it at a clause boundary fixed that and left the 21% where it is, because the 21% is the accustomed sense.
blocker_recorded: SEC EDGAR -- the genre solvency actually imitates -- 403s without a contact EMAIL in the User-Agent. I will not send the user's personal address to an unrelated service unasked and will not invent one. One line from the user unblocks it.
method_note: both corrections after the first were found by ADDING A GENRE, not by thinking harder about the list. No reason to believe a third genre finds nothing.

correcting_my_own_framing: today I wrote that a multi-valued channel is UNDETECTABLE and the only response left is fixing the reader. That over-stated it. Insensitivity needs no second source and no arity -- it is exactly what flood's link certificate and solvency's membership certificate do -- and I tested it for solvency's `owns` but never for scheduling's `has_capability`, which is the WORST channel measured all day: 0.210 accuracy lost, ALL 42 failures false-FEASIBLE, arity firing 0.000.
experiment: at most one has_capability is spurious.
